quiz.q: What is the format of the ISC2 AI Security pilot exam?
o: 125 multiple-choice items in three hours
160 multiple-choice items in three hours
150 multiple-choice items in four hours
100 scenario items in two and a half hours
quiz.why: The pilot exam outline specifies 160 multiple-choice items with a three-hour time limit.

quiz.q: Which domains carry the largest weight on the pilot exam?
o: Domain 1 and Domain 2
Domain 3 and Domain 5
Domain 4 and Domain 6
Domain 2 and Domain 6
quiz.why: Domain 3 (data management, privacy and model security) and Domain 5 (secure operations and incident response) are each weighted at 19%.

quiz.q: Roughly how much time does the exam allow per question?
o: About 45 seconds
About 67 seconds
About 90 seconds
About two minutes
quiz.why: Three hours is 10,800 seconds; divided by 160 items that is 67.5 seconds per item.

quiz.q: Which credential substitutes for the entire experience requirement?
o: An active CISSP certification
CompTIA Security+
A cloud provider’s associate certification
Any bachelor’s degree in computing
quiz.why: The outline lists CISSP, ISSAP, ISSEP, ISSMP, CCSP and CSSLP as substitutes for the whole requirement. A degree can waive only one year.

quiz.q: A candidate holds a master’s degree in computer science. How much of the experience requirement can it waive?
o: None
Up to one year
Up to two years
All four years
quiz.why: A relevant post-secondary degree may satisfy up to one year; only one year can be waived this way.

quiz.q: A question asks what a security manager should do FIRST after learning that a new AI tool has been adopted by a department. Which answer pattern is MOST likely correct?
o: Deploy a monitoring agent on the tool immediately to see how it is used
Understand the use case, data and ownership before choosing controls
Ban the tool across the organisation until it can be fully assessed
Ask the vendor for its latest penetration test report and certifications
quiz.why: FIRST questions usually reward understanding and assessment before action. Monitoring, bans and vendor reports may follow, but only once the situation is understood.

quiz.q: Two answer options are both technically accurate. How should you choose between them?
o: Pick the longer, more detailed option, since it covers more ground
Pick the option that addresses the stated qualifier and constraint
Pick the more technical option, since this is a security exam
Pick the option that mentions a recognised framework by name
quiz.why: When more than one statement is true, the qualifier (BEST, FIRST, MOST) and the scenario’s constraints decide which one actually answers the question.

quiz.q: Which study technique strengthens long-term recall MOST effectively?
o: Rereading your notes several times in one sitting
Highlighting key passages and reviewing them later
Testing yourself on it before reviewing the material
Watching every video twice in a row, at normal speed
quiz.why: Retrieval practice, recalling information from memory, produces stronger long-term retention than rereading or highlighting.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning?
o: Machine learning is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of AI
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
AI, machine learning and deep learning are three names for the same thing
Deep learning is a subset of AI that is unrelated to machine learning
quiz.why: AI is the broad field; machine learning is the part that learns from data; deep learning is machine learning using many-layered neural networks.

quiz.q: By capability, how are the AI systems in production today classified?
o: Artificial general intelligence
Artificial superintelligence
Narrow AI (weak AI)
Self-aware AI
quiz.why: Every deployed system, including large language models, is narrow AI. General AI and superintelligence remain hypothetical.

quiz.q: A model learns the distribution of its training data well enough to create new, realistic samples. What kind of model is it?
o: Discriminative
Generative
Symbolic
Reactive
quiz.why: Generative models learn what the data looks like and can produce new examples. Discriminative models learn the boundary between classes.

quiz.q: A team trains a model on 50,000 emails, each marked as spam or legitimate by analysts. Which learning paradigm is this?
o: Unsupervised learning
Federated learning
Supervised learning
Self-supervised learning
quiz.why: Training on inputs paired with correct labels is supervised learning, here a classification task.

quiz.q: Large language models are pretrained by predicting the next token across vast amounts of text. What kind of learning is this?
o: Self-supervised learning
Reinforcement learning from human feedback
Unsupervised clustering
Federated learning
quiz.why: The labels, the next tokens, come from the data itself, which makes pretraining self-supervised. RLHF is a later tuning stage.

quiz.q: An agent improves its strategy by taking actions in an environment and receiving scores for the outcomes. Which paradigm is this?
o: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Transfer learning
Semi-supervised learning
quiz.why: Learning a policy from rewards earned by acting in an environment is reinforcement learning.

quiz.q: During training, error on the training data keeps falling while error on the validation data starts to rise. What does this indicate?
o: Underfitting
Overfitting
A learning rate that is too low
Data drift
quiz.why: The model is memorising the training set and generalising worse to unseen data, the signature of overfitting.

quiz.q: Which step of training calculates how much each weight contributed to the error?
o: The forward pass
Backpropagation
Pooling
Tokenisation
quiz.why: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards through the network to compute each parameter’s gradient. Gradient descent then uses those gradients to update the weights.

quiz.q: In a genetic algorithm, what decides which candidate solutions survive into the next generation?
o: The learning rate
The fitness function
The activation function
The loss gradient
quiz.why: Each candidate is scored by a fitness function, and the fittest are selected as parents. No gradients are involved.

quiz.q: Which architecture uses learned filters that slide across an image to detect local patterns?
o: Recurrent neural network
Convolutional neural network
Transformer decoder
Graph attention network
quiz.why: Convolutional neural networks apply sliding filters to grid-like data, building from edges to whole objects.

quiz.q: What allows a transformer to weigh the relevance of every token to every other token in a sequence?
o: A hidden state passed between steps
Self-attention
Max pooling
A fitness function
quiz.why: Self-attention scores every pair of tokens and blends their information, processing the whole sequence in parallel.

quiz.q: Roughly how much memory is needed just to hold the weights of a 7-billion-parameter model at 16-bit precision?
o: About 3.5 GB
About 7 GB
About 14 GB
About 28 GB
quiz.why: Sixteen-bit precision uses 2 bytes per parameter: 7 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 14 GB. 28 GB would be 32-bit; 3.5 GB would be 4-bit.

quiz.q: During training, a model’s loss falls for a few steps, then swings up and down from step to step and never settles. Which change is MOST likely to help?
o: Adding more layers, so the model has greater capacity to learn
Lowering the learning rate, or using a schedule that reduces it
Raising the softmax temperature used when generating outputs
Removing the validation set, so more data is available for training
quiz.why: A loss that oscillates instead of settling is the classic sign of a learning rate that is too large: each step overshoots. More layers, sampling temperature and the validation set don’t address the step size.

quiz.q: A model’s final layer produces scores of 4, 2 and 1 for three possible outputs. What does applying softmax with a temperature below 1 do?
o: Spreads probability more evenly, so less likely outputs are chosen more often
Concentrates probability on the top output, making choices more predictable
Removes the lowest-scoring output from consideration before any sampling
Leaves the probabilities unchanged, as temperature only affects training
quiz.why: Dividing logits by a temperature below 1 widens the gaps between them, so softmax gives the top output a larger share. Temperatures above 1 flatten the distribution instead.

quiz.q: A provider is deciding whether its public API should return log-probabilities for many candidate tokens alongside each generated token. Which risk does this MOST increase?
o: Prompt injection, because attackers can read the system prompt from the values
Model extraction and membership inference, which exploit fine-grained scores
Denial of service, because log-probabilities double the cost of each request
Data poisoning, because users can submit their own scores back into training
quiz.why: Detailed scores reveal how confident the model is and where its decision boundaries lie, which helps attackers copy the model or test whether records were in its training data. Researchers used such API features to recover part of production models in 2024.

quiz.q: A language model’s average cross-entropy per token on a test set falls after further training. What happens to its perplexity on that set?
o: It rises, since perplexity grows as a model becomes more accurate
It decreases too, since perplexity is the exponential of that loss
It stays the same, since perplexity depends only on vocabulary size
It doubles, since perplexity is twice the average loss per token
quiz.why: Perplexity is the exponential of the average cross-entropy per token, so the two move together: lower loss means lower perplexity and better prediction.

exam.q: A bank trains a fraud model with federated learning across its branches, so customer data never leaves each branch. Which risk does this design introduce that centralised training does not?
o: Raw customer data must be copied to a central server
A compromised participant can submit harmful model updates
The model cannot be retrained once deployed
Labels are no longer required for training
exam.why: Federated learning combines updates from many participants. A malicious or compromised participant can send updates that degrade or manipulate the shared model, so the aggregation step needs safeguards.

exam.q: A vendor’s fraud engine combines a learned risk score with hard-coded rules that block transactions above regulatory limits. How is this design BEST described?
o: Purely symbolic, rule-based AI
Purely statistical machine learning
A hybrid of learned and symbolic approaches
An early form of general intelligence
exam.why: A learned model working alongside explicit, human-written rules is a hybrid design, common in regulated settings where some limits must be guaranteed.

exam.q: Why can gradient-free search methods, such as evolutionary algorithms, be used to probe a model deployed behind an API?
o: They need the model’s training data
They only need the model’s outputs to score candidate inputs
They require administrator access to the model’s weights
They work only on models trained with reinforcement learning
exam.why: Evolutionary search optimises against any score, and a model’s responses can serve as that score. That is why query limits, output minimisation and monitoring matter for exposed models.

exam.q: A log-analysis product uses a plain recurrent neural network on very long event sequences. Which limitation should you expect?
o: It can’t process text, only numerical event codes
Information from early in a long sequence tends to fade
It processes every event in parallel, losing their order
It requires labelled images rather than event sequences
exam.why: Plain RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients, so early information is lost over long sequences. LSTMs, GRUs and transformers were developed partly to address this.

exam.q: Several business units run AI workloads on the same pool of cloud GPUs. Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of one workload reading another’s data from accelerator memory?
o: Quantising every model to 4-bit precision, so less data sits in accelerator memory at once
Isolating workloads with dedicated or partitioned GPUs, and clearing memory between jobs
Moving all training jobs to CPUs, which keep each process’s memory strictly separate
Increasing GPU memory capacity so that workloads never have to share the same memory
exam.why: The risk is residual or shared memory between tenants. Isolation and memory clearing address it directly; quantisation and capacity are unrelated to confidentiality.

exam.q: An organisation must serve a large model on hardware with limited memory and can accept a small loss in accuracy. Which technique BEST fits?
o: Quantisation
Dropout
Backpropagation
Data augmentation
exam.why: Quantisation stores weights at lower precision, reducing memory needs at some cost in accuracy. Dropout and augmentation are training techniques; backpropagation computes gradients.

exam.q: Why does a transformer’s design make untrusted text anywhere in its context a security concern?
o: Transformers ignore text beyond the first sentence, so injected text replaces the real instructions
Self-attention lets every token influence every other, with no built-in trusted/untrusted distinction
Transformers execute any code they read in their context, as long as it is written in Python
Untrusted text in the context automatically retrains the model’s weights during inference
exam.why: All tokens in context can shape the output through self-attention. Separating trusted instructions from untrusted data has to be done by controls around the model.

exam.q: An organisation plans to publish the weights of its image-screening model so that partners can run it locally. Which consequence should the risk assessment highlight MOST?
o: The model will stop working if partners use different graphics processors
Anyone can compute input gradients, making strong evasion attacks far easier
Partners will gain the right to reuse the training data for other purposes
The model’s accuracy will fall, because weights degrade when they are copied
exam.why: Open weights give anyone white-box access, so gradient-based attacks such as PGD can craft evasions directly, and the model also becomes a substitute for transfer attacks. Hardware differences, data rights and copying don’t change the model in these ways.

exam.q: A red team reports that one prompt produced a policy violation in 3 of 50 attempts at a temperature of 0.8. The product owner argues that production uses a temperature of 0, so the finding can be closed. What is the BEST response?
o: Close the finding, as a temperature of 0 makes every output safe and fixed
Retest at production settings, with varied prompts, before deciding anything
Close the finding, since 3 failures in 50 is under a typical 10% tolerance
Keep it open only until the provider confirms the result was a glitch
exam.why: A low temperature makes output for one exact prompt more repeatable, not safe: real users vary their prompts, and settings and models change. Retesting under production settings with variations shows whether the risk is real.

exam.q: A SaaS provider batches requests from different customers through a shared mixture-of-experts model with fixed expert capacity. A customer asks whether another tenant could influence its results. What is the BEST response?
o: Reassure the customer, as one request’s output never depends on another’s
Assess the risk, and consider tenant isolation or a different routing design
Confirm there is no risk, since TLS encryption in transit prevents it
Advise the customer to send shorter prompts, so its tokens are routed first
exam.why: Research in 2024 showed that when routing depends on other requests in a batch, for example through fixed expert capacity, one user’s inputs can change another’s outputs. Encryption in transit and prompt length don’t remove that dependency.

quiz.q: What does a large language model fundamentally do at each step of generating a response?
o: Looks up the most relevant answer in an internal database of verified facts
Estimates the probability of every possible next token, then selects one
Retrieves the closest matching sentence from its stored training data
Executes a hand-written rule chosen for the topic it has detected
quiz.why: LLMs generate output one token at a time from a probability distribution over their vocabulary. They do not look facts up, which is why plausible errors occur.

quiz.q: An extraction task needs consistent, repeatable output. Which generation setting is MOST appropriate?
o: A high temperature
A low temperature
The largest possible maximum-token limit
No stop sequences
quiz.why: Low temperature concentrates sampling on the most likely tokens, giving more focused and repeatable output. High temperature increases variety.

quiz.q: A prompt includes three worked examples of input and the expected output before the real request. What is this technique called?
o: Zero-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
Fine-tuning
Prompt chaining
quiz.why: Including demonstrations in the prompt is few-shot prompting, also called in-context learning. No weights change.

quiz.q: Which statement about system prompts is MOST accurate from a security standpoint?
o: They are enforced by the model in the same way as access control rules
They guide the model’s behaviour but can’t guarantee compliance or keep secrets
They are encrypted, so users can never discover or extract their contents
They block prompt injection, provided they are written clearly and firmly
quiz.why: System prompts shape behaviour probabilistically. Anything that must hold, such as data access, needs enforcement outside the model, and secrets shouldn’t be placed in prompts.

quiz.q: Why is retrieval-augmented generation usually preferred over fine-tuning for knowledge that changes frequently?
o: It stores new knowledge permanently in the model’s weights, so it is never forgotten
Updating the index changes answers immediately, with citations, and content can be removed
It needs no data pipeline, because the model reads source systems directly at runtime
It enlarges the model’s context window, so more knowledge fits into every response
quiz.why: RAG supplies current knowledge at request time. Index updates take effect immediately, answers can cite sources, and removing a document stops it influencing answers.

quiz.q: In a RAG system, an attacker hides instructions in a document that the assistant later retrieves and follows. What is this attack?
o: Direct prompt injection
Indirect prompt injection
Model extraction
Membership inference
quiz.why: When the malicious instructions arrive through content the system processes, rather than from the user’s own input, it is indirect prompt injection.

quiz.q: How does LoRA reduce the cost of fine-tuning?
o: It trains a smaller replacement model from scratch with fewer layers and parameters
It freezes the original weights and trains small low-rank matrices that are added to them
It prunes rarely used weights from the base model so fewer parameters need updating
It replaces costly real training data with cheaper synthetic data generated by the model
quiz.why: LoRA keeps the base weights frozen and learns the change as the product of two small matrices, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of QLoRA?
o: To quantise a model’s outputs so its answers become shorter and cheaper to generate
To fine-tune large models on limited GPU memory by training LoRA adapters on a 4-bit base
To encrypt LoRA adapters at rest so they can be shared safely between teams
To compress a fine-tuned model to 4-bit precision after training is finished, so it serves faster
quiz.why: QLoRA quantises the frozen base model to 4 bits and trains LoRA adapters on top, so large models can be fine-tuned on modest hardware.

quiz.q: In an agent that uses tool calling, which component actually executes a tool?
o: The language model itself, which runs the function inside its own weights
The application or orchestration layer, after deciding whether to run the call
The end user’s browser, which receives the call and runs it locally in every case
The vector database, which stores the tool definitions and triggers them on retrieval
quiz.why: The model only outputs a structured request. The surrounding application decides whether to execute it, which is where authorisation and approval checks belong.

quiz.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
o: A tokenisation scheme that lets one model process text, images and audio together
An open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources
A method for compressing long context windows so that more history fits in each request
An EU regulation that sets privacy rules for AI agents that connect to external systems
quiz.why: MCP standardises how AI applications connect to tools, resources and prompts exposed by MCP servers.

quiz.q: Which NLP technique is MOST commonly used to find personal data such as names and account numbers for redaction?
o: Stemming and lemmatisation
Named entity recognition
Part-of-speech tagging
Byte-pair tokenisation
quiz.why: Named entity recognition identifies and classifies entities such as people, organisations, email addresses and account numbers, which is why DLP tools rely on it.

quiz.q: How is the similarity between two text embeddings most commonly measured?
o: Word overlap
Cosine similarity
Comparing their token counts
Comparing their file sizes
quiz.why: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors: values near 1 mean very similar meaning, even without shared words.

quiz.q: Roughly how many English words fit in 1,000 tokens?
o: About 250
About 750
About 1,500
About 4,000
quiz.why: A token averages about four characters of English, roughly three quarters of a word, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words.

quiz.q: A multi-department assistant retrieves from one shared vector index. Which control BEST ensures each user receives only chunks they are entitled to?
o: Instructing the model in its system prompt not to mention or quote from restricted documents
Filtering retrieval results by the requesting user’s permissions stored as metadata
Lowering the number of retrieved chunks so less restricted content can appear
Using a larger embedding model that separates departments’ content more cleanly
quiz.why: Permission-aware retrieval stops restricted chunks reaching the prompt at all. The model can’t be relied on to withhold information it has been shown.

quiz.q: A help desk wants every incoming ticket routed automatically as billing, technical or account security. Which NLP task does this describe?
o: Named entity recognition, finding people and places in text
Text classification, assigning a label to each whole passage
Lemmatisation, reducing each word to its dictionary form
Tokenisation, splitting each ticket into subword pieces
quiz.why: Assigning one of a set of labels to a whole piece of text is text classification. Entity recognition finds spans within text, and lemmatisation and tokenisation are preprocessing steps.

quiz.q: Why can a language model struggle to count the letters in a long word?
o: Stop-word removal deletes letters before the model sees them
It sees token IDs, and several letters may share a single token
Its context window is too small to hold a whole word at once
Lemmatisation changes words into different words first
quiz.why: Models work on token IDs, and a token often covers several characters, so individual letters may be invisible to the model. Modern LLMs don’t apply stop-word removal or lemmatisation, and a word fits easily in any context window.

exam.q: A business unit wants to self-host an open-weight model so that no data leaves the organisation. Which consideration is MOST specific to this choice?
o: The model provider may silently update or retire the model version without notice
Verifying the weights’ provenance and securing the serving stack become the organisation’s job
Prompts and outputs will be retained by the provider and may be used for training
Open-weight licences prohibit fine-tuning, so the model can’t be adapted to the business’s own needs
exam.why: Self-hosting open weights moves almost all security responsibility in-house, including verifying where the weights came from, patching the serving stack, and accepting that safeguards can be altered. Provider-side changes and retention apply to hosted APIs.

exam.q: A reviewer treats a model’s displayed step-by-step reasoning as proof of how it reached a high-stakes recommendation. What is the BEST response?
o: Accept it, because chain-of-thought output is a complete record of the model’s computation
Treat it as a useful trace, but verify the recommendation independently before relying on it
Disable visible reasoning, since a hidden chain of thought is more faithful to the computation
Ask the model to restate its reasoning at a higher temperature to get a more honest account
exam.why: Displayed reasoning helps review but is generated text, not a guaranteed account of the computation. High-stakes outputs need independent verification.

exam.q: An assistant’s RAG index includes a company wiki that any employee can edit. An attacker edits a page to plant a false approval procedure, which the assistant then repeats. Which control MOST directly addresses this?
o: Increase the number of chunks retrieved so that the false page is outvoted by true ones
Restrict who can edit indexed sources, vet high-impact content and track provenance of changes
Add a system prompt rule telling the assistant to ignore any approval procedures that it finds in the wiki
Re-embed the wiki weekly with a newer model so that edited pages are detected as outliers
exam.why: This is knowledge-base poisoning through an open write path. Controlling and auditing who can change indexed content, and reviewing high-impact pages, addresses the cause.

exam.q: After fine-tuning a safety-tuned model on customer-service transcripts, testers find it now complies with requests it used to refuse. What should become a mandatory step in the pipeline?
o: Fine-tuning for more epochs so the model fully absorbs the customer-service style
Comparing safety evaluations of the base and tuned models and blocking release on regressions
Merging the adapter into the base weights so the original safety behaviour is restored
Increasing the LoRA rank so the adapter captures refusals as well as transcript style
exam.why: Fine-tuning can erode safety behaviour even with benign data, so before-and-after safety evaluation with a release gate belongs in every fine-tuning pipeline.

exam.q: An agent writes facts it reads on web pages into long-term memory. A malicious page plants a false instruction that the agent keeps following in later sessions. Which control BEST addresses this?
o: Give the agent a larger context window so it can re-read the original page each time
Check provenance before writing to memory, keep untrusted memories separate, and expire them
Increase the agent’s autonomy so that it can detect and correct the false instruction by itself over time
Encrypt the memory store at rest so that attackers can’t read or alter saved entries
exam.why: This is memory poisoning. Validating what enters memory, tracking where it came from, isolating untrusted entries and expiring them limits how long a planted instruction can persist.

exam.q: A helpdesk agent uses a service account that can reset any user’s password. A junior employee asks it to reset an executive’s password, and it does. Which design flaw does this BEST illustrate?
o: An insufficient context window, so the agent forgot the requester’s role
A confused deputy: the agent used more privilege than the requester holds
Model collapse, caused by training on the agent’s own earlier outputs
Excessive temperature, which made the agent ignore its reset policy
exam.why: The agent performed an action the requester couldn’t perform directly, because its own privileges were broader. Tool calls should be authorised against the requesting user’s entitlements.

exam.q: Long conversations with an assistant gradually stop following its safety rules. Investigation shows the application drops the oldest messages when the context window fills. What is the BEST fix?
o: Use a model with a lower temperature so it sticks more closely to its rules
Pin the system instructions in every request and summarise or trim older turns instead
Silently restart the conversation every ten messages so the rules are always recent
Move the safety rules into the first user message so that they are always kept with the conversation history
exam.why: Naive truncation removed the instructions themselves. Pinning instructions and managing history by summarising or trimming keeps safeguards in force.

exam.q: Why should an organisation attribute LLM token usage to individual users, applications and purposes?
o: It improves the model’s accuracy by tailoring every response to each individual user’s history
It supports cost control, detection of abuse such as unbounded consumption, and audit
It is technically required for the tokeniser to split text into the right tokens
It reduces how much context each request needs, which lowers latency for users
exam.why: Token accounting shows who is consuming what, which enables chargeback, spotting abnormal consumption and providing evidence for audits.

exam.q: A SaaS provider stores all customers’ document embeddings in a single vector index. Which control MOST directly prevents one customer’s content appearing in another customer’s answers?
o: Using a newer embedding model that keeps customers’ documents far apart in vector space
Separate indexes or namespaces per tenant, with tenant filters enforced on every query
Retrieving fewer chunks per question so other customers’ content is less likely to appear
Instructing the model to ignore any content that belongs to other customers
exam.why: Tenant isolation at the storage and query layer prevents cross-tenant retrieval. Instructions to the model are not an isolation control.

exam.q: A DLP rule blocks prompts that contain confidential project names. Staff bypass it by writing the names with Cyrillic letters that look identical to Latin ones. Which control BEST closes the gap?
o: Remove stop words from prompts before the rule is applied
Map confusable characters to a common form before matching
Apply sentiment analysis to flag prompts with a negative tone
Lowercase every prompt before comparing it against the list
exam.why: Look-alike letters from other alphabets are different code points, which standard Unicode normalisation and lowercasing leave unchanged. Confusable-character mapping, as defined in Unicode Technical Standard #39, maps them to a common form so the rule matches again.

quiz.q: A research assistant confidently cites a court decision that does not exist. What is this failure called?
o: Prompt injection (indirect)
Hallucination (confabulation)
Concept drift (model decay)
Training data poisoning
quiz.why: Fluent, plausible but fabricated output is hallucination, which the NIST Generative AI Profile calls confabulation. No attacker or data change is needed for it to happen.

quiz.q: A summary states that a project was approved, but the source report says it was rejected. Which type of hallucination is this?
o: Extrinsic hallucination
Intrinsic hallucination
Aleatoric uncertainty
Model collapse
quiz.why: An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the source the model was given. An extrinsic hallucination adds claims the source cannot support.

quiz.q: Why can an LLM produce slightly different outputs for the same prompt even with temperature set to 0?
o: Temperature 0 maximises randomness, so the model deliberately picks a different token each time
Floating-point operations can run in different orders across hardware and batches, and providers may update models
The model permanently learns from every request, so each new answer reflects the previous conversations
Tokens are randomly reassigned to new IDs on each call, so the same prompt is encoded differently every time
quiz.why: Low temperature removes most sampling randomness, but numerical differences from batching and hardware, and provider-side changes, can still alter outputs.

quiz.q: Which type of uncertainty can be reduced by collecting more or better training data?
o: Aleatoric uncertainty
Epistemic uncertainty
Irreducible measurement noise
Label ambiguity in the data itself
quiz.why: Epistemic uncertainty reflects gaps in the model’s knowledge and shrinks with better data. Aleatoric uncertainty is inherent noise or ambiguity in the data.

quiz.q: A hosted LLM application starts answering differently after the provider updates the model behind the same API name. What is this called?
o: Concept drift
Behavioural drift
Model collapse
Label (prior) shift
quiz.why: Behavioural drift is a change in a generative system’s outputs caused by changes to the model, prompts, retrieval or tools. Version pinning and regression testing control it.

quiz.q: Which monitoring approach gives the EARLIEST warning that a model is seeing inputs unlike its training data?
o: Waiting for the quarterly accuracy report, which shows whether predictions are still correct
Comparing production input distributions with the training baseline using statistics such as PSI
Counting how many model versions have been deployed since the original training run
Reviewing the training code each month to confirm that nothing in the pipeline has changed since launch
quiz.why: Input distribution monitoring needs no labels, so it detects data drift immediately. Performance metrics need true outcomes, which often arrive late.

quiz.q: What is model collapse?
o: A sudden outage of a model-serving cluster when demand exceeds the available accelerator capacity
Progressive degradation when models train on earlier models’ outputs, losing rare patterns and diversity
The loss of earlier skills when a model is fine-tuned on a new task, also called catastrophic forgetting
A model refusing too many harmless requests after safety tuning has been applied too aggressively
quiz.why: Model collapse results from recursive training on model-generated data. Losing earlier skills during new training is catastrophic forgetting, a different problem.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of model collapse?
o: Training each new model only on the previous model’s outputs, which are cleaner than human data
Tracking data provenance and keeping and accumulating genuine human data alongside any synthetic data
Raising the model’s temperature during data generation so that synthetic outputs are more varied and diverse
Deleting older human training data to save storage and keep each training set focused on recent outputs
quiz.why: Provenance lets you know what is synthetic, and accumulating rather than replacing real data preserves the tails of the distribution.

quiz.q: For a malware detector, which metric measures the share of actual malware that was detected?
o: Precision
Recall rate
Specificity
Accuracy
quiz.why: Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) is TP ÷ (TP + FN): the proportion of real positives caught. Precision is the proportion of alerts that are real.

quiz.q: A detector produces 200 alerts, of which 50 are real attacks. What is its precision?
quiz.why: Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP) = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. Three in four alerts are false positives.

quiz.q: What is benchmark contamination?
o: Malware hidden in benchmark software that tampers with the scores it reports
Benchmark test items appearing in a model’s training data, inflating its score
Benchmarks that mix too many languages, which makes the results hard to compare
A benchmark run on unpatched hardware, which leaves the evaluation results open to tampering
quiz.why: If a model has seen the test items during training, its score reflects memorisation rather than capability.

quiz.q: Reviewers approve 99.8% of AI recommendations, spending a few seconds on each. Which risk does this MOST suggest?
o: Model collapse from synthetic data
Automation bias and rubber-stamp oversight
Data drift in the recommendations
Unbounded token consumption during the review
quiz.why: Near-universal, very fast approval suggests reviewers are deferring to the system rather than exercising judgement, which defeats the purpose of a human in the loop.

exam.q: Two analysts use the same LLM tool to summarise the same incident ticket and receive noticeably different summaries. What is the BEST first step?
o: Report the tool to the vendor as compromised, since a sound model should give identical summaries
Check the logged model version, prompt and sampling settings, then standardise them for this task
Ban the tool for incident work immediately until the vendor can guarantee fully deterministic outputs
Retrain the model on the organisation’s own incident tickets so it learns a single house summary style
exam.why: Variation is expected from sampling, version changes and context differences. Diagnosing the cause from logs and then pinning versions, lowering temperature and standardising prompts is proportionate. Treating it as a compromise or retraining is premature.

exam.q: A developer installs a library recommended by a code assistant. The library name was invented by the model, and an attacker had registered it with malicious code. How is this BEST classified?
o: A pure model limitation with no security relevance, because the model itself never installed anything
A hallucination that became a supply-chain vulnerability because the output was used without verification
A denial-of-service attack on the code assistant, because its recommendations were deliberately flooded
Concept drift in the code assistant, because package ecosystems changed after its training cut-off date
exam.why: Hallucinated package names are a limitation; attackers exploit them by registering the names. Dependency verification turns the limitation back into a harmless error.

exam.q: A fraud model’s precision has declined steadily for three months, but its input distributions are stable. True fraud labels arrive about 60 days after each transaction. What is the MOST likely cause and BEST response?
o: Data drift; collect more recent inputs and retrain immediately on the unlabelled transactions as they arrive
Concept drift; retrain on recent labelled data, and watch leading indicators such as overrides while labels lag
Model collapse; find and delete any synthetic transactions that have entered the training data pipeline
Label drift; lower the decision threshold sharply so the model flags far more transactions as fraud
exam.why: Stable inputs with falling performance points to a changed relationship between inputs and outcomes: concept drift. Because labels are delayed, leading indicators help detect it sooner.

exam.q: Which event should MOST clearly trigger re-evaluation of a deployed LLM application before it continues in production?
o: A scheduled backup of the application’s vector index, prompts and configuration completing successfully
The provider announcing that a new model version will replace the current one behind the same endpoint
A redesign of the colour scheme and layout of the user interface that the assistant is embedded in
A 20% increase in the number of employees who are licensed to use the application each month
exam.why: A model change can alter behaviour, including safety behaviour. The golden test set and safety evaluations should be re-run before accepting it.

exam.q: A company plans to train its next customer-support model mainly on conversations generated by its current model and to discard older human transcripts. Average answer-quality scores are expected to stay the same. What is the BEST advice?
o: Proceed, because average answer quality is the measure that matters most to customers and the business
Keep and accumulate human transcripts, label and limit synthetic data, verify it, and test rare and hard cases
Use a different vendor’s model to generate the synthetic conversations, so the training data is more diverse
Generate ten times more synthetic conversations, so the extra volume compensates for losing the human data
exam.why: Replacing real data with recursive synthetic data risks model collapse, which hides behind stable averages. Provenance, accumulation, curation and tail evaluation are the mitigations.

exam.q: A SOC is tuning an AI alert-triage model. Analysts can handle about 200 escalations a day, and a missed intrusion is very costly. How should the decision threshold be set?
o: Maximise overall accuracy, since that balances missed intrusions against false alarms
Maximise precision regardless of recall, so that analysts only ever see alerts that are genuine incidents
Favour recall within analyst capacity, and measure both precision and recall at the chosen threshold
Leave the default threshold of 0.5, because the vendor has already calibrated it for SOCs
exam.why: Costly misses call for high recall, constrained by realistic alert volume. Accuracy is misleading for rare events, and a default threshold ignores the cost of errors.

exam.q: A team evaluates a RAG assistant using an LLM judge. Scores are excellent, but users complain of unsupported answers. Investigation shows answers contain text praising their own accuracy. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Ask the judge to be much stricter by adding firm instructions to penalise any answer that praises its own accuracy
Isolate graded text from judge instructions, check faithfulness to sources, and calibrate against human ratings
Replace the LLM judge with BLEU scores, which compare each answer’s wording with a reference answer
Stop automated evaluation and rely on user complaints, which reflect real problems more accurately
exam.why: Model judges can be biased and manipulated by the content they grade. Isolation, task-specific faithfulness checks and human calibration make the evaluation trustworthy.

exam.q: An insurer automatically denies some claims based on a model’s output, with significant effects on claimants. What is MOST important from a compliance and governance perspective?
o: Publishing the model’s overall accuracy on the company website so claimants can judge its reliability
Ensuring meaningful human review is available, by reviewers with the evidence, time and authority to change it
Raising the model’s confidence threshold to 99%, so that only very certain denials are issued automatically
Adding a clear disclaimer to denial letters explaining that the decision was produced by an AI model
exam.why: Decisions with legal or similarly significant effects attract safeguards such as the right to human intervention (for example, GDPR Article 22). Oversight must be meaningful, not a rubber stamp.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prohibited practice under the EU AI Act?
o: A customer-service chatbot that clearly discloses to users that it is an AI system
Social scoring that leads to detrimental treatment of people
Credit scoring of loan applicants based on their financial history
An email spam filter that uses machine learning
quiz.why: Social scoring leading to detrimental or unjustified treatment is banned under Article 5. Credit scoring is high risk, a disclosed chatbot is limited risk, and spam filters are minimal risk.

quiz.q: In the NIST AI RMF, which function is cross-cutting and informs all the others?
o: Map
Measure
Manage
Govern
quiz.why: Govern establishes culture, policies, roles and accountability, and runs through Map, Measure and Manage.

quiz.q: What MOST distinguishes ISO/IEC 42001 from the NIST AI RMF?
o: ISO/IEC 42001 is an EU law with fines, while the NIST AI RMF is a US federal regulation
ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard; the NIST AI RMF is voluntary, uncertified guidance
The NIST AI RMF applies only to US federal agencies, while ISO/IEC 42001 applies to every organisation
ISO/IEC 42001 only covers generative AI, while the NIST AI RMF covers every other kind of AI system
quiz.why: Both are voluntary, but 42001 sets auditable requirements for an AI management system that accredited bodies certify. The RMF is flexible guidance for any organisation.

quiz.q: An EU employer uses a vendor’s AI tool to rank job applicants. Under the EU AI Act, the employer is MOST likely:
o: The provider of a minimal-risk system
The deployer of a high-risk system
Outside the scope of the Act
A general-purpose AI model provider
quiz.why: Employment and recruitment uses are listed in Annex III as high risk, and an organisation using such a system under its authority is a deployer, with its own obligations.

quiz.q: Which characteristic MOST distinguishes AI governance from traditional IT governance?
o: AI systems always cost more than traditional systems, so they need tighter budget control
AI behaviour is learned and probabilistic, and it can change through drift without a code release
AI systems rarely process personal data, so privacy governance plays a smaller role than in IT
AI systems are retrained automatically, so they never need formal change management
quiz.why: Learned, probabilistic behaviour and drift break the assumption that tested, released code behaves predictably, which drives continuous monitoring and reassessment.

quiz.q: Which document type sets mandatory, specific and measurable requirements that support a policy?
o: Guideline
Standard
Procedure
Charter
quiz.why: Standards are mandatory and specific. Policies state intent, procedures give steps, and guidelines are advisory.

quiz.q: “Consider removing customer names before pasting text into an AI tool.” What kind of document statement is this?
o: A policy
A standard
A guideline
A baseline
quiz.why: The word “consider” signals advice. Guidelines recommend good practice but are not mandatory.

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a centralised AI use-case inventory?
o: To showcase the organisation’s AI capabilities to customers, investors and regulators
To give visibility of every AI system, its owner, risk tier and controls, so it can be governed
To replace individual risk assessments with a single register of all approved AI systems
To store every model’s weights and training data securely in one central, access-controlled location
quiz.why: Every other governance activity depends on knowing what AI exists, who owns it and how risky it is.

quiz.q: Who should be accountable for an AI use case’s outcomes and risks?
o: The vendor that supplied the model
A named business owner
The most senior data scientist
The AI tool itself
quiz.why: Accountability belongs to a named business owner who benefits from the use case and can make decisions about it. Technical teams and vendors have responsibilities, but not ownership of the business risk.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN role of AI champions?
o: To approve all high-risk AI use cases on behalf of the governance committee
To act as trained advocates in their teams and a first point of contact for safe AI use
To conduct independent audits of AI systems and report findings directly to the board
To replace the chief AI officer in business units that don’t have their own AI leadership
quiz.why: Champions extend the governance programme into business units. Approval of high-risk uses sits with the committee, and independent assurance with internal audit.

exam.q: A US software company with no EU offices sells an AI hiring tool to employers in the EU. Which statement is MOST accurate?
o: The EU AI Act doesn’t apply, because the company has no establishment anywhere in the EU
As a provider placing a high-risk system on the EU market, the company must meet provider obligations
Only the GDPR applies, because the tool processes candidates’ personal data rather than products
Only the EU employers have obligations under the Act, because they are the ones using the tool
exam.why: The AI Act applies to providers placing systems on the EU market regardless of where they are established. Hiring tools are high risk, so provider duties such as risk management, documentation and conformity assessment apply. Deployers have separate duties.

exam.q: A multinational must meet EU AI Act duties, GDPR requirements and customer demands for assurance. Which approach is MOST efficient and defensible?
o: Run a separate compliance programme for each requirement, so each has a dedicated owner and budget
One AI management system with an obligations register and crosswalks, so shared controls evidence everything
Adopt the NIST AI RMF across the group, since a recognised framework satisfies the EU AI Act and GDPR
Meet the strictest requirement in each area and assume that this automatically satisfies all the others
exam.why: A single management system, for example aligned to ISO/IEC 42001, with obligations mapped to shared controls, avoids duplication and produces consistent evidence. Frameworks never override legal obligations.

exam.q: A CIO proposes governing AI solely through the existing change advisory board, which reviews releases before deployment. What is the MOST significant gap?
o: Change boards are too slow for AI, so AI releases should bypass them and go through the data science team
Release review misses drift, impact on people, bias, legal review and monitoring after deployment
Change boards can’t review cloud-hosted systems, so any hosted model would fall outside their remit
AI systems rarely change after deployment, so a change board would have too little to review
exam.why: AI outcomes can change without releases and raise harms beyond CIA. Governance needs risk and impact assessment, cross-functional decisions and ongoing monitoring in addition to change control.

exam.q: Employees are pasting customer records into consumer AI chatbots, despite a high-level responsible AI policy. Which action is MOST effective?
o: Re-issue the existing policy with stronger wording and a reminder of the disciplinary consequences
Provide an approved enterprise tool, an acceptable-use standard by data class, training and technical controls
Block all AI websites on the corporate network and ban AI use permanently until further notice
Ask every employee to re-read and sign the policy, and have managers audit a sample of signatures each quarter
exam.why: Policies need actionable standards, a sanctioned alternative and enforcement. Banning AI typically drives use underground, and re-issuing the same policy changes nothing.

exam.q: Internal audit finds the AI inventory lists 40 systems, but SaaS discovery tools show 130 AI-enabled applications in use. What is the BEST next step?
o: Block all 90 unregistered applications immediately until each one has been fully assessed
Triage them into the inventory through risk-based intake, assign owners and tiers, and fix the intake gaps
Redefine “AI” in the policy to exclude AI features embedded in SaaS products, which vendors manage
Ask each vendor to confirm in writing that its AI features are safe and compliant, and record each confirmation
exam.why: A risk-based triage brings unknown AI under governance proportionately. Blanket blocking disrupts the business and drives shadow use, and vendors don’t carry the organisation’s accountability.

exam.q: A high-impact AI credit model has residual risk above the team’s authority after all planned controls. Who should decide whether to accept it?
o: The lead data scientist, who understands the model and its limitations best
The CISO, because AI risk is ultimately a technology and information security risk that the CISO owns
A senior executive with authority under the risk appetite, advised by the governance committee
The model vendor, which is accountable for the risks of the product it supplies
exam.why: Residual risk must be accepted by someone with authority matching its level, usually a senior business executive acting within board-approved risk appetite. Technical leads and the CISO advise but don’t own business risk.

quiz.q: Which principle is MOST directly served by telling users they are interacting with an AI system?
o: Fairness
Transparency
Reliability
Inclusiveness
quiz.why: Disclosing AI use is a core transparency measure, and a legal duty under Article 50 of the EU AI Act for systems that interact with people.

quiz.q: What is “ethics washing”?
o: Removing personal data from training sets before a model is published or shared
Projecting ethical AI through published principles without requirements, controls or accountability
Retraining a model on rebalanced data to reduce bias before an external audit
Commissioning an independent audit of AI ethics and publishing a short summary of its findings on the website
quiz.why: Ethics washing is the appearance of responsible AI without substance: principles that have no owners, metrics or effect on decisions.

quiz.q: Which principle focuses on ensuring AI works well for people of different abilities, languages and backgrounds?
o: Accountability
Inclusiveness
Privacy
Security
quiz.why: Inclusiveness means designing and testing for diverse users, including people with disabilities and speakers of different languages and dialects.

quiz.q: A hiring tool shortlists 30% of female applicants and 50% of male applicants. What is the impact ratio, and what does it suggest under the four-fifths rule?
o: 1.67; no concern, because women are shortlisted more efficiently
0.6; potential adverse impact requiring investigation
0.8; exactly at the threshold, so there is no concern
0.2; proof that the tool discriminates intentionally
quiz.why: Impact ratio = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6, below 0.8, which is a common indicator of potential adverse impact. It requires investigation but is not, on its own, proof of discrimination.

quiz.q: Which fairness metric requires equal true positive rates across groups?
o: Demographic parity
Equal opportunity
Predictive parity
Calibration
quiz.why: Equal opportunity requires that qualified (actually positive) people in each group are correctly selected at the same rate.

quiz.q: Why does removing protected attributes from a model’s inputs often fail to prevent discrimination?
o: Models give little weight to demographic inputs, so removing them changes nothing
Other features, such as postcode, act as proxies carrying the same information
Protected attributes are legally required inputs in every high-risk model
Removing inputs makes the model so accurate that small groups are overlooked
quiz.why: Features such as postcode, name or career gaps can correlate strongly with protected characteristics and reproduce the same disparities.

quiz.q: What does a counterfactual explanation describe?
o: The model’s full architecture, including its layers and the weights that matter most
The smallest change to the inputs that would have produced a different outcome
The average importance of each feature across all of the model’s predictions
The training data used to build the model and how each record influenced it
quiz.why: Counterfactuals are local and actionable: “if X had been different, the decision would have been Y”.

quiz.q: How does transparency differ from explainability?
o: They mean the same thing: both describe publishing a model’s source code and weights
Transparency is openness about a system’s use, design and limits; explainability gives reasons for outputs
Transparency applies only to open-source code, while explainability applies to every AI system
Explainability applies only to simple linear models, while transparency applies to deep learning models as well
quiz.why: Transparency operates at the system and organisational level; explainability addresses why the system produced a specific output or behaves as it does.

quiz.q: Which practice MOST reduces an AI service’s energy footprint while maintaining quality?
o: Always using the largest available model, because it completes tasks in fewer attempts
Choosing the smallest model that meets requirements, with efficient inference such as quantisation and caching
Running heavy workloads at peak grid demand, when renewable energy supply is usually at its very highest level
Retraining the model every day on fresh data so that it never wastes energy on outdated answers
quiz.why: Right-sizing models and efficient inference cut energy and cost, often with little or no quality loss for the task.

quiz.q: What does “monoculture” risk mean in the context of AI?
o: A training dataset that contains text in only one language, which limits fairness for other speakers
Many organisations relying on the same model share its flaws, so one failure can cause correlated harm
A model trained for a single narrow task, which can’t adapt when the business needs change
A team that depends on a single data scientist, creating key-person risk for every AI project
quiz.why: Widespread dependence on the same foundation model concentrates risk: a single jailbreak, vulnerability or outage affects everyone built on it.

exam.q: An AI ethics board concludes that a planned customer-scoring system breaches the organisation’s fairness principle, but the product team launches anyway because the board is advisory. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Publish the fairness principle more prominently on the intranet, so that product teams can’t claim they were unaware of it
Give a designated body authority to block failing high-risk launches, or require documented executive risk acceptance
Disband the ethics board, since advice that teams can ignore has no effect on outcomes
Ask the product team to self-certify fairness for future launches, with spot checks by the board
exam.why: Principles need decision rights. Either a body with authority to stop non-compliant launches, or an explicit, documented acceptance by an accountable executive, turns ethical review into governance.

exam.q: A bank’s model has similar overall accuracy for two groups, but one group experiences far more wrongful denials. When choosing a fairness metric to monitor, what is MOST important?
o: Choosing the metric on which the model performs best, so that monitoring produces few false alarms
Choosing the metric that reflects the main harm, here unequal error rates, agreed by accountable owners
Using overall accuracy, since it is already equal across the two groups and is easy to explain
Monitoring every available fairness metric equally, so that no possible form of bias can be missed
exam.why: Fairness metrics conflict when base rates differ, so tracking every metric equally can’t settle which one matters; the choice is a governance decision tied to the harm in context. Overall accuracy hides unequal errors.

exam.q: To test a model for ethnic bias, the data science team needs ethnicity data that the organisation doesn’t normally collect. The privacy officer is concerned. What is the BEST approach?
o: Abandon bias testing, because processing sensitive data creates more risk than it removes
Infer ethnicity from customers’ names and postcodes, avoiding the need to collect new data
Process it only where lawful and strictly necessary for bias testing, with safeguards, documented in a DPIA
Collect ethnicity data from all customers and add it as a model input, so that bias can be corrected directly
exam.why: Bias can’t be measured without some group data. Laws such as the EU AI Act permit strictly necessary processing for bias detection with safeguards. Using ethnicity as an input, or uncontrolled inference, creates new harms.

exam.q: A regulator asks a lender to explain why its deep-learning model declined a particular applicant. What is the BEST response?
o: Provide the full model weights and code, so the regulator can reproduce the decision independently
A validated local explanation (reason codes or a counterfactual), with model documentation and the review record
State that deep-learning models can’t be explained, but that the model is accurate on average
Provide the model’s global accuracy and its fairness metrics, which show that it treats applicants consistently
exam.why: A faithful local explanation addresses the specific decision; documentation and the review record show how the system and oversight work. Weights are neither meaningful nor appropriate to share, and “can’t be explained” fails the duty.

exam.q: Auditors plan to rely on the step-by-step reasoning that an LLM writes in its output as evidence of how decisions were made. What is the MAIN concern?
o: Reasoning text is usually too short to show every step the model took
A model’s self-explanation may not reflect how it actually produced the output
LLMs can only produce reasoning text when they are run at a high temperature
Reasoning text belongs to the model provider, so auditors can’t rely on it as evidence
exam.why: Generated reasoning is itself model output. Stronger evidence includes logged inputs, retrieved sources, model versions, decision records and the human review trail.

exam.q: A city council plans to use AI to flag possible benefit fraud. Which approach BEST addresses the societal trade-offs?
o: Deploy quickly to a pilot area, then fix any problems as complaints arrive from affected residents and advocates
Assess who is harmed and how, weigh alternatives, require human review before action, and offer appeals and monitoring
Use the system only for claimants in deprived areas, where the council assumes fraud risk is higher
Keep the system’s existence confidential, so that claimants can’t learn how to avoid being flagged by it
exam.why: Public-sector fraud systems have caused serious harm to vulnerable people when deployed without safeguards. A structured trade-off analysis with oversight, recourse and monitoring is essential; targeting vulnerable groups would be discriminatory.

quiz.q: Which formula gives the annualised loss expectancy (ALE)?
o: ALE = AV × ARO
ALE = SLE × ARO
ALE = SLE ÷ EF
ALE = AV + SLE
quiz.why: ALE is the single loss expectancy multiplied by the annualised rate of occurrence. SLE itself is asset value × exposure factor.

quiz.q: What is the difference between inherent and residual risk?
o: Inherent risk is financial in nature, while residual risk is reputational
Inherent risk is before controls; residual risk is what remains after controls
Inherent risk applies only to AI systems, while residual risk applies to all IT
They describe the same risk, measured by different teams at different times
quiz.why: Inherent risk ignores controls; residual risk is the exposure left once controls operate. Residual risk is never zero.

quiz.q: Which model quantifies risk by decomposing it into loss event frequency and loss magnitude?
o: STRIDE
FAIR
RACI
MITRE ATLAS
quiz.why: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) is a quantitative model built on loss event frequency and loss magnitude, often estimated as ranges.

quiz.q: Which assessment does the EU AI Act require of certain deployers, such as those assessing creditworthiness, before using high-risk AI?
o: An independent penetration test
A fundamental rights impact assessment
A business continuity and recovery plan
A software bill of materials (SBOM)
quiz.why: Article 27 requires a FRIA from public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring and certain insurance systems.

quiz.q: What determines an AI system’s blast radius?
o: Its intended purpose, as described in the approved design document and policy
The data, actions and connections it can actually reach, and the scale it operates at
The size of its underlying model in parameters, which sets how much it can do
The number of developers who built it and the number of teams who maintain it
quiz.why: Blast radius depends on permissions and integrations. A system intended for a narrow task but given broad access has a broad blast radius.

quiz.q: Which two dimensions are commonly combined to tier AI use cases?
o: Cost and speed
Human impact and technical complexity
Model size and vendor
Number of users and colour of the interface
quiz.why: Human impact captures potential harm to people; technical complexity captures how hard the system is to predict, control and secure.

quiz.q: A model approved for a low-risk use is proposed for a high-impact use. What is the correct approach?
o: Reuse the original approval, as long as the model version hasn’t changed
Tier and assess the new use case on its own impact and its complexity
Approve it, since the model has already passed a full risk assessment
Reject all future uses of the model to keep the approval process simple
quiz.why: Risk attaches to the use, not the tool. A new purpose, population or decision type needs its own tier and assessment.

quiz.q: Buying insurance to cover losses from AI errors is an example of which treatment?
o: Avoidance (termination)
Mitigation (reduction)
Transfer (risk sharing)
Acceptance (retention)
quiz.why: Insurance shares financial consequences with another party. Accountability to regulators and affected people remains with the organisation.

quiz.q: Removing an agent’s ability to execute payments, because the risk is too high, is an example of:
o: Risk avoidance
Risk transfer
Risk acceptance
Risk tolerance
quiz.why: Removing the capability that creates the risk avoids it. Adding approval steps instead would be mitigation.

quiz.q: Which event should MOST clearly trigger a reassessment of a deployed AI system?
o: A routine backup of the system’s configuration and logs completing
The provider replacing the model version behind the API
The development team moving to a new office in another city
A change to the application’s colour theme and branding
quiz.why: Model changes can alter behaviour, including safety and fairness, so they are a standard reassessment trigger.

exam.q: An AI-enabled fraud scenario has an SLE of £250,000 and an ARO of 0.4. A control costing £40,000 a year would reduce the ARO to 0.1. What is the annual value of the control?
exam.why: ALE before = £250,000 × 0.4 = £100,000. ALE after = £250,000 × 0.1 = £25,000. Reduction = £75,000. Minus the £40,000 cost, the control is worth £35,000 a year.

exam.q: In an AI risk workshop, almost every risk is rated “medium” on a three-point scale, and the board cannot prioritise. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Rate every uncertain risk as high, so that the board treats all of them as priorities for funding
Define clear likelihood and impact criteria, including impact on people, and map risks to components and owners
Replace the three-point scale with a ten-point scale so that small differences between risks can be shown
Ask each risk owner to re-rate their own risks without the workshop, to avoid groupthink in the room
exam.why: Vague scales produce undifferentiated ratings. Defined criteria, quantification where possible, and mapping to components and owners make prioritisation and action possible.

exam.q: An EU bank will deploy a high-risk creditworthiness model and already has a GDPR DPIA for it. What is the MOST efficient way to meet the fundamental rights impact assessment duty?
o: Skip the FRIA, since the GDPR DPIA already covers every risk to fundamental rights that the AI Act requires of deployers
Build the FRIA on the DPIA, adding affected groups, rights risks, oversight and responses, then notify the authority
Commission a separate team to start the FRIA from scratch, so that it is independent of the privacy work
Ask the model provider to complete the FRIA, since the provider designed the system and knows its risks
exam.why: The AI Act lets a FRIA build on a DPIA, but it must still address fundamental rights beyond data protection, and the deployer must notify the authority. The duty belongs to the deployer, not the provider.

exam.q: An impact assessment finds that an email-handling agent with a broad service account has a very large blast radius. Which treatment is MOST effective?
o: Add a sentence to the system prompt asking the agent to take great care with high-impact actions
Reduce permissions to least privilege, segment access, and add limits and approval for high-impact actions
Increase the agent’s context window so that it can see the full history before acting on any email
Monitor the agent’s actions every week, and quickly roll back any harmful changes that the security review identifies
exam.why: Blast radius shrinks only when reach shrinks. Least privilege, segmentation, limits and approvals reduce both likelihood and impact; prompts don’t enforce, and weekly review is too slow.

exam.q: Teams are bypassing AI governance because every request, however small, requires a 40-page assessment. What is the BEST fix?
o: Enforce the 40-page assessment more strictly, with sanctions for teams that skip it
Introduce risk-based tiers with proportionate requirements, and second-line review of tiers
Stop assessing low-value AI use cases altogether and focus only on externally facing systems
Let each team decide for itself whether governance applies to its particular use of AI
exam.why: Proportionate tiering lets low-risk uses move quickly and concentrates effort on high-impact ones, removing the incentive to bypass governance. Review of classifications prevents gaming.

exam.q: Threat intelligence reports a new indirect prompt injection technique affecting RAG applications built on a particular open-source framework. What should the risk owner do FIRST?
o: Wait for the next scheduled review of each affected system, when the new technique can be considered properly and in full
Use the inventory and AIBOM to find affected systems, triage the change in risk, and reassess or add controls
Shut down every AI system in the organisation until the framework’s maintainers release a patch
Ask each development team to confirm whether they use the framework, and record their answers
exam.why: A vulnerability disclosure is a reassessment trigger. Identifying exposure and triaging comes first, then a proportionate response; blanket shutdowns or waiting are disproportionate either way.

quiz.q: Which of these is special category data under the GDPR?
o: A customer’s postal address and phone number
A person’s biometric data used to identify them
A company’s quarterly revenue and profit figures
A product’s serial number and warranty date
quiz.why: Biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is special category data under Article 9, alongside health, ethnicity, religious beliefs and sexual orientation.

quiz.q: Why might sharing export-controlled technical data with a cloud AI service be a problem?
o: Export controls apply only to physical goods, so cloud services raise data protection issues instead
Sending controlled technical data to a service hosted abroad, or seen by foreign persons, can be an export
Cloud services are exempt from export controls, but providers may still refuse to process technical data
Export controls matter only for consumer products, so business use of cloud AI services is unaffected
quiz.why: Export regimes such as ITAR and EAR control technical data, not just hardware. Where data is processed and who can access it matter.

quiz.q: In the United States, whether training a model on copyrighted works is lawful is mainly assessed under:
o: The EU text and data mining exception, with machine-readable opt-outs
The fair use doctrine, decided case by case on four factors
Automatic permission for any publicly available content
Trademark law and the protection of registered brands
quiz.why: Fair use weighs purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used and market effect. Outcomes depend on the facts.

quiz.q: Under the EU’s commercial text and data mining exception, when may content NOT be mined?
o: When the content was first published more than ten years ago
When the rightsholder has reserved their rights in a machine-readable way
When the content is written in English rather than an EU language
When the content is hosted on servers that are located outside the European Union
quiz.why: Article 4 of the DSM Directive allows TDM for any purpose unless rightsholders opt out, for online content in a machine-readable way.

quiz.q: Under US copyright law, what is required for a work to be protected?
o: Generation by an advanced AI model
Human authorship of the work
Registration within 24 hours
Use of an open-source licence
quiz.why: The US requires human authorship; purely AI-generated material is not protected, though human selection and arrangement can be.

quiz.q: What is “regulatory contamination” in AI?
o: Malware hidden in a training dataset that spreads into every model trained on it
Regulated data entering an AI pipeline, so its obligations attach to models and outputs
A regulator’s audit of an AI system that finds problems across several of its components
Training data leaking into the test set, which makes regulatory evaluations unreliable
quiz.why: Once regulated data is in a model or index, obligations such as erasure, residency, export control and licence terms can follow it.

quiz.q: Why should embeddings of personal data be treated as personal data?
o: Embeddings are usually stored unencrypted in vector databases, so they are easy to steal
Embeddings can be partly inverted to reconstruct the original text and its meaning
Embeddings are kept for longer than the source documents, so retention rules apply
Embeddings contain only numbers, so they are anonymous unless linked to user IDs
quiz.why: Embedding inversion can recover meaningful parts of source text, so embeddings inherit the classification of their source.

quiz.q: Which technique makes encrypted data unrecoverable across many copies, including backups, by destroying the keys?
o: Tokenisation
Crypto-shredding
Salted hashing
Format-preserving encryption
quiz.why: Crypto-shredding destroys the encryption keys, rendering all ciphertext copies unreadable, which is useful where data is replicated widely.

quiz.q: Where is personal data hardest to delete once it has been used?
o: In a relational database
In a trained model’s weights
In a cloud object store with versioning
In an email archive
quiz.why: Training diffuses data through the weights. Removal requires retraining, machine unlearning or output suppression, so prevention before training matters.

quiz.q: Which statement about publicly available personal data is MOST accurate?
o: It can be used for any purpose without restriction, because individuals chose to publish it
Privacy law still applies, so its use needs a lawful basis, transparency and respect for rights
It becomes anonymous once published, because anyone could link it to the person anyway
Only data published by government bodies is regulated; other public data can be reused freely
quiz.why: Regulators have stated that publicly accessible personal data remains protected; scraping it is processing under privacy law.

exam.q: A hospital wants to use a hosted LLM to summarise patient discharge notes. What is MOST important before any data is sent?
o: Choosing the most accurate model available, so summaries don’t introduce clinical errors
Confirming the provider will sign a BAA and its retention, training and security terms meet HIPAA
Asking clinicians to shorten the notes so that less patient information is sent to the provider
Testing the model on a sample of real discharge notes to compare summary quality across vendors
exam.why: Sending PHI to a vendor makes it a business associate under HIPAA. A BAA and suitable retention, no-training and security commitments are prerequisites.

exam.q: An organisation discovers that a widely shared internal model was fine-tuned on documents containing export-controlled technical data. What is the BEST immediate action?
o: Continue sharing the model, since the controlled data now exists only as numerical weights
Restrict access and distribution pending legal review, find all copies through lineage, and plan retraining
Delete the original documents from the training store, which removes the export-control concern for the model entirely
Add a disclaimer to the model’s outputs stating that they may contain export-controlled information
exam.why: The model may itself be controlled. Containing distribution, scoping copies through lineage, and obtaining expert review come first; deleting the source documents doesn’t fix the model.

exam.q: A product team plans to embed an open-weight model in a commercial app with millions of users. What should happen FIRST?
o: Deploy it, since open-weight models are free to use commercially at any scale
Review the licence and acceptable use policy for restrictions, and record the obligations
Fine-tune it on company data, since a fine-tuned derivative isn’t bound by the original licence
Ask the model’s community forum whether this kind of commercial use is allowed, and keep the reply
exam.why: Open-weight licences vary and may restrict commercial use above thresholds, certain applications, or training other models on outputs. Licence review is a supply-chain and IP control.

exam.q: Marketing wants to rely on copyright protection for images generated entirely by an AI model with a one-line prompt. What is the BEST advice?
o: The images are automatically protected by copyright, because the company paid for the AI service
Purely AI-generated images may lack protection in places like the US; add human creative work and get advice
Register the images as trade secrets instead, which protects them from being copied by competitors worldwide
Copyright in AI outputs belongs to the AI provider, so the company should request a licence from it
exam.why: US law requires human authorship. Human selection, arrangement and modification may create protectable elements; legal advice is needed for important assets.

exam.q: A vendor’s standard terms allow it to retain prompts for 30 days for abuse monitoring and to use them to improve its models. The organisation will send confidential contracts. What is the BEST action?
o: Accept the standard terms, since 30-day retention for abuse monitoring is normal across the industry
Negotiate no training on customer data, minimal retention and deletion commitments, or choose another service
Ask employees to remove contract titles and party names before pasting contracts into the service
Encrypt the prompts before sending them, so the vendor can’t read the contracts it receives
exam.why: Vendor retention and training use must match the organisation’s policy and confidentiality duties. Encrypting prompts would stop the model processing them, and partial redaction doesn’t address training use.

exam.q: A research team plans to scrape profile photos and posts from a public social network to train a recognition model. Which response BEST reflects privacy obligations?
o: Proceed, because the photos and posts are public, and the network’s users agreed to its terms
Stop until a DPIA assesses lawful basis, transparency, minimisation and platform terms; biometrics are high risk
Proceed if the photos are downsampled to low resolution, so individuals are harder to recognise
Proceed, but keep the dataset confidential and delete it as soon as the recognition model has been fully trained
exam.why: Public availability doesn’t remove obligations. Biometric processing is special category and high risk, regulators have fined scrapers, and platform terms may prohibit scraping.

quiz.q: A vendor’s ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers only its corporate offices. What does this mean for an assessment of its AI platform?
o: The platform is fully assured, because ISO/IEC 27001 certification applies to the whole company
