It offers little assurance for the AI platform, so further evidence covering the platform is needed
Certificates never matter in AI assessments, because AI platforms change too quickly to certify
The vendor must be rejected immediately, because a partial scope means the certificate is invalid
quiz.why: Certification scope matters. Assurance must cover the systems and facilities that actually deliver the AI service.

quiz.q: Which framework provides vendor-neutral AI security and governance control objectives, mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act?
o: PCI DSS v4.0.1
The CSA AI Controls Matrix
ITIL 4 for AI services
COBIT 2019 with AI extensions
quiz.why: The Cloud Security Alliance’s AI Controls Matrix (AICM) underpins its STAR for AI programme and maps to major AI frameworks.

quiz.q: Why should an AI vendor contract require advance notice of model version changes?
o: To reduce licence costs, because older model versions are priced lower
Silent model updates can change behaviour, including safety, and invalidate your testing
Because each new model version changes the vendor’s tax position in the different countries it operates in
It is a GDPR requirement for all software that processes personal data in the EU
quiz.why: Notice, plus the ability to pin versions, lets you re-test before a changed model reaches your users.

quiz.q: Under NIS2, how quickly must an essential or important entity send an early warning of a significant incident?
o: Within 24 hours
Within 7 days
Within 30 days
There is no deadline
quiz.why: NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours, and a final report within one month. Vendor terms must fit inside these clocks.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, what is the general deadline for providers to report a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system?
o: 72 hours
15 days
30 days
6 months
quiz.why: Article 73 sets 15 days generally, with shorter limits of 2 days for widespread infringement or critical-infrastructure incidents and 10 days for a death.

quiz.q: What does an AIBOM add to a traditional SBOM?
o: Nothing; an AIBOM is simply an SBOM generated by an AI tool rather than by hand
Models, datasets, adapters, training lineage and related licences, alongside software
Only the hardware serial numbers of the GPUs and servers used to train each model
Only the vendor’s performance claims, such as benchmark scores, for each model version
quiz.why: An AIBOM extends software inventories to AI-specific components and their provenance, which incident response and licence compliance depend on.

quiz.q: Which formats support machine-readable AI or ML bills of materials?
o: CSV and XLSX spreadsheets with a standard column layout
CycloneDX (ML-BOM) and SPDX 3.0 (AI and Dataset profiles)
OpenAPI 3.1 and JSON Schema for model interfaces
PDF/A documents that are digitally signed by the model’s publisher
quiz.why: Both major SBOM standards have extended to AI: CycloneDX with ML-BOM and SPDX 3.0 with AI and Dataset profiles.

quiz.q: An organisation uses a SaaS copilot that can read too many internal document libraries. Under the shared responsibility model, who is primarily responsible for fixing this?
o: The SaaS provider, because it built the copilot and controls the AI model
The customer, because data access configuration is on the customer’s side
The cloud data centre operator that hosts the SaaS provider’s infrastructure
The model developer, because the copilot’s retrieval behaviour comes from training
quiz.why: In SaaS, customers own their data, identities and configuration, including which content the copilot may access.

quiz.q: What does remote attestation provide in confidential computing?
o: Faster processing of encrypted data, because the TEE decrypts it in hardware
A hardware-signed proof of what code and configuration are running in a TEE, verified before trust
Automatic encryption of every backup and snapshot taken from the confidential virtual machine at rest
A secure copy of the model weights that the relying party can inspect before sending data
quiz.why: Attestation lets a client or key broker verify the environment before releasing data or keys to it.

quiz.q: Which threat does confidential computing NOT address?
o: A cloud operator reading data in memory
A malicious hypervisor
Prompt injection against the application
Another tenant reading GPU memory
quiz.why: TEEs protect data and code from the infrastructure layer. Application-layer attacks such as prompt injection work the same inside a TEE.

exam.q: A business unit wants to adopt an AI meeting-transcription service for board meetings. Which due diligence question is MOST important?
o: How accurate are its transcripts for board members with different accents and speaking styles?
Are transcripts retained or used for training, where are they processed, and by which sub-processors?
How many languages does it support, and can it translate transcripts for overseas board members?
Does it integrate with the company’s calendar and board portal so meetings are recorded automatically?
exam.why: Board discussions are highly confidential. Data retention, training use, location and sub-processors determine the confidentiality risk; features are secondary.

exam.q: A vendor will notify incidents “within a reasonable time”. The organisation is subject to GDPR and NIS2. What is the BEST contractual change?
o: Accept the term, since vendors act in good faith and “reasonable” is a well-understood legal standard
Require notice within the shortest regulatory clock (for example, 24 hours), with set content and cooperation
Require monthly incident summaries, which give the organisation a complete picture of the vendor’s incidents
Replace the clause with a right to audit the vendor annually, which covers incident handling more fully
exam.why: Vague notification can make the organisation miss its own deadlines (24-hour NIS2 early warning, 72-hour GDPR notification). A specific, short clock with defined content is needed.

exam.q: An advisory reports that a widely used embedding model contains a backdoor. The CISO asks which production systems use it. The organisation has SBOMs for its applications but no records of models or datasets. What is the BEST long-term improvement?
o: Ask developers to keep a shared spreadsheet of every model and dataset they use, updated at each release cycle
Extend SBOMs into AIBOMs recording models, versions, hashes, datasets and lineage, linked to the inventory
Ban third-party embedding models and require every team to train its own from scratch in future
Ask every AI vendor to email the CISO whenever a security issue affects one of their models
exam.why: SBOMs cover software libraries but not models or datasets. AIBOMs linked to the inventory make this question answerable in minutes.

exam.q: A team builds an application on a hosted model API. A user extracts confidential data from the application’s retrieval index through crafted questions. Under shared responsibility, who must primarily address this?
o: The model API provider, because it hosts the model that generated the confidential answers
The customer, because the app, retrieval data, access controls and filters are on its side
The end user who crafted the questions, who is legally responsible for the extraction
The internet service provider, which should have detected the unusual queries in transit
exam.why: With a model API, the customer owns the application layer, including retrieval data and its permissions, prompts and output filtering. Accountability for outcomes stays with the customer in every model.

exam.q: A bank wants to use a cloud LLM to analyse confidential customer documents, but its regulator is concerned about cloud operator access to data during processing. Which control MOST directly addresses this concern?
o: Encryption at rest with customer-managed keys held in the bank’s own on-premises hardware security modules
Confidential computing with verified attestation, so documents are decrypted only inside TEEs
A longer contract with stronger confidentiality clauses, audit rights and penalties for any operator access
Daily backups of all processed documents to an on-premises location
exam.why: The concern is data in use. Encryption at rest and in transit don’t protect data while it is processed; attested TEEs do.

exam.q: A provider claims its confidential AI service is secure because it runs in TEEs. Which follow-up question is MOST important?
o: Which certifications does the data centre hold, and how often are its physical controls audited?
How is attestation verified, how are TEE flaws patched, and what application-layer controls exist?
How many GPUs does the provider own, and can it guarantee capacity during peak demand periods?
Is the confidential service cheaper than competitors, and does the price include attestation?
exam.why: TEE assurance depends on verified attestation and patched hardware, and TEEs don’t cover application-layer risks. These questions test whether the claim holds.

quiz.q: What MOST distinguishes human-on-the-loop from human-in-the-loop oversight?
o: HOTL means no human is involved at all; HITL means a human reviews a random sample of the decisions made afterwards
In HOTL the system acts while a person supervises and can intervene; in HITL a person approves each decision
HOTL is used only for chatbots, while HITL is used for every other type of high-risk AI system
HITL requires the system to run offline in batches, while HOTL lets it run in real time
quiz.why: The difference is when the human acts: before each decision (HITL) or during operation with the ability to intervene (HOTL).

quiz.q: A claims handler replaces a model’s “deny” recommendation with an approval. Which authority is being exercised?
o: Sign-off
Override
Stop
Audit
quiz.why: Override authority replaces an AI output with a human decision in an individual case. Overrides should be recorded with a reason and analysed for patterns.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST ensures an emergency stop can be used when needed?
o: Requiring a committee vote before any system is stopped, to prevent unnecessary disruption
Giving stop authority to several available, trained people, with a tested kill switch and protection
Keeping the kill switch procedure confidential, so attackers can’t learn how to trigger it
Allowing only the CEO to stop systems, so that stop decisions are always taken at the top
quiz.why: Stops must be fast. Available holders, practised controls and a no-blame policy make the authority real.

quiz.q: Which is an example of shadow AI?
o: An enterprise chatbot approved through governance and listed in the inventory
An employee using a personal public chatbot account to summarise confidential reports
A model listed in the AI inventory that has not been reassessed for two years
A vendor tool with a signed data processing agreement that staff use for translation
quiz.why: Shadow AI is AI used without the organisation’s knowledge, approval or governance, often with consumer terms that offer no data protection.

quiz.q: Which source is MOST useful for discovering third-party AI apps that users have connected to corporate accounts?
o: Building access logs showing which staff were on site
OAuth and app-consent records from the identity platform and SaaS discovery tools
Printer and scanner logs showing documents that were digitised
An annual staff survey asking which AI tools and browser extensions people use at work
quiz.why: App-consent records show which third-party applications have been granted access to corporate identities and data, and with what scopes.

quiz.q: What must an exception record include to keep exceptions under control?
o: Only the requester’s name and the date the exception was requested
The requirement waived, justification, compensating controls, approver and expiry date
The model’s source code and configuration at the time the exception was first raised by the team
A copy of the policy being waived, signed by everyone affected by the exception
quiz.why: Without compensating controls and expiry-driven review, temporary exceptions become permanent unmanaged risk.

quiz.q: Which document describes a model’s intended use, training data, performance across groups and limitations?
o: A datasheet for datasets
A model card
An SBOM
A risk acceptance
quiz.why: Model cards provide transparency about a specific model. Datasheets describe datasets; system documentation describes the whole deployed system.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, who must disclose that an image is a deepfake?
o: Nobody, provided the image is clearly artistic or satirical
The deployer who uses the system to generate or manipulate the content
Only the cloud provider that hosts the image generation service
Only the person depicted, who must label every published image of themselves
quiz.why: Article 50 places the deepfake disclosure duty on deployers; providers must ensure generated content is machine-readably marked.

quiz.q: Which marking technique records a signed history of how content was created and edited?
o: Visible captions added to the image
Provenance metadata such as C2PA content credentials
Detection classifiers run by social media platforms on upload
Lossy compression that leaves editing artefacts
quiz.why: C2PA content credentials attach cryptographically signed provenance. Their weakness is that platforms often strip metadata.

quiz.q: Why is independence essential to an AI audit?
o: It makes audits faster, because independent auditors don’t need to learn the system
Assurance is only credible when the auditor is independent of those who built and run the system
Independent auditors can rely on their own judgement, so they need less evidence from the team
It removes the need for remediation, because independent findings are advisory rather than binding
quiz.why: Self-assessment is useful but isn’t assurance. Independence, plus evidence, makes audit conclusions trustworthy.

quiz.q: Which technique BEST addresses the non-determinism of generative AI during an audit?
o: Running each test once on the latest model version to save time
Repeating tests many times with pinned versions and assessing rates
Accepting the vendor’s published test results for each model version
Setting temperature to zero, which makes generative outputs fully repeatable
quiz.why: Because outputs vary, single runs prove little, and even temperature 0 doesn’t guarantee identical outputs. Repeated runs against pinned versions give rates that can be compared with thresholds.

exam.q: A bank assigns HOTL supervision of an automated fraud-blocking model to one analyst, who also handles 150 customer calls a day. Blocked-account complaints rise for weeks before anyone acts. What is the MOST significant governance flaw?
o: The model’s blocking threshold was set too high, so too many genuine customers were blocked
Oversight was assigned without the time, alerting and authority needed to supervise effectively
Customers complained too much, which made genuine fraud alerts harder for the analyst to spot
The model should have been human-in-the-loop for every decision, however small the amount involved
exam.why: HOTL needs real-time visibility, meaningful alerts and people with capacity and authority to intervene. Nominal oversight by an overloaded analyst provides no protection.

exam.q: Who should normally hold sign-off authority for deploying a tier-3 (high-risk) AI system to production?
o: The developer who built it, who best understands its design and limitations
The governance committee or a designated senior owner, after required assessments and tests
The business users of the system, who will be accountable for its day-to-day outcomes and benefits
The cloud provider hosting the model, which is responsible for its production environment
exam.why: Sign-off authority must match the risk tier and be independent of the builders, with evidence that prerequisites are met.

exam.q: Secret scanning finds an API key for an external model in a sales team’s repository. The key is used by an unregistered agent that reads customer emails. What should happen FIRST?
o: Delete the repository and the agent’s code, then investigate who created them
Rotate the exposed key, then register, tier and assess the agent before it continues
Leave the agent running, since sales depends on it, and add it to next quarter’s review
Move the key to a private repository and ask the sales team to register the agent soon
exam.why: An exposed credential must be rotated immediately. The agent then needs to come under governance, with an inventory entry, tier and assessment, because it processes customer data.

exam.q: An auditor asks why a high-risk model was deployed without the required adversarial test. The team says the CTO verbally agreed. What does this reveal?
o: Nothing significant; verbal approval from a senior executive is sufficient for a one-off deviation
A missing exception record: deviations need justification, compensating controls, an approver and expiry
The auditor lacks the authority to question decisions approved by members of the executive leadership team
Adversarial testing is optional for high-risk models, so long as the CTO agrees the risk is low
exam.why: Undocumented deviations can’t be verified, reviewed or closed. Exception records make deviations visible, controlled and time-bound.

exam.q: A company uses AI to generate a realistic video of its CEO for a marketing campaign shown in the EU. What is required?
o: No disclosure, because the CEO consented to the use of their likeness in the campaign
Disclosure that the content is AI-generated or manipulated, plus machine-readable marking
Registration of the video in the EU database as the output of a high-risk AI system
Prior approval of the video from the data protection authority in each EU country
exam.why: Content resembling real people is a deepfake under Article 50. Deployers must disclose it, and generative systems must mark outputs. Consent doesn’t remove the transparency duty.

exam.q: An organisation’s annual AI audit keeps finding that drift had gone unnoticed for months. Which change BEST addresses this?
o: Audit every two years instead, with a larger sample of systems examined in much more depth on each occasion
Introduce continuous auditing using monitoring data and automated control checks, plus periodic reviews
Remove drift from the audit scope, since drift is a model quality issue rather than a control failure
Rely on vendor assurances about drift monitoring, since vendors have the best view of their models
exam.why: AI systems change between periodic audits. Continuous auditing detects control failures, such as missed drift alerts, much sooner.

quiz.q: Which assessment method gives the MOST reliable picture of a reviewer’s ability to oversee an AI system?
o: Self-rating questionnaires about confidence with AI
Practical exercises reviewing realistic AI outputs for errors and bias
Course completion records for mandatory AI training
Years of experience in the role, in the organisation and with similar AI systems
quiz.why: Practical exercises show what people can actually do. Self-ratings tend to be optimistic, and completion records show attendance only.

quiz.q: In a skills gap analysis, how should gaps be prioritised?
o: By how many people in each team lack AI training
By the risk of the AI-related decisions and activities each role performs
By the size of each team, so the largest groups are trained first
By seniority, starting with executives and working down to front-line staff
quiz.why: Gaps among people overseeing high-impact systems, building agents or handling regulated data carry the most risk.

quiz.q: What does Article 4 of the EU AI Act expect of providers and deployers?
o: That every employee who uses AI holds a recognised AI certification
That they take measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others using AI for them
That AI training is delivered by accredited trainers approved by the national regulator
That staff complete a fixed number of hours of AI training each year, recorded centrally
quiz.why: Article 4, as amended by the 2026 Omnibus, requires measures to support AI literacy, taking into account people’s knowledge, experience and context of use.

quiz.q: Which training is MOST appropriate for ML engineers building agents with tool access?
o: A general video on what AI is and how large language models work
Hands-on labs in threat modelling, secure tool integration and least privilege
A board-level briefing on the organisation’s AI risk appetite and governance
Annual phishing awareness training, refreshed with examples of AI-written emails
quiz.why: Builders need practical, role-specific skills for the risks they create, such as excessive agency and insecure tool integration.

quiz.q: Which feature MOST improves the behavioural impact of AI awareness training?
o: A single comprehensive annual course that covers every AI policy in depth
Short, scenario-based, role-specific content with just-in-time prompts at the point of use
Generic content identical for all roles, so that every employee hears the same message
Content that stays unchanged from year to year, so staff can easily compare their progress
quiz.why: Practical, contextual and frequent training changes behaviour; one-off generic courses rarely do.

quiz.q: In the Kirkpatrick model, which level measures whether people apply what they learned at work?
o: Level 1: Reaction
Level 2: Learning
Level 3: Behaviour
Level 4: Results
quiz.why: Level 3 measures on-the-job behaviour, for example DLP events or use of sanctioned tools; level 4 measures organisational results.

quiz.q: After an AI awareness campaign, reports of AI near misses rise sharply. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: The campaign increased risk by encouraging more staff to experiment with AI tools
Improved recognition and trust in reporting, a sign of a healthier safety culture
The reporting system is malfunctioning and logging the same events more than once
Staff are over-reporting minor issues to show compliance with the new campaign
quiz.why: More reporting typically reflects better awareness and psychological safety; incidents were probably happening before but went unreported.

quiz.q: Which is a leading indicator of AI security risk among staff?
o: The number of regulatory fines received last year
The share of AI use going through sanctioned tools
The total cost of the most recent AI incident
The number of findings in last year’s audit report
quiz.why: Leading indicators predict future risk. Sanctioned-tool adoption signals reduced shadow-AI exposure; fines, costs and past findings are lagging.

exam.q: An organisation plans AI training for 8,000 staff but has a limited budget. A gap analysis shows the most serious gaps among 40 claims reviewers who oversee a high-impact AI model. What is the BEST plan?
o: Spread the budget evenly across all 8,000 staff, so everyone receives the same training standard
Prioritise intensive, practical training for the 40 reviewers, with lighter awareness for everyone else
Train executives first, so that leadership can cascade AI knowledge down through the organisation
Delay training until the budget increases, so the programme can be delivered properly to all staff
exam.why: Risk-based prioritisation focuses resources where gaps matter most, while still providing baseline awareness for all staff.

exam.q: A company’s AI training is a single 60-minute generic module each year. Shadow AI and data-leak events remain high. Which change is MOST likely to help?
o: Extend the annual module to 120 minutes, so that it covers every AI policy and approved tool in much more detail
Role-specific, scenario-based modules, just-in-time prompts in AI tools, and an approved tool with guidance
Remove training and rely on blocking every unapproved AI website at the network perimeter
Require staff to re-sign the AI policy twice a year, with managers tracking who has not signed
exam.why: Behaviour changes when training is relevant, practical and delivered at the point of use, and when people have a sanctioned alternative.

exam.q: The board asks for evidence that the AI security awareness programme reduces risk. Which report BEST answers the question?
o: Course completion of 99% across the organisation, with all overdue staff followed up by managers
Trends in AI data events, simulation results and human-caused incidents against the pre-programme baseline
Average satisfaction of 4.7 out of 5, with most staff saying the training was relevant to their role
The number of training sessions delivered, broken down by business unit, region and job family
exam.why: Behaviour and results measures, against a baseline, show whether risk changed. Completion, satisfaction and activity counts don’t.

exam.q: A manager proposes disciplining every employee who reports pasting confidential data into an AI tool by mistake. What is the MOST likely effect?
o: Fewer actual incidents, because staff will become more careful
Fewer reports while incidents continue unseen, harming culture and metrics
Better training completion, because staff will want to avoid disciplinary action
Little effect, because most employees already report mistakes voluntarily
exam.why: Punishing self-reporting drives incidents underground. A no-blame reporting route, combined with coaching and technical controls, preserves visibility.

quiz.q: Who should approve the use of a dataset to fine-tune a model?
o: The data custodian
The dataset’s data owner
Any data scientist on the project
The model vendor
quiz.why: The data owner is accountable for permitted uses of the data. Custodians operate controls on the owner’s behalf.

quiz.q: A model provider uses customers’ prompts to train its own future models. What is its GDPR role for that processing?
o: Processor
Controller
Data subject
Custodian
quiz.why: Using data for its own purposes means the provider determines purposes and means, so it acts as a controller for that processing.

quiz.q: Which term describes a legal requirement that certain data must remain within a country’s borders?
o: Data residency
Data localisation
Data minimisation
Data stewardship
quiz.why: Localisation is a legal mandate. Residency is where data actually sits, often chosen to satisfy localisation or sovereignty concerns.

quiz.q: Which AI-specific factor is MOST often overlooked when assessing cross-border data transfers?
o: The location of the provider’s head office and the law of its contract
Where inference happens, including failover regions and abuse-monitoring logs
The number of users in each country who will have access to the AI system
The model’s parameter count, which determines which export rules apply
quiz.why: Prompts may be processed or logged in other regions, including during failover, which can create unplanned transfers.

quiz.q: What classification should embeddings generated from Confidential documents normally receive?
o: Public, because embeddings can’t be read by people
Internal, one level below their source documents
Confidential, the same as their source documents
Unclassified until a separate assessment is completed
quiz.why: Derived artefacts inherit their source classification; embeddings can be partly inverted and are used to retrieve the original text.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN purpose of a sensitive data impact assessment for AI?
o: To estimate the dataset’s commercial value before it is licensed to a third party
To assess purpose fit, derivation risks and safeguards before sensitive data is used in AI
To replace the DPIA and other assessments with a single AI-specific review document
To label every file in the dataset manually with its sensitivity and retention period
quiz.why: An SDIA examines whether and how sensitive data can safely be used for an AI purpose, and sets conditions.

quiz.q: Which record shows which models were trained on a particular dataset version?
o: Provenance
Lineage records
A retention schedule
A classification label
quiz.why: Lineage tracks the flow from sources through transformations and dataset versions to training runs and models.

quiz.q: What should provenance for a synthetic dataset include?
o: Nothing; synthetic data is generated rather than collected, so it has no provenance to record
The generator model and version, seed data and its provenance, parameters and validation results
Only the file size, record count and date of generation, which identify each synthetic dataset
Only the name of the team that generated it, which is enough to answer any later questions about it
quiz.why: Synthetic data’s trustworthiness depends on how it was generated and validated, including the source of its seed data.

quiz.q: Which control BEST proves a dataset was not altered between two custodians?
o: A signed letter from each custodian confirming the data is unchanged
Matching cryptographic hashes or signatures recorded at each hand-off
Identical file names, sizes and timestamps at each stage of the transfer
Compressing the dataset into a password-protected archive before transfer
quiz.why: Hashes and signatures provide tamper evidence; recorded at each hand-off, they form the chain of custody.

quiz.q: At which lifecycle stage is poisoned or corrupted data cheapest to stop?
o: After deployment, when monitoring reveals unusual outputs
During collection and validation, before any training begins
During model retirement, when all the training data is archived
During the annual audit of the model’s training pipeline
quiz.why: Catching bad data before it is trained into a model avoids costly retraining and incident response.

quiz.q: Who should be able to edit or delete entries in the chain-of-custody log for a training dataset?
o: The data custodian, who keeps the log accurate as transfers happen
No one: entries are append-only and protected from those they record
Any data scientist who handled the dataset during a training run
The vendor that labelled the data, since it knows what it changed
quiz.why: A custody log is only trustworthy if it is append-only and tamper-evident, protected even from the administrators and custodians whose actions it records. Corrections are added as new entries.

quiz.q: A labelled dataset arrives from a supplier, and its hash doesn’t match the value recorded when it was sent. What should happen FIRST?
o: Recompute the hash on a faster machine and use the new value instead
Quarantine it and investigate the cause before it is used for training
Use it for training, but flag the resulting model for later review
Ask the supplier to resend a hash value that matches the received file
quiz.why: A mismatch means the data changed in transit or at rest, through corruption or tampering. Quarantine stops it reaching training until the cause is known. Replacing the expected hash would defeat the control.

exam.q: A data science team wants to reuse three years of customer call transcripts, collected for quality assurance, to train a sales-recommendation model. What should happen FIRST?
o: Start training, since the data is already held in-house and was lawfully collected from customers
Get the data owner’s approval for the new purpose, backed by a privacy assessment of compatibility and basis
Ask the data custodian to copy the transcripts to the training cluster, with access restricted to the team
Anonymise a sample of the transcripts, check the results, and proceed if no names remain in the sample
exam.why: Reuse for a new purpose needs the owner’s decision and an assessment of compatibility and lawful basis. Being in-house doesn’t make a new purpose lawful.

exam.q: A public-sector client requires that its data never leaves the UK. The AI service’s standard configuration routes requests to the nearest available region worldwide. What is the BEST approach?
o: Accept the routing, since all requests are encrypted in transit and the provider is certified
Restrict processing, logging and failover to UK regions in contract and configuration, and verify it
Tell users to work only during UK business hours, when the nearest available region is in the UK
Store all outputs and logs in the UK only, since stored data is what the residency requirement covers
exam.why: Residency must cover processing, logging and failover, not just storage of outputs, and must be verified. Encryption doesn’t change where data is processed.

exam.q: A RAG pipeline splits labelled documents into chunks, but the chunks lose their sensitivity labels. Users start receiving restricted content in answers. What is the root cause and BEST fix?
o: The model is too large and memorises restricted content, so switch to a smaller model
Labels weren’t carried into chunks; propagate labels to the index and filter retrieval by clearance
Users asked questions outside their role, so retrain them on acceptable use of the assistant
The documents were over-classified, so relabel them at a lower level to match how they are used
exam.why: Without labels on chunks, retrieval can’t enforce access. Propagating labels and filtering retrieval fixes the cause.

exam.q: After a supplier reveals that one of its datasets included scraped content without permission, an organisation must find every affected model. Which capability is MOST important?
o: A data classification policy that labels every dataset by sensitivity
Lineage linking source datasets and versions to training runs and model versions
Encryption at rest for every training dataset and model artefact
Model cards for every model, describing its intended use, training data and known limitations
exam.why: Lineage traces each dataset forward to every model it influenced, enabling targeted retraining or withdrawal.

exam.q: A team proposes replacing sensitive customer data with synthetic data and reclassifying it as Public. What should happen before reclassification?
o: Nothing; synthetic data contains no real people, so it can safely be reclassified as soon as it has been generated
Test for leakage of real records, evaluate fidelity and bias, record provenance, and get the owner’s approval
Delete the original customer data first, so that the synthetic dataset can’t be linked back to it
Publish a sample of the synthetic data internally to see whether anyone recognises real customers
exam.why: Generators can memorise and reproduce real records. Privacy, fidelity and bias must be validated, and the owner must approve any reclassification.

exam.q: A customer’s erasure request is fulfilled in the CRM, but their data remains in a fine-tuning dataset, a vector index and backups. Which practice would have prevented this?
o: Encrypting the CRM and every downstream copy with the same customer-specific key, held centrally
Lineage-driven deletion propagation covering datasets, indexes, models, backups and vendors
Annual privacy training for staff who handle erasure requests and customer records
A written erasure procedure for the CRM team, reviewed by the DPO every year
exam.why: Deletion must follow data downstream. Lineage identifies every copy and derived artefact, so deletion can be propagated and verified.

exam.q: Investigators find that a poisoned dataset reached production. Custody records show it passed through three teams, but its integrity was checked just once, when it first arrived from the supplier. What is the MOST important improvement?
o: Reduce the number of teams, so fewer hand-offs need any records
Hash and verify the data at every hand-off, before each team uses it
Encrypt the dataset in transit between each of the three teams
Ask each team to confirm in writing that it changed nothing
exam.why: Hashing and verifying at every hand-off pinpoints where data changed and stops altered data moving on. Encryption in transit protects data on the wire, not changes made while a team holds it, and written assurances prove nothing.

quiz.q: Under GDPR Article 25, what does data protection by default require?
o: Privacy-protective settings must be available for users who choose to switch them on
By default, only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed
All personal data must be encrypted by default, wherever it is stored or sent
Default passwords on systems that process personal data must be changed before use
quiz.why: By default means protection applies without the person doing anything: only necessary data, limited access and limited retention. Optional privacy features and encryption alone don’t meet the requirement.

quiz.q: A retailer collected purchase data to fulfil orders. It now wants to train a model that infers customers’ health conditions from what they buy. Which principle is MOST directly at stake?
o: Storage limitation, because order data would be kept for longer than needed
Purpose limitation, because inferring health is a new and incompatible purpose
Accuracy, because some of the inferred conditions might turn out to be wrong
Integrity, because the model might be tampered with after it is deployed
quiz.why: Inferring health conditions is unrelated to fulfilling orders, and it creates special category data. It needs its own assessment and lawful basis; the other principles matter but are secondary.

quiz.q: Where consent is the lawful basis for training a model on personal data, which statement is correct?
o: Consent can be included in the general terms of service if they are clearly written
Consent must be specific, informed and unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give
Consent stays valid indefinitely once given, even if the training purpose changes
Pre-ticked boxes are acceptable if the privacy notice explains the training use
quiz.why: GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative act, and withdrawable at any time. Bundled terms, pre-ticked boxes and open-ended consent all fail.

quiz.q: Which statement about pseudonymised data under the GDPR is correct?
o: It is anonymous once direct identifiers are replaced, so the GDPR no longer applies
It remains personal data for a controller who holds the means to re-identify it
It may be published freely, provided the re-identification key is encrypted
It is a category defined only for health and genetic data used in clinical research
quiz.why: Pseudonymisation is a safeguard, not anonymisation. Whoever can re-identify the data, using a key or other information, is processing personal data.

quiz.q: In differential privacy, what does choosing a smaller epsilon (ε) do?
o: Adds less noise, giving more accurate results and weaker privacy
Adds more noise, giving stronger privacy and less accurate results
Removes noise entirely once enough records have been collected
Shrinks the dataset so that fewer records need to be protected
quiz.why: ε bounds how much any one person’s data can change the output. A smaller ε needs more noise, which strengthens privacy and reduces accuracy.

quiz.q: An organisation uses unsalted SHA-256 hashes of customers’ phone numbers as identifiers in a shared dataset. What is the MAIN weakness?
o: SHA-256 is too slow to compute for large datasets of phone numbers
Phone numbers are predictable, so hashing every possible number reverses them
Hashed values can’t be joined with other datasets for analysis
SHA-256 hashes are too long to store efficiently in most databases and analytics tools
quiz.why: The set of possible phone numbers is small enough to enumerate. Use a keyed hash (HMAC) or tokenisation, with the key held separately, and treat the result as pseudonymous personal data.

quiz.q: Which technique lets authorised payment systems recover card numbers while keeping them out of AI and analytics pipelines?
o: Generalising card numbers into ranges
Vaulted tokenisation of card numbers
Differential privacy on transactions
Suppressing the card number field
quiz.why: Tokenisation replaces card numbers with tokens downstream, while the vault lets a small set of authorised systems detokenise. Generalisation, noise and suppression can’t recover the original.

quiz.q: Under the GDPR, when must a controller normally notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach?
o: Within 24 hours of the breach occurring, in every case
Within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless unlikely to result in risk
Within 60 days of discovery, in line with the deadline for HIPAA breaches
Only once affected individuals have already been told
quiz.why: Article 33 requires notification without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people.

quiz.q: Which statement about PCI DSS is correct?
o: It is a US federal law enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and state regulators
It is an industry standard enforced through card brands and acquirers
It applies only to banks that issue payment cards to consumers
It allows card security codes to be stored if they are encrypted
quiz.why: PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard. It applies to any entity that stores, processes or transmits card data, and it prohibits storing sensitive authentication data after authorisation, even encrypted.

quiz.q: Which HIPAA de-identification method relies on a qualified expert’s documented statistical analysis?
o: Safe Harbor
Expert Determination
Limited data set
Minimum necessary review
quiz.why: Expert Determination uses a qualified expert to conclude that re-identification risk is very small. Safe Harbor removes 18 identifier types instead.

quiz.q: A person’s data was used to fine-tune a large model, and they ask for erasure. Which option gives the HIGHEST assurance that the model no longer reflects their data?
o: Adding an output filter that blocks responses naming the person
Retraining the model on a dataset with their records fully removed
Applying an approximate unlearning method to the existing weights
Lowering the model’s temperature so it is less likely to regurgitate
quiz.why: A retrained model has never seen the data. Approximate unlearning is hard to verify, filters leave the data in the weights, and temperature changes remove nothing.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes a model’s prediction that an identifiable person has a particular health condition?
o: It isn’t personal data, because the person never provided it
It is personal data, and can be special category data too
It belongs to the model provider as intellectual property
It is anonymous, because it is only a statistical estimate
quiz.why: Inferences about identifiable people are personal data, and an inferred health condition is special category data, whether or not the inference is accurate.

quiz.q: A count is released with the Laplace mechanism at ε = 1. The analyst now wants to release it at ε = 0.25 instead. How does the noise change?
o: Its scale shrinks to a quarter of its size
Its scale grows fourfold, from 1 to 4
Its scale doubles, as it depends on √ε
It is unchanged; only δ is affected
quiz.why: The Laplace noise scale is sensitivity ÷ ε. For a count, the sensitivity is 1, so the scale rises from 1 to 4 as ε falls from 1 to 0.25: more noise, stronger privacy.

quiz.q: A health service releases one private statistic per region, each at ε = 0.5. Every patient belongs to exactly one region. What is the total privacy loss for any one patient?
o: ε = 0.5 multiplied by the number of regions
ε = 0.5, because the regions don’t overlap
ε = 1, the usual cap for any two releases
Unknown, since separate releases can’t be bounded
quiz.why: Under parallel composition, releases computed on disjoint groups of people cost only the largest ε, because each person’s data affects just one release.

quiz.q: What does the per-example gradient clipping step in DP-SGD achieve?
o: It removes duplicate records before each training step
It caps how much any single record can change each update
It encrypts the gradients so the server can’t read them
It stops the learning rate from becoming too large
quiz.why: Clipping bounds each example’s contribution, which sets the sensitivity that the Gaussian noise must hide. De-duplication, encryption and learning rate limits are separate matters.

quiz.q: A vendor’s differential privacy guarantee protects each record, but some customers contribute thousands of records each. What is the concern?
o: Those customers are protected more, since their records are averaged
Those customers are protected far less than the stated ε suggests
The guarantee is void unless every customer contributes one record
The guarantee applies, but only to the most recent record of each
quiz.why: Record-level protection weakens for people with many records, because their combined influence can be much larger than one record’s. User-level differential privacy protects everything a person contributes.

exam.q: A bank’s marketing team wants to reuse customer service chat transcripts, collected to resolve complaints, to fine-tune a model that writes personalised sales offers. The privacy notice mentions only complaint handling. What should the privacy lead recommend FIRST?
o: Proceed, since the bank already holds the transcripts lawfully and the fine-tuned model will stay in-house
Run a DPIA covering purpose compatibility and lawful basis, then update notices and offer opt-out or consent as needed
Strip names and account numbers from the transcripts and proceed, since de-identified free text falls entirely outside the GDPR
Ask the vendor to confirm in writing that the fine-tuning data won’t be used to improve its other models
exam.why: Marketing is a new purpose that needs a compatibility assessment and a lawful basis. Removing names doesn’t anonymise free-text transcripts, holding data lawfully for one purpose doesn’t cover another, and vendor terms address a different risk.

exam.q: A health research team plans to publish a dataset of patient visits with names removed but full postcodes, dates of birth and visit dates retained. What is the BEST assessment?
o: The dataset is anonymous, because names and record numbers have been removed and no direct identifiers remain
Postcodes, birth dates and visit dates allow linkage; generalise or suppress them and assess risk before release
The dataset can be published safely if downloaders must register and agree not to attempt re-identification
The dataset can be published once the file is encrypted and the key is sent only to approved researchers
exam.why: Combinations of quasi-identifiers single out most people. Generalisation, suppression or differential privacy, plus a re-identification risk assessment, are needed. Registration terms help but don’t anonymise, and encryption protects confidentiality, not identifiability.

exam.q: A company wants to publish weekly statistics on how staff use its internal AI assistant, broken down by department, without revealing any individual’s behaviour. Some departments have only three or four people. Which approach BEST meets the goal?
o: Publish exact counts for every department, since the statistics contain no names or employee identifiers
Apply differential privacy to the statistics, tracking the total privacy budget spent across weekly releases
Round every count to the nearest ten before publishing, which hides each individual’s behaviour each week
Share the department-level figures only with senior managers, who are trusted not to misuse them
exam.why: Small groups make exact or rounded counts revealing, and repeated releases compound the risk. Differential privacy gives a provable limit per release, and an accountant tracks the cumulative loss. Rounding offers no guarantee and can be undone by comparing releases.

exam.q: A European retailer uses an AI model to reject online credit applications automatically below a score threshold, with no human review. A rejected applicant asks why. Which response BEST meets GDPR requirements?
o: Decline to explain, because the scoring model is a trade secret that the retailer is entitled to protect in full
Explain the main factors and logic involved, and offer human review and a clear way to contest the decision
Confirm the decision was made by a validated algorithm, which on its own meets the GDPR’s transparency duty
Offer a manual reapplication route instead, since Article 22 only applies to decisions made by public bodies
exam.why: A solely automated credit refusal falls under Article 22. The applicant is entitled to meaningful information about the logic involved, and to safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest. Trade secrets can’t justify a blanket refusal.

exam.q: A retailer’s new voice assistant takes phone orders and records every call for model improvement. Customers read out their card number and security code during the call. What is the MOST important change?
o: Encrypt the call recordings with strong keys, which makes it acceptable to retain the security codes they contain
Keep card data out of recordings with keypad entry or pause-and-resume, and purge any stored security codes
Restrict access to the recordings to the data science team that uses them for model training and evaluation
Keep the recordings for no more than 12 months before deletion, in line with the retailer’s retention schedule
exam.why: PCI DSS prohibits storing sensitive authentication data after authorisation, even when encrypted. The fix is to stop capturing it and remove what has been stored; access limits and retention schedules don’t make the storage permissible.

exam.q: A lender’s data scientists want to check whether their credit model treats ethnic groups differently, but the training data contains no ethnicity information. The DPO is concerned about minimisation. What is the BEST approach?
o: Abandon fairness testing, because collecting ethnicity data for any purpose would breach the minimisation principle
Use ethnicity data for testing only where strictly necessary, under a legal basis, segregated, then delete it
Add ethnicity as a permanent model input, so that the model can learn to correct for any bias automatically
Infer each applicant’s ethnicity from their name and postcode, and keep it on file for future credit decisions
exam.why: Bias can’t be measured without group information, but sensitive data should be used only where strictly necessary, with a legal basis and safeguards, and deleted afterwards. The EU AI Act provides for this. Using ethnicity in decisions, or keeping inferred ethnicity, creates new risks.

exam.q: An AI assistant repeatedly tells users that a named private individual has a criminal conviction. This is false, and the individual complains. What should the provider do FIRST?
o: Explain that outputs are probabilistic predictions, so the GDPR’s accuracy principle doesn’t apply to model outputs
Suppress false outputs about them now, fix any grounding sources, investigate, and answer the rectification request
Begin a full retraining of the model, and reply to the complaint only once the new version is deployed
Ask the individual to provide proof of a clean criminal record before considering any change to outputs
exam.why: False personal data in outputs engages the accuracy principle and the right to rectification. Immediate suppression limits ongoing harm while the cause is fixed; waiting for retraining or demanding proof leaves the harm in place.

exam.q: A product team plans to let analysts run unlimited differentially private queries against an HR dataset, each at ε = 0.1, with no record kept of how many have been run. What is the MOST significant problem?
o: An ε of 0.1 adds too little noise to protect anyone in the dataset
Repeated queries add up, so the overall privacy loss has no upper bound
Analysts could see the noise values and subtract them from results
Each query must use a different noise mechanism to remain private
exam.why: Privacy loss composes: with unlimited queries the total ε grows without limit, and averaging repeated answers can cancel the noise. A privacy accountant must track and cap the budget.

exam.q: A data scientist tuned DP-SGD hyperparameters by training 40 models on the private dataset, then reported the ε of the final run only. What should the privacy reviewer conclude?
o: The ε is accurate, since only the final model will ever be deployed
The ε is understated, as tuning on the private data also spends budget
The ε is overstated, since the earlier runs were all discarded
The ε is irrelevant, as DP-SGD protects privacy regardless of settings
exam.why: Every training run on the private data leaks information, including through the choice of the best run. Tuning must be included in the accounting, or done on public or separate data.

exam.q: A team releases a differentially private model. It then publishes an adjusted version, derived only from the private model’s weights and public data, with no further access to the training data. What happens to the privacy budget?
o: The budget doubles, since a second model has now been released
No extra budget is spent, as post-processing can’t weaken the guarantee
The guarantee is lost, since the model was modified after training
The new version needs a fresh budget, set by the team that adjusted it
exam.why: Anything computed from a differentially private output without touching the private data again is post-processing, so it keeps the original guarantee at no extra cost.

quiz.q: What does integrity mean for AI training data?
o: The data is encrypted at rest and in transit at every stage of the pipeline
The data is accurate, complete and free from unauthorised modification
The data is available to every team that needs it, without delay
The data is anonymised so that no individual can ever be identified
quiz.why: Integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and protection from unauthorised change. Encryption, availability and anonymisation address other properties.

quiz.q: Why is separation of duties important for training data?
o: It lets one expert both make and approve changes quickly, reducing delays
It stops one person from both changing training data and approving it for use
It ensures that every dataset is stored in two separate geographic regions
It divides training data into separate training, validation and test sets
quiz.why: Separating the ability to change data from the authority to approve it means a single insider or compromised account can’t silently alter what models learn.

quiz.q: Which practice MOST directly ensures a model is trained on exactly the dataset that was approved?
o: Storing all datasets on encrypted disks with regular, tested backups held in a second region
Pinning the run to a dataset version by content hash and verifying its signed manifest
Giving every data scientist write access so problems can be fixed quickly
Naming each dataset folder with the date it was approved by its owner
quiz.why: A content hash changes if any data changes, and verifying a signed manifest at training time blocks unapproved versions. Names and backups prove nothing about content.

quiz.q: Which type of poisoning is HARDEST to detect through normal accuracy testing?
o: Availability poisoning
Backdoor poisoning
Random label noise
Train–test leakage
quiz.why: A backdoored model behaves normally unless the trigger appears, so it passes standard evaluations. Availability poisoning shows up as lower accuracy.

quiz.q: What did a 2025 study find about the number of poisoned documents needed to backdoor LLMs of different sizes?
o: It rose in proportion to model size, so the largest models were effectively immune
It stayed roughly constant, so the poisoned share of data fell as models grew
It fell to zero for the largest models, which developed backdoors on their own
It depended only on the number of training epochs, not on the poisoned data
quiz.why: Around 250 documents sufficed across models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters, so poison isn’t diluted by more clean data.

quiz.q: Which factor MOST increases the likelihood that a model memorises a specific piece of training text?
o: The text being written in a formal, professional style
The text appearing many times in the training data
The text being placed near the end of the training dataset
The text being stored in a compressed file format
quiz.why: Duplication is one of the strongest drivers of memorisation, which is why de-duplication is a key control. Model size and uniqueness also matter.

quiz.q: What distinguishes training data extraction from model extraction?
o: Training data extraction steals the model’s weights, while model extraction steals its training data
Training data extraction recovers what a model learned from; model extraction copies the model
They are two names for the same attack against hosted model APIs
Training data extraction needs physical access; model extraction works only remotely
quiz.why: Training data extraction targets the data behind a model; model extraction replicates the model’s functionality or weights (Module 3.6).

quiz.q: Which control BEST detects an annotator who is deliberately mislabelling items?
o: Paying annotators per item, so that they have a strong incentive to work quickly
Mixing in gold-standard items and comparing each annotator with the consensus
Letting annotators approve their own work to reduce the review workload
Encrypting the labels at rest inside the annotation platform’s database
quiz.why: Gold items and consensus comparison reveal annotators whose labels are systematically wrong. Self-approval and encryption don’t detect manipulation.

quiz.q: Why are some dataset and model file formats a security risk to load?
o: They are too large to scan with standard antivirus and endpoint tools
Some serialisation formats can execute code when the file is loaded
They can’t be compressed, so they consume excessive storage
They store data in plain text, which anyone can read
quiz.why: Formats such as Python pickle can run arbitrary code on load. Prefer safe formats, or load files only inside an isolated sandbox.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST prevents model collapse when using synthetic data?
o: Replacing human data with synthetic data each generation, to keep the data fresh
Accumulating real human data alongside a capped, labelled share of synthetic data
Generating the synthetic data with the same model that will be trained on it
Filtering synthetic data with an AI judge and discarding the human originals
quiz.why: Research shows collapse is avoided when real data accumulates rather than being replaced. Capping and labelling synthetic data keeps it controllable.

quiz.q: Which is the BEST evidence that a synthetic dataset protects privacy?
o: The generator vendor’s statement that its outputs contain no personal data
Tests showing no near-duplicates of real records and low membership inference risk
The fact that every record was produced by a model rather than collected
A visual review of 50 records by the data science team, which found no names or addresses
quiz.why: Generators can memorise seed data, so privacy must be tested, not assumed. Vendor statements and small manual reviews are weak evidence.

exam.q: A fraud team discovers that a contractor with write access to the training data store altered several thousand historical labels before leaving. Which control would MOST likely have stopped the altered data reaching production models?
o: Annual security awareness training for contractors on the acceptable use of training data
Immutable approved snapshots, separation of duties, and training jobs that verify signed manifests
Encryption of the training data store at rest, with keys held by the security team
Exit interviews for departing contractors, with a signed statement that no training data was changed
exam.why: Immutable approved versions and manifest verification make unauthorised changes detectable and unusable, and separation of duties removes the single point of abuse. Encryption doesn’t stop an authorised user, and training and exit statements don’t prevent tampering.

exam.q: An image classifier that screens uploaded documents performs normally in testing, but a red team finds that any image with a small logo in one corner is always classed as “safe”. What is the MOST likely cause and BEST response?
o: Overfitting to the test set; collect more test images and re-run the standard evaluation
A backdoor from poisoned training data; trace lineage, retrain from verified data and add trigger testing
Concept drift in uploaded documents; lower the classification threshold for every image
An availability attack on the screening service; add servers so the classifier can handle the extra load
exam.why: Normal behaviour except when a specific pattern is present is the hallmark of a backdoor. Lineage finds the poisoned data and affected models; retraining from verified data removes it; trigger testing guards against recurrence.

exam.q: A law firm fine-tuned an LLM on its case files. Testers find the model sometimes reproduces client names and case details verbatim when asked about similar matters. Which response is MOST appropriate?
o: Raise the temperature so the model paraphrases rather than repeating text word for word
Restrict the model, add output filters, then retrain on minimised, de-duplicated data with privacy tests
Add a disclaimer that outputs may contain confidential information, and continue using the model as before
Move the model to a larger GPU cluster so that it can handle the longer context of case files
exam.why: Verbatim reproduction is memorisation of confidential data. Containment and output filtering limit immediate harm; retraining on minimised, de-duplicated data with extraction and membership tests addresses the cause. Temperature changes don’t remove memorised data.

exam.q: An ML engineer downloads a dataset from a public hub that ships with a custom loader script. The script requests network access while loading. What should happen?
o: Run the script on a workstation with antivirus enabled, since antivirus will block anything malicious
Stop: review the script, and load in an isolated sandbox without network access or use a safe-format copy
Run the script as normal, since the hub hosts thousands of datasets and scans everything uploaded
Allow the network access but log it, so that any data the script sends out can be reviewed later
exam.why: Loader scripts are code from an untrusted source, and unexpected network access is a red flag. Review and isolation, or a safe-format alternative, prevent code execution and exfiltration.

exam.q: After an incident, investigators must show exactly which data trained a model that is now in production. Which capability is MOST critical?
o: A naming convention that includes the training date and the responsible data scientist’s initials
Content-hashed dataset versions linked to training runs and model versions in a registry
Daily backups of the training data store, kept for 30 days in a second region
A wiki page on which each team describes the datasets it generally uses for training
exam.why: Only content-addressed versions linked through lineage prove what a specific model was trained on. Names, backups and wiki pages can’t demonstrate the exact data.

exam.q: A vendor offers a cheap synthetic dataset of “realistic customer records” for training a fraud model, but gives no information about how it was generated. What should the security lead require BEFORE use?
o: A discount, since synthetic data carries no privacy obligations and is worth less than real data
Generator provenance and seed data details, plus fidelity, privacy and bias validation results
Confirmation that the dataset is larger than the organisation’s own real transaction history
A guarantee that the records were generated recently, so they reflect current fraud patterns
exam.why: Without provenance and validation, synthetic data may leak real records, miss the rare cases fraud models need, or carry the generator’s biases and flaws.

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of data security posture management (DSPM)?
o: To block sensitive data as it leaves the network, in real time
To discover and classify data stores and assess who can reach them
To check cloud infrastructure against configuration benchmarks
To encrypt every data store automatically with customer-managed keys
quiz.why: DSPM is data-centric: it finds and classifies data, maps access and prioritises exposure. Real-time blocking is DLP; configuration checks are CSPM.

quiz.q: Which AI-related store is MOST often missed when inventorying sensitive data?
o: The production customer database behind the main application
Prompt and response logs kept by AI applications and gateways
The finance team’s accounting system and its nightly backups
The HR system that holds employee contracts and pay records
quiz.why: Prompt and response logs often hold large volumes of sensitive data outside normal controls, and are frequently overlooked.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN advantage of semantic filtering over pattern-based DLP for AI prompts?
o: It is faster and cheaper to run on every single request
It can recognise sensitive meaning in paraphrased or summarised text
It never produces false positives on legitimate business content
It works without any policy decisions about what counts as sensitive
quiz.why: Semantic filters judge meaning, so they catch sensitive content that patterns miss. They are slower and costlier, and still produce false positives.

quiz.q: In a “tokenise and restore” DLP pattern for an external model, what happens?
o: The model provider stores the real values and returns only tokens to users
Sensitive values are swapped for tokens before the model and restored in the response
The prompt is encrypted end to end, so that the model can’t read any part of it at all
All sensitive prompts are blocked, and the user is asked to rewrite them
quiz.why: Tokens replace sensitive values on the way out, so the external model never sees them, and the gateway restores the real values in the response.

quiz.q: Which control protects data while it is being processed by an AI model on a cloud host?
o: Full-disk encryption on the host’s storage volumes
A trusted execution environment with verified attestation
TLS 1.3 between the client and the model endpoint
Encrypted backups of the model, its weights and its configuration
quiz.why: Data in use is protected by confidential computing. Disk encryption covers data at rest, and TLS covers data in transit.

quiz.q: Why is envelope encryption used for large AI artefacts such as checkpoints?
o: It removes the need for a key management service or an HSM anywhere in the architecture
Data keys encrypt artefacts locally, while KMS-held keys protect the data keys
It compresses the artefact so that it takes up less storage space
It lets anyone with read access to the bucket decrypt the artefact
quiz.why: Bulk data is encrypted quickly with local data keys; only small wrapped keys go to the KMS, where policy and logging control their use.

quiz.q: What distinguishes hold-your-own-key (external key management) from BYOK?
o: HYOK keys are generated by the provider on request, whereas BYOK keys are generated by the customer
With HYOK, keys stay in the customer’s system; with BYOK, they are imported into the provider’s KMS
HYOK protects only data in transit, whereas BYOK protects only data at rest
There is no real difference; providers use the two terms interchangeably
quiz.why: BYOK imports customer-generated keys into the provider’s KMS. HYOK keeps keys outside the provider, which must request each use, so the customer can cut off access.

quiz.q: Where should an AI agent’s credentials for calling external tools be kept?
o: In the agent’s system prompt, so that it always has them available
In a secrets vault, issued short-lived and scoped to the agent and tool
In the source code repository, protected by branch permissions
In a shared configuration file that all agents on the platform read
quiz.why: Vault-held, short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials limit exposure. Prompts can be extracted, and repositories and shared files spread secrets widely.

quiz.q: What does purpose-based access control add to role-based access control?
o: It grants access according to seniority within the organisation
It ties access to the declared and approved purpose of each request
It removes the need to authenticate users and service accounts
It gives every member of a role access to all data in their domain
quiz.why: PBAC checks that each request’s purpose is approved for that data, which directly enforces purpose limitation.

quiz.q: Why should an agent acting for a user use delegated (on-behalf-of) access?
o: It lets the agent see more data than the user, which improves its answers
It ensures the agent can never access more than that user could
It removes the need to log the agent’s individual data requests
It lets the agent share one credential safely with other agents
quiz.why: Delegation caps the agent at the user’s own permissions, preventing the confused deputy problem.

quiz.q: Why can ordinary shredding be insufficient for high-density solid-state media?
o: Solid-state drives are too hard for commercial shredders to cut cleanly
Fragments can contain intact flash chips holding large amounts of data
Shredding triggers firmware that copies the data to a hidden partition
Shredded drives can’t be recycled under environmental regulations
quiz.why: Dense flash means a small fragment can hold a lot of data, so destruction needs very small particle sizes, incineration or melting.

quiz.q: When is cryptographic erase a valid purge method?
o: Whenever a drive supports encryption, even if encryption was switched on after data had been written
When all data was encrypted from the first write and every key copy is verifiably destroyed
Only for magnetic hard drives that have also been degaussed beforehand
Only when the drive has first been overwritten three times with random data
quiz.why: Crypto erase relies on there being no plaintext on the media and no surviving key copies. Overwrites and degaussing are separate techniques.

exam.q: A DSPM scan finds a full copy of the customer database in a data scientist’s notebook storage, made for an experiment eight months ago and since forgotten. What is the BEST response?
o: Leave the copy in place but encrypt it, since the experiment might be needed again later
Confirm the owner and need, then delete or secure the copy, and fix how such copies are created
Move the copy to a larger shared bucket where the data team can manage it centrally
Report the data scientist for disciplinary action and close the finding as resolved
exam.why: Stale shadow copies should be deleted or brought under control by an accountable owner, and the root cause (uncontrolled extracts) fixed so they don’t recur. Encrypting or moving the copy keeps unnecessary data; discipline alone fixes nothing.

exam.q: A company’s AI gateway uses pattern-based DLP in front of external LLMs. Users start uploading screenshots of customer records instead of pasting text. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Block all image uploads to every AI service, including the approved internal tools staff rely on
Add text extraction and image analysis to the gateway’s inspection, with policies for uploads
Ask users to sign a declaration that screenshots contain no customer information
Add more regular expressions to catch customer numbers in pasted text
exam.why: Inspection must cover the formats people actually use. OCR and image analysis extend DLP to uploads; blanket blocking pushes users elsewhere, and more text patterns miss images entirely.

exam.q: A team trains models on highly sensitive data in a GPU cluster whose high-speed interconnect doesn’t support encryption without unacceptable performance loss. What is the BEST compensating approach?
o: Accept the risk without further action, since interconnect traffic never leaves the physically secured data centre
Isolate the cluster physically and logically: dedicated hardware, segmented networks, restricted management access
Encrypt the training data at rest, which also protects it while it moves between GPUs
Move the training to CPUs only, so that no traffic crosses the GPU interconnect at all
exam.why: Where encryption in transit isn’t feasible, isolation limits who can reach the traffic. Encryption at rest doesn’t protect data in transit, and abandoning GPUs isn’t proportionate.

exam.q: A cloud AI provider will store fine-tuning data encrypted with provider-managed keys. The organisation must be able to cut off access instantly and prove every key use to auditors. Which option BEST meets this?
o: Accept provider-managed keys, and request the provider’s annual audit report as evidence of how keys are used
Use customer-managed or, better, external keys, with key-use logging under the organisation’s control
Encrypt the files with a password before uploading them, and share the password with the provider
Ask the provider to rotate its managed keys monthly, which gives the organisation effective control over access
exam.why: Customer-controlled keys give revocation and auditable key-use logs; external keys offer the strongest ability to cut off access. Provider reports and provider-side rotation don’t give the organisation control.

exam.q: A platform team wants to let internal AI agents query any table in the data lake through one broad service account, to speed up development. Which design BEST balances speed with control?
o: Use the broad account in development and production, and review agent queries at the end of each quarter
Agents discover governed data products through a catalog, with delegated, purpose-bound and logged access
Give each agent its own copy of the data lake, so that agents can’t interfere with each other’s queries
Instruct agents in their system prompts to use only the tables they need for each task they perform
exam.why: A catalog of governed data products with policy-based, delegated access lets agents find data quickly while enforcing least privilege and purpose. Broad accounts, copies and prompt instructions all fail to limit access.

exam.q: A company must return 400 leased NVMe drives from a training cluster that held special category data. All drives were self-encrypting from first use. What is the BEST approach?
o: Delete the files and reformat each drive, then return them to the lessor
Crypto erase each working drive, verify and certify it, and retain and destroy any that fail
Overwrite each drive three times with random data, as older sanitisation guidance recommended
Return the drives, since the lessor’s contract requires it to wipe them before reuse
exam.why: Self-encrypting drives support verified cryptographic erase, a purge method suited to media leaving your control. Drives that fail must be kept and destroyed. Reformatting is not sanitisation, and multi-pass overwrites miss remapped flash blocks.

exam.q: An organisation is ending its use of a cloud AI platform where training data and fine-tuned models were stored. How can it BEST sanitise data on media it doesn’t own?
o: Ask the provider to shred the specific disks that held the organisation’s data
Delete the data, destroy the customer-managed keys protecting it, and obtain deletion confirmation
Overwrite the stored files with random data before deleting the account
Rely on the provider’s standard terms, which state that deleted customer data is removed within 30 days
exam.why: In the cloud, crypto erase through key destruction is often the only practical purge method, supported by contractual deletion evidence. Disks are shared and can’t be singled out, and overwriting files doesn’t reach replicas or backups.

quiz.q: Who should be accountable for a production model’s use and outcomes?
o: The data scientist who trained the most recent version of the model
A named model owner, usually in the business area that relies on it
The vendor that supplied the base model the system was built on
The security team, because it reviews every model before deployment
quiz.why: Accountability sits with a named business owner, supported by technical owners. Developers, vendors and security teams contribute, but they don’t own the model’s use and outcomes.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN purpose of classifying models into risk tiers?
o: To decide which models can skip documentation and approval altogether
To scale validation, approval and monitoring to each model’s potential impact
To rank data science teams by the commercial value of the models they build
To choose which cloud provider should host each model once it reaches production
quiz.why: Risk tiers make governance proportionate: higher-impact models get deeper validation, more senior approval and closer monitoring. Even low-tier models still need basic records.

quiz.q: Which content is MOST essential in a model card?
o: The full training code and every hyperparameter tried during model development
Intended and out-of-scope uses, results across groups, and known limitations
The names and contact details of everyone who labelled the training data
Marketing claims comparing the model’s accuracy with competing products
quiz.why: A model card tells users and reviewers what a model is for, how it performs across groups and conditions, and where it shouldn’t be used. Code, personal details and marketing claims don’t belong there.

quiz.q: How does an approved model registry act as a security control?
o: It stores model weights in encrypted form, so that nobody can steal them
Deployment pipelines accept only registry-approved versions with valid signatures
It retrains models automatically whenever their measured performance starts to decline
It lets any engineer update an approved version in place, keeping one record
quiz.why: Gating deployment on approval status and verified signatures stops unapproved or tampered models reaching production. Approved versions should be immutable, so changes create new versions.

quiz.q: Why should the same signed artefact be promoted through test and production, rather than rebuilt at each stage?
o: Rebuilding the model at every stage would use more storage space in the registry
It guarantees that exactly what was tested is what is deployed in production
Signed artefacts load faster on inference servers than freshly rebuilt ones do
Regulators forbid rebuilding a model once its first version has been signed
quiz.why: Promoting one signed artefact preserves integrity: any rebuild could introduce differences, accidental or malicious, that testing never saw.

quiz.q: Where should a model-serving container get its database credentials?
o: From environment variables written into the container image when it is built
From a secrets vault at start-up, using the workload’s own cloud identity
From a configuration file stored alongside the model weights in the registry
From the system prompt, so the model can connect whenever it needs data
quiz.why: Runtime injection from a vault, authenticated by workload identity, keeps secrets out of images, packages and prompts, where they can be extracted or copied.

quiz.q: Which risk does OWASP call improper output handling in LLM applications?
o: Users receiving answers that are too long or detailed for their needs
Model output passed to other components without validation or encoding
Models refusing too many legitimate requests because filters are too strict
Replies arriving slowly because the serving cluster is badly overloaded
quiz.why: LLM05: Improper Output Handling covers output that reaches browsers, databases, shells or tools without validation, leading to injection, privilege escalation or code execution.

quiz.q: What should a rollback plan for an LLM application restore?
