o: Only the model weights, because nothing else changes during an update
The full tested bundle: model, prompts, settings, guardrails and index
Only the system prompt, because it is the easiest component to change
Only the guardrail filters, because that is where most failures occur
quiz.why: Behaviour depends on the whole system. Restoring only one component can leave an untested combination running in production.

quiz.q: Why is model performance often hard to measure directly in production?
o: Production systems can’t record the predictions that a model makes
True outcomes, such as defaults or fraud, may arrive weeks or months later
Performance metrics are meaningful only during the training and testing phases
Monitoring tools can’t measure the accuracy of classification models
quiz.why: Ground truth is often delayed, so teams watch proxies such as data drift and prediction drift until real outcomes arrive.

quiz.q: Overnight, one account sends tens of thousands of systematically varied queries to a model’s API. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: A routine batch job, which should be excluded from monitoring
An attempt to extract the model or probe its decision boundaries
Concept drift caused by a change in the customer population
A fairness problem that affects one group of users in particular
quiz.why: High-volume, systematic querying from one identity is a classic sign of extraction or boundary probing. It needs investigation and rate limiting (Module 3.6).

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, what record-keeping must high-risk AI systems support?
o: Manual logging by operators, reviewed by the provider once a year
Automatic recording of events (logs) over the system’s lifetime
Storage of every prompt and output for at least ten years
Logging that starts only once an incident has been reported
quiz.why: Article 12 requires high-risk systems to technically allow automatic event logging throughout their lifetime. Providers and deployers keep the logs for at least six months, unless other law provides otherwise.

quiz.q: Why should a hash of prompt content in an audit log be keyed, for example with an HMAC?
o: Keyed hashes are shorter, which reduces the cost of storing logs
Without a key, short or predictable content could be guessed and confirmed
Keyed hashes can be reversed to recover the original prompt whenever it is needed
Regulations require every hash in a log to use one public key
quiz.why: An unkeyed hash of predictable text can be brute-forced by hashing likely inputs. A secret key prevents this, while still letting authorised investigators match retained content to the log.

exam.q: A bank’s data science team has deployed 40 models over three years. An internal audit finds that 12 have no identified owner, and several are used for decisions their documentation doesn’t mention. What should the CISO recommend FIRST?
o: Retire all 12 unowned models immediately, whatever disruption that causes to the business
Build a model inventory with named owners and risk tiers, then review each model’s use against its approval
Require model cards for all 40 models before the team is allowed to make any further deployments
Commission an external penetration test of the 12 unowned models to find out whether they are vulnerable
exam.why: Governance starts with knowing what exists and who is accountable. An inventory with owners and risk tiers lets the bank prioritise reviews of models used beyond their approval. Retiring everything is disproportionate, and documentation and testing follow ownership and classification.

exam.q: A vendor’s model card says the model was evaluated only on English-language data and must not be used for medical advice. A business unit wants to use it to answer patients’ questions in Spanish. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Proceed, because a vendor’s model card is guidance rather than a contractual restriction
Treat it as an out-of-scope use: assess the risk, test for the actual use, and get approval first
Translate the patients’ questions into English first, which keeps the use within the card’s scope
Add a disclaimer to every answer stating that it isn’t medical advice, and then deploy it
exam.why: The use falls outside the documented scope on two counts, language and medical advice, so it needs its own risk assessment, testing for the real use and approval. Translation and disclaimers don’t make an out-of-scope use safe.

exam.q: An auditor finds that the pipeline deploying models to production authenticates with one long-lived cloud access key, stored in the pipeline settings and shared by every stage. What is the BEST remediation?
o: Rotate the access key every 90 days, and restrict who can view the pipeline settings
Use short-lived workload identity credentials scoped to each stage, with approval for production
Encrypt the access key within the pipeline settings, using the pipeline tool’s built-in secret masking
Move the access key into the model package, so that it travels with the approved artefact
exam.why: Workload identity removes long-lived secrets, per-stage scoping stops a compromised stage reaching production, and approvals add a human check. Rotation and masking still leave one powerful shared key, and embedding keys in packages spreads them further.

exam.q: A retailer releases a new version of its product-description LLM. Within an hour of the full release, customers report offensive descriptions; the previous version had no such problem. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Patch the system prompt in production with stricter instructions, and monitor the results closely
Roll back to the previous approved bundle under the pre-agreed procedure, then investigate fully
Take the whole website offline until the base model’s vendor explains the change in behaviour
Add the reported phrases to the output blocklist, and keep the new version running meanwhile
exam.why: A pre-planned rollback quickly restores a known-good state and limits harm; root-cause analysis and re-approval follow. Hot-patching prompts or blocklists treats symptoms and may miss other failures, and taking the site offline is disproportionate when a safe version exists.

exam.q: An AI agent summarises incoming supplier emails and can create purchase orders through an API. A red team shows that an email containing hidden instructions can make the agent raise an order. Which control BEST limits the impact?
o: A stronger system prompt that tells the agent to ignore any instructions it finds inside supplier emails
Treat the agent’s proposed actions as untrusted: validate them, and require human approval for orders
Scan all incoming email with antivirus software before the agent is allowed to read it
Train procurement staff to report suspicious supplier emails promptly to the security team
exam.why: Prompt injection can’t be reliably filtered, so impact must be limited outside the model: validating proposed actions and requiring human approval for orders stops a manipulated agent acting alone. Prompt instructions can be overridden, and antivirus doesn’t detect instructions written in natural language.

exam.q: Monitoring shows that a hiring model’s false negative rate for older applicants has doubled in six months, breaching its tolerance. The team retrains the model on recent data, and offline tests show the gap has closed. What should happen BEFORE the retrained model replaces the current one?
o: Deploy it straight away, because the offline tests show the gap has now closed
Validate and approve it as a new version for its tier, and update the registry, risk record and model card
Delete the monitoring data from the breach period, to limit the organisation’s legal exposure
Lower the fairness tolerance for the next six months to compensate for the breach period
exam.why: A retrained model is a material change, so it needs the validation and approval its tier requires, and governance records must capture the breach, its cause and the fix. Deleting evidence is improper, and adjusting tolerances doesn’t address the cause.

exam.q: A hospital’s clinical summarisation assistant must keep audit records for incident investigations. The privacy officer worries that the logs will become a new store of patient data. Which design BEST meets both needs?
o: Store full prompts and outputs in the general application log, where investigators can search them easily
Log metadata with pseudonymous IDs in tamper-evident storage; keep redacted content in a restricted vault
Log nothing about how the assistant is used, so that no patient information can ever leak from logs
Keep complete logs only on clinicians’ own devices, where device encryption protects them from theft
exam.why: Separating pseudonymised metadata (in tamper-evident storage) from redacted content (in a restricted vault with break-glass access and retention limits) supports investigations while minimising exposure. Full logs in a general store create a sensitive trove, no logs lose traceability, and device-held logs are neither controlled nor reliable.

quiz.q: Why can strong access controls on model weights matter legally as well as technically?
o: They allow the weights to be patented once enough controls are in place
Trade secret protection usually requires reasonable steps to keep information secret
They transfer legal ownership of the weights from individual developers to the organisation
They make the model’s outputs exempt from data protection law in most jurisdictions
quiz.why: Trade secret protection usually requires reasonable secrecy measures, so access controls, NDAs and need-to-know practices support the legal position as well as security.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST reduces the risk of a single insider exporting a model’s weights?
o: Asking staff to sign an annual acceptable use statement that covers model files
A two-person rule and just-in-time access for exporting or downloading weights
Storing the weights in a different cloud region from the one used for training
Renaming the weight files so that they look like ordinary application log files
quiz.why: Requiring a second authorised person, and granting access only when needed, stops one rogue or compromised account acting alone. Statements, regions and renaming don’t restrict access.

quiz.q: What should be assumed about a production system prompt?
o: It is fully protected, because users can’t see it anywhere in the interface
It may leak, so it must not hold secrets or be the only security control
It is encrypted by the model provider, so it can safely hold API keys
It is ignored by the model whenever a user gives conflicting instructions
quiz.why: System prompts can often be extracted (OWASP LLM07:2025). Keep credentials out of them, and enforce security in controls outside the model.

quiz.q: What does a model extraction attack MAINLY produce?
o: A copy of the training data, recovered record by record from the provider’s storage
A substitute model that imitates the target, trained on the target’s own answers
A denial of service against the model’s API that takes it offline for a while
A backdoor inserted into the target model through its training pipeline
quiz.why: Extraction queries a model and trains a substitute on its outputs, copying functionality without touching the weights.

quiz.q: Why doesn’t encrypting model weights at rest prevent model extraction?
o: Encryption slows the model down so much that attackers have more time to query it
Extraction works through the public API and never touches the stored weights
Encrypted weights are easier to copy, because encryption also compresses them
Attackers can always recover the encryption keys from the API’s responses
quiz.why: Extraction uses legitimate queries and answers. Controls must therefore act on the API: authentication, output minimisation, rate limits and detection.

quiz.q: What is the core difference between a model watermark and a passive fingerprint?
o: A watermark is visible to users, while a fingerprint is always hidden from them
A watermark is embedded on purpose; a passive fingerprint is an existing trait
A watermark proves who trained a model, while a fingerprint proves who used it
A watermark applies only to images, while a fingerprint applies only to text
quiz.why: Watermarks are deliberately embedded signals. Passive fingerprints identify a model from characteristics it already has, without changing it.

quiz.q: Why should a watermark detector’s result be treated as evidence rather than proof?
o: Detectors work only on text written in English, not on other languages
Detection can give false positives, and paraphrasing can weaken watermarks
Courts never accept technical evidence about AI-generated content
Watermarks become invalid as soon as the model is updated to a new version
quiz.why: Detection is statistical and watermarks can be degraded, so results should be combined with logs, contracts and other evidence.

quiz.q: Why is a model package verified with a signed manifest rather than a single file hash?
o: A manifest compresses the model, which makes deployment noticeably faster
Models are usually many files, and the signature covers every file’s digest
A single hash can’t be computed for files larger than four gigabytes
A signed manifest removes the need to keep models in a registry at all
quiz.why: Weight shards, tokenizer and configuration files all shape behaviour. Hashing each one and signing the list protects the whole package.

quiz.q: Which risk is MOST relevant when loading a third-party pickle-based model checkpoint?
o: The checkpoint may take up too much disk space on the inference server
Pickle files can execute arbitrary code at the moment they are loaded
Pickle files hide extra layers that only activate outside office hours
Pickle checkpoints always lose accuracy when they are decompressed
quiz.why: Pickle deserialisation can run code, so untrusted checkpoints should be scanned in a sandbox and converted to a data-only format such as safetensors.

quiz.q: Why should rate limits for LLM APIs count tokens as well as requests?
o: Token counts are easier for customers to understand than request counts
One very long request can use as much capacity as thousands of short ones
Request counts can’t be measured accurately at an API gateway
Tokens are the only unit that model providers allow in their contracts
quiz.why: Cost and capacity scale with tokens, so request-only limits miss resource-heavy prompts and long outputs.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly limits denial-of-wallet attacks on a pay-per-use AI service?
o: A web application firewall that inspects every request for known attack signatures
Per-identity quotas and budget caps that alert and then stop excess usage
Encrypting all prompts in transit with TLS 1.3 between client and API
A longer timeout on the model server, so that requests rarely fail
quiz.why: Denial of wallet exhausts budgets through legitimate-looking use, so quotas and spending caps per identity are the direct control.

quiz.q: What should autoscaling for an AI inference service include, to stay resilient against abuse?
o: No upper limit, so that capacity always matches demand however high it goes
A maximum scale with budget alerts, alongside rate limits and usage quotas
Scaling based only on the number of users who are currently logged in
Manual approval before every scaling event, at any time of day or night
quiz.why: Unlimited autoscaling turns an attack into a cost problem. A ceiling, budget alerts and per-identity limits keep both capacity and spend under control.

exam.q: A start-up fine-tunes an open-weight base model on proprietary customer-service data and serves it from a third-party GPU cloud. The board’s main concern is theft of the fine-tuned weights. Which approach BEST addresses this?
o: Publish the fine-tuned weights openly, since the base model they came from is already open-weight
Encrypt with customer-managed keys, restrict access, and serve in attested confidential computing
Rely on the cloud provider’s standard terms, which state that customer data won’t be accessed
Rename the model files and keep them in an unlisted storage bucket that only the engineering team knows about
exam.why: The fine-tune embodies proprietary data and effort, whatever the base model’s licence. Customer-controlled encryption, least privilege and confidential computing with attestation protect it at rest and in use on infrastructure the start-up doesn’t control. Contract terms and obscurity are not technical controls.

exam.q: Monitoring of a fraud-scoring API shows that three keys belonging to one customer together send two million queries a day with near-random feature values, far more than any other customer. What is the BEST immediate response?
o: Take no action, because the customer is paying for every query that it sends to the API
Throttle the linked keys, investigate the account, and review whether full scores need returning
Retrain the model immediately, so that any copy the customer is building will be out of date
Publish the model openly instead, because extraction can never be fully prevented anyway
exam.why: The pattern (very high volume, synthetic-looking inputs, linked keys) suggests extraction. Throttling contains it, investigation confirms it, and output minimisation reduces future leakage. Paying for queries doesn’t make extraction acceptable, and retraining or publishing is disproportionate.

exam.q: A provider finds that a competitor’s new chatbot gives its model’s planted answers to most of the provider’s secret trigger prompts. What does this MOST strongly indicate, and what should the provider do?
o: Coincidence, since models trained on similar public data usually behave in the same ways
Likely derivation from its model; preserve evidence and pursue legal and contractual remedies
A breach of the provider’s own training data, which must now be deleted and rebuilt at once
That its watermark has failed, so it should be removed from all of the provider’s future models
exam.why: Trigger-set answers far above chance are strong evidence of copying or distillation. The provider should preserve evidence (test results, logs, terms of service) and pursue remedies, treating the watermark as one part of the case.

exam.q: An incident review finds that a production assistant’s system prompt was edited directly on the server six weeks ago, weakening its refusal rules, and nobody knows who made the change. Which control would MOST likely have prevented this?
o: Encrypting the system prompt at rest on the inference server with a managed key
Managing prompts as code: versioned, peer-reviewed and deployed only through the signed pipeline
Asking the model to report any changes to its own instructions at the start of each reply
A monthly manual comparison of the deployed prompt against a printed copy kept on file
exam.why: Treating prompts as configuration under change control (versioning, review, signed deployment, no direct server edits) prevents unreviewed changes and records who changed what. Encryption doesn’t stop authorised-path edits, and monthly checks only detect problems late.

exam.q: A data science team downloads a popular pre-trained model from a public hub. The files are pickle-based and carry no publisher signature. What should security require BEFORE the model is loaded on internal systems?
o: Nothing further, because popular models on public hubs are reviewed by the community
Scan it in an isolated sandbox, convert it to a safe format, and verify provenance where possible
Load it on one developer’s laptop first, to check whether anything unusual happens
Rename the files with a safe extension, so that internal systems won’t treat them as executable code
exam.why: Pickle files can execute code on load, so untrusted files must be scanned in isolation and converted to a data-only format such as safetensors, with provenance checked (Module 3.7). Popularity isn’t assurance, a laptop isn’t a sandbox, and renaming changes nothing.

exam.q: A public chatbot’s costs triple overnight. Logs show a few accounts repeatedly sending maximum-length prompts and requesting maximum-length answers. Request-count rate limits are in place and weren’t exceeded. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Double the request-count limits, so that legitimate users aren’t affected by any change
Add token-based rate limits, per-identity quotas, output length limits and budget caps
Move every user permanently to a much cheaper model, whatever the impact on quality
Turn the chatbot off until the account holders responsible can be identified in court
exam.why: The abuse used heavy requests, not many requests, so controls must count tokens and cap output, with quotas and budget caps limiting each identity and total spend. Raising limits makes it worse, and the other options are disproportionate.

exam.q: An insurer’s claims-triage assistant depends on a third-party LLM API, which suffers a four-hour outage. Claims must still be triaged within a regulatory deadline. Which resilience design is BEST?
o: Wait for the provider to restore service, because its contract includes a 99.9% availability SLA
A circuit breaker that switches to an approved fallback model, then to a manual triage queue
Switch automatically to whichever public model is cheapest and available at the time
Queue the claims and triage them all once the API returns, accepting the missed deadline
exam.why: Graceful degradation keeps the essential service running: a circuit breaker, a pre-approved fallback model, then a non-AI path. An SLA gives compensation, not continuity, and an unapproved fallback bypasses governance.

quiz.q: Why is a dataset distributed as a list of URLs especially exposed to poisoning?
o: URL lists are too large to store, so they are rarely backed up anywhere
The content behind each URL can change after curation, including on expired domains
URL lists can only be downloaded over unencrypted connections, never over TLS
Search engines index URL lists, which reveals the dataset’s full contents to attackers
quiz.why: Whoever controls a URL controls what later downloaders receive. Hashes recorded at curation time let users reject changed content.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly ensures that a model is trained on exactly the data that was reviewed?
o: Downloading the dataset again at the start of every training run
Pinning each item by content hash in an internal, access-controlled mirror
Choosing the datasets with the most downloads on the public hub
Asking data scientists to record the exact date they downloaded each dataset
quiz.why: Content hashes and a controlled mirror fix the training data and make any change detectable. Live downloads, popularity and dates don’t.

quiz.q: A purchased dataset of consumer profiles is offered for model training. Which question is MOST important to answer first?
o: How many columns the dataset contains, and which file format it uses
How the data was collected, and whether there is a lawful basis for training
Whether the vendor can deliver the data faster than its competitors can
Whether other companies in the same sector have already used the dataset
quiz.why: Personal data collected without a lawful basis, or permission for this use, creates legal risk that no technical control fixes later.

quiz.q: Why is synthetic data generated by another model not automatically low-risk?
o: Synthetic data is always much larger than the real data it replaces
It can inherit the generator’s biases and errors, and carry its licence terms
Regulators prohibit training models on any data that other AI models have generated
Synthetic data can’t be stored in the same systems as real customer data
quiz.why: Synthetic data reflects the model that made it, including its flaws, and the generating model’s terms may restrict how outputs are used.

quiz.q: What does a valid digital signature on a model file prove?
o: That the model contains no backdoors or known vulnerabilities
That the holder of the key or identity signed it, and it hasn’t changed since
That the model performs as well as its model card claims it does on every benchmark
That the model’s licence permits your intended commercial use
quiz.why: Signatures prove origin and integrity, not safety or quality. A compromised publisher can still sign a malicious release.

quiz.q: What is model namespace reuse?
o: Two internal teams deploying the same model under different names
Re-registering a deleted publisher’s name, so name-based references pull an impostor
Fine-tuning a public model and then republishing it under the original publisher’s name
Reusing a model’s tokenizer with a completely different set of weights
quiz.why: Pipelines that reference models by publisher and name trust whoever holds that name. Pinning by hash and internal mirrors prevent substitution.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST prevents dependency confusion attacks on internal ML packages?
o: Automatically installing the newest available version of every package, every time
Private indexes with scoped names, so internal names can’t resolve publicly
Asking developers to check package names carefully before installing
Allowing package installation only during normal business hours
quiz.why: Dependency confusion relies on installers preferring a public package with an internal name. Scoped private indexes and pinned sources remove that path.

quiz.q: Which evidence shows HOW a third-party model artefact was built?
o: A marketing brochure that describes the model’s capabilities in detail
A signed provenance attestation describing the source, inputs and pipeline
A list of well-known customers that already use the model in production
A screenshot of the model’s download page on a popular public hub
quiz.why: Provenance attestations record how an artefact was produced, and their signatures let you check that they match the artefact you received.

quiz.q: Why should a fine-tuned model be re-evaluated for safety, even if its base model passed?
o: Fine-tuning always reduces a model’s accuracy on its main task
Fine-tuning, even on a small amount of data, can weaken safety behaviour
Regulators require a new licence for every fine-tuned model version
Fine-tuned models can’t be stored in the same model registry as their base models
quiz.why: Research shows that fine-tuning can erode safety training, sometimes with very few examples, so every fine-tune is a new model to evaluate.

quiz.q: Which statement about backdoors in pre-trained models is MOST accurate?
o: Standard safety training reliably removes any backdoor that a pre-trained model contains
Testing can’t rule out hidden triggers, so provenance and monitoring matter too
Backdoors exist only in models that are distributed in pickle format
Backdoors can always be found by reading the model card carefully
quiz.why: Backdoors can survive safety training and evade testing, so trusted provenance, least privilege and production monitoring complement evaluation.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN risk of calling a hosted foundation model through an unpinned alias such as “latest”?
o: The provider may charge more for calls made through an alias
The model behind the alias can change without your testing or approval
Aliases always point to older, deprecated versions of the model
Calls made through aliases bypass the provider’s safety systems and content filters
quiz.why: An alias lets the provider swap the underlying model. Pin dated versions, and re-test before moving to a new one.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of general-purpose AI models give downstream providers?
o: Full copies of their training data, whenever a downstream provider asks
Information and documentation on the model’s capabilities and limitations
A guarantee that the model will never produce incorrect or harmful output
Exclusive rights to use the model within the downstream provider’s sector
quiz.why: Article 53 requires general-purpose AI model providers to give downstream providers the information they need to understand the model and meet their own obligations.

exam.q: A healthcare start-up wants to fine-tune a diagnostic model on a large open medical imaging dataset found on a public hub. The dataset page has no licence, no datasheet and an anonymous uploader. What should the security and privacy lead recommend?
o: Use it, because publicly available data can be used freely for both research and products
Don’t use it until provenance, licence, consent and content are established; find a documented source
Use it only for internal testing, which removes the legal and privacy obligations that would apply
Use a random 10% sample, which reduces the legal exposure and the poisoning risk proportionately
exam.why: Medical images are special category data, and an undocumented, unlicensed dataset from an anonymous source fails provenance, rights and lawful-basis checks. Public availability doesn’t grant rights, internal use is still processing, and sampling doesn’t fix legality or poisoning.

exam.q: An AI team learns that a public dataset it trained on six months ago has been withdrawn after illegal content was found in it. What should happen FIRST?
o: Nothing, because the models were trained before the dataset was withdrawn
Assess exposure: identify affected models and data copies, and involve legal and compliance
Delete every model in production immediately, whatever the impact on the business
Publish a statement saying the organisation wasn’t aware of the content when it trained the models
exam.why: Lineage and the AIBOM let the team find every affected copy and model; legal and compliance decide on obligations such as deletion, reporting and retraining. Doing nothing ignores the risk, mass deletion is premature, and statements come after the facts are known.

exam.q: A vendor delivers a fine-tuned model signed with its own key, but with no provenance attestation or model card. The vendor says the model “passed all internal tests”. What is the BEST next step?
o: Accept it, because the valid signature shows that the model is safe to deploy
Request provenance and documentation, and test the model independently in a sandbox
Reject the vendor permanently, because missing documents prove the model is malicious
Deploy it to a small group of customers, and gather their feedback before deciding
exam.why: A signature proves origin, not safety. Documentation and provenance support the assessment, and independent testing in isolation verifies the vendor’s claims before approval. Permanent rejection is disproportionate, and customer pilots expose users to an unverified model.

exam.q: A popular model-loading library was briefly replaced on the public package registry by a malicious version. An organisation’s builds install the latest version automatically. Which control would MOST have reduced its exposure?
o: A policy requiring developers to read the library’s changelog every month before each release
Dependencies pinned by version and hash, installed from a verified internal mirror
Running builds less often, so that fewer malicious versions get installed
Switching to a different library that has fewer outside contributors
exam.why: Pinned, hash-verified dependencies from an internal mirror don’t change when the public registry does. Changelogs, build frequency and contributor counts don’t stop a malicious version being installed.

exam.q: A bank plans to use a hosted foundation model to triage customer complaints, a process with regulatory deadlines. Which combination BEST manages the foundation model risk?
o: Rely on the provider’s strong reputation and on its standard terms of service
Pin the version, evaluate on the bank’s data, agree change notice, and keep a fallback
Adopt each new model version as soon as it is released, to get the best accuracy
Ask staff to double-check every triage decision, so that no other controls are needed
exam.why: Pinning prevents silent changes, the bank’s own evaluation tests fitness for its use, contractual notice gives time to re-test, and a fallback protects the deadline. Reputation isn’t a control, chasing versions skips testing, and manual checks alone don’t address availability or change.

exam.q: A product team wants to build on an open-weight model whose licence restricts use by companies above a set number of monthly active users. The product is expected to pass that threshold within a year. What should happen?
o: Proceed, because the licence terms of open-weight models can’t be enforced
Have legal review the licence first, and pick a model or agreement that fits the scale
Proceed now, and negotiate a commercial licence only if the model provider complains later
Remove the model’s attribution notices, so that the licence no longer applies to it
exam.why: Licence terms are part of the supply chain risk assessment. Legal review before adoption avoids building on a model the product will soon be barred from using. Ignoring or evading terms creates legal exposure.

quiz.q: Under Zero Trust, how should downstream systems treat an AI model’s output?
o: As trusted, because the model runs inside the organisation’s own network
As untrusted input to validate, because the model can be manipulated
As trusted once the system prompt instructs the model to behave safely
As untrusted only when an external provider hosts the model
quiz.why: The model can be steered by injected content, so its output is untrusted input to everything downstream, wherever it runs.

quiz.q: Which layer of defence in depth MOST reliably limits harm when a prompt injection succeeds?
o: A longer, more detailed system prompt that defines forbidden behaviour
Action limits: least-privilege tools, scoped credentials and approval
An input classifier trained to recognise every known injection pattern
A larger model that is better at recognising malicious instructions
quiz.why: Action limits hold even when the model is fooled. Prompts, classifiers and model choice all reduce the chance of success, but can be bypassed.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a secure default for a newly created AI agent?
o: Full access to every internal tool, so it can be useful immediately
Read-only tools, with write actions enabled only after explicit approval
Logging switched off, so that no sensitive prompts are ever stored
Web browsing and code execution switched on, with monitoring afterwards
quiz.why: Secure defaults keep risky capabilities off until deliberately enabled. Logging should be on by default, with privacy protections.

quiz.q: In an AI threat model, where should analysts look hardest?
o: At the user interface, because that is where users notice problems first
Where data flows cross trust boundaries, such as app to model or to tools
At the model weights alone, because they are the single most valuable asset
At the system documentation, because it is most often out of date
quiz.why: Boundary crossings are where untrusted data enters or authority changes hands, so they concentrate the threats and the controls.

quiz.q: Which STRIDE category does a prompt injection that drives an over-privileged tool MOST clearly represent?
o: Repudiation of actions
Elevation of privilege
Denial of service
Spoofing of identity
quiz.why: The attacker gains the tool’s authority through the model, which is elevation of privilege.

quiz.q: Why does permission-aware filtering belong in the retrieval layer of a RAG system?
o: It makes retrieval faster, because fewer documents need to be ranked
It stops unauthorised content reaching the model, whatever the prompt says
It removes the need for authentication on the vector database itself
It means the system prompt no longer needs to mention confidentiality at all
quiz.why: Content the model never receives can’t be leaked by it. Filtering in prompts or outputs relies on controls that can be bypassed.

quiz.q: Why does streaming model replies to users complicate security?
o: Streaming always uses unencrypted connections between client and server
Text appears before the full reply can be checked by the output filters
Streaming doubles the token cost of every reply that a model generates
Streamed replies can’t be logged, so there is no audit trail of them
quiz.why: Streaming shows partial output immediately, so designs need buffering, chunk-by-chunk checks, or no streaming for high-risk replies.

quiz.q: What is the BEST way to reconcile a tight latency budget with strong output checks?
o: Remove output checks from every request, so that the latency budget is always met
Route by risk: cheap checks everywhere, expensive checks for high-risk requests
Apply the most expensive check to every request, whatever the delay
Check a sample of stored conversations once a month instead
quiz.why: Risk-based routing keeps typical requests fast while applying stronger assurance where impact is high.

quiz.q: What MOST often decides whether a hosted model API is acceptable for a use case?
o: Whether the provider’s model is the largest one available on the market
Whether the data may leave, and the provider’s terms on use and retention
Whether the provider offers a free tier for testing and evaluation
Whether developers already have personal accounts with the provider
quiz.why: Data sensitivity and contractual terms determine whether external processing is permissible and safe.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, when can a deployer of a high-risk AI system become its provider?
o: Whenever it has used the system in production for more than a year
When it rebrands, substantially modifies, or repurposes it as high-risk
When it signs a long-term support contract with the system’s original provider
Whenever it trains its own staff to operate the system day to day
quiz.why: Article 25 makes a deployer the provider if it puts its name or trademark on the system, substantially modifies it, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

quiz.q: What is a rug pull in the context of MCP tool integrations?
o: A server that suddenly stops responding, leaving the agent without tools
A tool whose definition or behaviour changes after review and approval
A user who withdraws consent for an agent to act on their behalf
A token that expires partway through a long-running agent task
quiz.why: Rug pulls exploit one-time approval. Pinning reviewed definitions and alerting on changes defeats them.

quiz.q: Why must an MCP server not pass a client’s access token straight through to a downstream API?
o: Passing tokens through makes every request noticeably slower for users
It lets tokens be used beyond their intended audience and breaks audit trails
Downstream APIs can’t read tokens that were issued using OAuth 2.1
Token passthrough is allowed only for local servers that use standard input and output
quiz.why: The MCP specification forbids token passthrough: servers accept only tokens issued for them, and use their own credentials downstream.

exam.q: A customer assistant can issue refunds through a tool. A red team makes it refund an attacker-controlled account using instructions hidden in a product review that the assistant retrieved. Which change BEST applies defence in depth?
o: Rewrite the system prompt to forbid any refunds that customers didn’t request themselves
Enforce refund limits and ownership checks in the refund service, with approval above a threshold
Remove all product reviews from the knowledge base, because they were the source of the attack
Switch to a newer model that scores better on published prompt injection benchmarks
exam.why: Controls in the refund service hold even when the model is manipulated: ownership checks stop refunds to the wrong account and approval thresholds cap impact. Prompt rules and better models reduce but don’t remove injection, and removing reviews treats one source among many.

exam.q: A team is designing an agent that reads incoming invoices, looks up suppliers in the ERP system and schedules payments. What should the security architect do FIRST?
o: Choose the AI guardrail product with the best published detection rates
Threat model the design: components, data flows, trust boundaries and the payment tool
Write a detailed system prompt that describes exactly how the agent should behave
Ask the model vendor for its latest independent penetration test report and certifications
exam.why: Threat modelling identifies where untrusted invoices enter, what the payment tool can do and which controls are needed, before products or prompts are chosen. Vendor reports cover the vendor’s scope, not this design.

exam.q: A multi-tenant SaaS company keeps all customers’ embeddings in one vector index and filters results by tenant ID in application code. A bug in a new release left out the filter on one query path. Which design change MOST reduces the impact of such bugs?
o: Add a sentence to the system prompt reminding the model to use only the current tenant’s data
Isolate tenants at the data layer, with separate indexes or namespaces that the database enforces
Encrypt all of the embeddings with a single key that is shared across every tenant
Return more results per query, so that the right tenant’s documents are always included
exam.why: Enforcing isolation in the data layer means one missed filter in application code can’t expose another tenant’s data. Prompts don’t enforce anything, a shared key doesn’t separate tenants, and more results increase exposure.

exam.q: A chatbot streams replies word by word. An audit finds that account numbers sometimes appear briefly before the output DLP filter removes them. What is the BEST fix?
o: Accept the risk, because the numbers are visible for only a fraction of a second
Buffer and check each chunk before display, or stop streaming account-related replies
Raise the DLP filter’s sensitivity so that it flags more patterns once the reply ends
Warn customers in the terms of service that replies may briefly show other data
exam.why: The trade-off must favour checking before display where sensitive data is possible: buffer and filter chunks, or don’t stream those replies. A brief exposure is still disclosure, and post-display filtering or disclaimers don’t prevent it.

exam.q: A retailer with a two-person security team wants to self-host an open-weight model for a marketing copy tool that uses only public product information. What is the BEST advice?
o: Self-host it, because self-hosting a model is always more secure than using a provider
Use a hosted API or managed platform, as the data is low-risk and the team is small
Train a new model from scratch, so that the retailer controls every part of it
Avoid AI entirely until the security team has grown to at least ten people
exam.why: Low-sensitivity data removes the main reason to self-host, and a small team would struggle to secure and operate a model platform. A hosted service shifts that work to a specialist provider. Self-hosting isn’t inherently more secure.

exam.q: Reviewing an MCP server from a public registry, an analyst finds that one tool’s description contains hidden instructions telling the model to read private key files and include them in its requests. What does this indicate, and what should happen?
o: A documentation error; correct the description and approve the server for use
Tool poisoning; reject the server, report it, and check whether it was used before
Normal behaviour for developer tools; approve it, but only for the engineering team
A rug pull; approve it, but monitor the definition closely for any further changes
exam.why: Hidden instructions in tool descriptions are tool poisoning. The server must be rejected and reported, and any prior use investigated for exposed keys. Approving it in any form accepts a malicious component.

exam.q: An organisation chains three agents: a planner delegates to a research agent, which delegates to a purchasing agent. The planner passes the user’s full-access token down the chain. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Keep using the token, but encrypt it before each agent in the chain passes it to the next one
Give each hop its own task-scoped, short-lived grant, and validate each agent’s results
Let each agent decide for itself which actions the user would probably approve of
Merge the three agents into one agent that holds the same full-access token
exam.why: Forwarding a full-access token gives every agent, and anyone who manipulates one, the user’s full authority. Task-scoped grants per hop and validated results contain each agent. Encryption in transit doesn’t limit authority.

quiz.q: Why are ML tools such as notebooks and distributed compute dashboards frequent targets?
o: They always run on the most expensive hardware the organisation owns
They are often exposed without authentication and hold credentials and data
They can’t be patched, because their vendors never release security updates
They are used mainly by external contractors, who tend to be less careful
quiz.why: Many ML tools assume a trusted network, ship with weak or no authentication, and accumulate secrets, data and access to valuable compute.

quiz.q: Which cloud control MOST directly prevents teams creating publicly readable buckets of training data?
o: A monthly reminder email about storage good practice for all engineers
An organisation-level policy that blocks public access to storage
A naming convention that clearly marks which buckets are sensitive
Encrypting every bucket with its own customer-managed key
quiz.why: A preventive guardrail applied across the organisation stops the misconfiguration from being possible. Reminders and naming rely on people; encryption doesn’t stop public read access to decrypted objects.

quiz.q: What does a hybrid AI deployment add to hardening work?
o: Nothing, because each environment can simply be hardened on its own
Securing the links between environments, with consistent identity and policy
A requirement to move all model training back into on-premises data centres permanently
A need to switch off identity federation between the different sites
quiz.why: Hybrid adds connections and the risk of inconsistent controls, so unify identity, connect privately and apply one policy everywhere.

quiz.q: Why are plain containers a weak boundary for untrusted, agent-generated code?
o: Containers can’t limit how much memory a process is allowed to use
Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape them
Containers always have unrestricted internet access by default
Containers can only run programs written in compiled languages
quiz.why: A shared kernel means one vulnerability can break the boundary. Micro-VMs and sandboxed runtimes add a separate kernel layer.

quiz.q: Which feature is MOST characteristic of an isolated training environment for sensitive data?
o: Direct internet access, so engineers can download packages more quickly
No direct internet egress, with packages from approved internal mirrors
Shared credentials, so that any engineer can resume any training job
Public endpoints, so that research partners can submit training jobs
quiz.why: Blocking egress stops exfiltration and unreviewed downloads; dependencies come through scanned internal mirrors instead.

quiz.q: Why should prompt or key-value caches on a multi-tenant inference service be scoped per tenant?
o: Shared caches use far more memory than separate per-tenant caches would use
Shared caches can leak other tenants’ prompts through timing side channels
Per-tenant caches remove the need to authenticate requests at all
Caches can store responses in only one language at a time
quiz.why: Research in 2025 found shared prompt caches at some providers, allowing timing attacks that reveal whether others sent similar prompts.

quiz.q: Which control lets production inference keep running when experiments compete for the same GPUs?
o: A higher maximum autoscaling limit for experimental workloads
Priority classes with preemption, combined with per-team quotas
A single shared queue in which every job has equal priority
Requiring administrator approval before any experiment can run
quiz.why: Priorities with preemption guarantee capacity for production, and quotas stop any team from taking everything. Manual approval doesn’t stop runaway jobs.

quiz.q: Why should autoscaling for AI workloads have a maximum and budget alerts?
o: Autoscaling can’t add GPU nodes unless a maximum has been set
So that an attack or a bug can’t grow capacity and costs without limit
Because cloud providers forbid their customers from using unlimited autoscaling
So that experiments always receive more capacity than production
quiz.why: Unbounded autoscaling turns abuse or runaway jobs into unbounded cost. Maximums and alerts keep both in check.

quiz.q: Which way of sharing a GPU gives each workload its own memory and compute, enforced in hardware?
o: Time-slicing
Hardware partitioning
Multi-process sharing
Spot instances
quiz.why: Hardware partitioning, such as multi-instance GPU, splits a device into isolated instances with dedicated memory, cache and compute.

quiz.q: What did the 2024 LeftoverLocals research show?
o: That GPUs overheat when more than four users share them at once
That data left in GPU memory by one process could be read by another
That GPU drivers can be updated safely without rebooting servers
That time-slicing makes GPUs immune to side-channel attacks
quiz.why: Researchers recovered fragments of another process’s data, including language model output, from uncleared GPU local memory on several vendors’ devices.

quiz.q: What does 2N redundancy mean for data centre power?
o: Twice the normal number of operations staff on each shift
Fully duplicated systems and paths, either able to carry the full load
One spare component for every two that are in service
Two generators shared between all of the facility’s data halls and offices
quiz.why: 2N duplicates the entire power path, unlike N+1, which adds a single spare component.

quiz.q: Why do liquid-cooled AI racks call for leak detection?
o: Liquid cooling makes racks louder, which can drown out alarms
Coolant runs close to the electronics, so leaks can cause damage or outages
Leak sensors are needed to measure how much power the rack draws
Liquid-cooled racks have no fans, so the room’s smoke detectors stop working
quiz.why: Liquid near high-value electronics introduces a new failure mode, so leak sensors in and under racks are a standard control.

exam.q: A review of an ML platform finds a model registry with public read access, notebook servers reachable from the internet with token authentication, and GPU nodes running two-year-old drivers. What should be fixed FIRST?
o: Upgrade the GPU drivers, since outdated drivers may have known vulnerabilities
Remove public access to the registry and notebooks, and check for unauthorised use
Write a complete new hardening standard for the platform before changing anything
Rename the registry and notebook servers so that their addresses are harder to guess
exam.why: Public exposure of models and notebooks is the most immediate risk and may already have been exploited, so removing it and checking for compromise comes first. Driver updates follow quickly; standards come after the urgent fix, and obscurity isn’t a control.

exam.q: An organisation runs inference partly in its own data centre and partly in a public cloud. Audits find different firewall rules, separate identity stores and inconsistent logging. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Move everything back on premises, where the team has more direct control
Federate identity, connect privately, and apply one policy and logging standard
Accept the differences, because each environment has its own team of administrators
Ask each team to document its own rules in a shared spreadsheet for reference
exam.why: Hybrid risk comes from inconsistency. One identity system, private connectivity and a common policy and logging standard close the gaps. Retreating on premises is disproportionate, and documentation alone fixes nothing.

exam.q: A start-up’s AI service runs customer-supplied Python plugins on its inference hosts, inside the same container as the model server. Which change MOST reduces the risk?
o: Review each plugin by hand before customers are allowed to upload it
Run plugins in ephemeral micro-VM sandboxes with no network or model server access
Ask customers to sign terms promising not to upload any malicious plugins
Run the model server as root, so that it can kill any misbehaving plugins immediately
exam.why: Untrusted code needs strong isolation from the model server and the network. Manual review doesn’t scale or catch everything, terms don’t stop attackers, and running as root makes compromise worse.

exam.q: A public AI chatbot’s GPU cluster autoscaled to ten times its normal size overnight during traffic from a few hundred newly created accounts, producing a large cloud bill. Which combination BEST prevents a repeat?
o: Switch off autoscaling, so that the cluster always stays at its normal size
Per-identity token limits and quotas, an autoscaling maximum, and budget alerts
Require a credit card for every new account, and take no other action
Move the chatbot to a cloud provider that charges less for GPU time
exam.why: Per-identity limits stop a few accounts consuming capacity, the maximum caps scale, and alerts catch anomalies early. Disabling autoscaling hurts legitimate peaks, and payment checks or cheaper GPUs don’t limit consumption.

exam.q: A bank’s fraud-scoring model must respond within 50 milliseconds around the clock. It runs on spot GPU instances shared with batch analytics. What is the BEST change?
o: Keep the spot instances but add more of them, so that reclaim events matter less
Move it to reserved, dedicated capacity across zones, with a fallback model
Time-slice the GPUs more aggressively, so that the model gets more turns
Run the model on analysts’ laptops whenever there is a GPU shortage
exam.why: Critical, latency-sensitive services need capacity that can’t be reclaimed or crowded out, spread for resilience, with a fallback. More spot instances still share the reclaim risk, and time-slicing adds unpredictability.

exam.q: A colocation provider hosting a company’s AI training hardware proposes removing the mantrap at the data hall entrance and relying on badge access alone. What should the company’s security lead do?
o: Accept the change, because the badge readers already record who enters the hall
Object: layered entry controls stop tailgating to high-value hardware; check the contract
Accept, provided the provider adds a sign reminding staff not to hold the doors open for others
Object, but only because removing it might affect the fire suppression system
exam.why: Badges record a card, not the people who follow it in. A mantrap prevents tailgating to high-value hardware, and the contract and audit reports should require it. Signs aren’t controls, and fire suppression isn’t the issue.

exam.q: The facilities team proposes gaseous fire suppression throughout a new AI data hall, including an area where technicians routinely work. What is the MAIN additional consideration?
o: Gaseous systems leave a residue that damages GPUs and network equipment
People safety: alarms, discharge delays, evacuation procedures and room sealing
Gaseous systems can’t be combined with any form of early smoke detection
Gaseous suppression is prohibited in every building that uses liquid cooling
exam.why: Gas systems are effective and leave no residue, but occupied spaces need pre-discharge alarms, delays, evacuation and safety procedures, and rooms must be sealed for the agent to work. They are commonly paired with early detection.

quiz.q: What is poisoned pipeline execution?
o: A training dataset poisoned before it ever reaches the pipeline
Untrusted code running inside a pipeline with the pipeline’s privileges
A pipeline that fails because a dependency has been deleted upstream
A build that produces a corrupted container image entirely by accident
quiz.why: PPE lets an attacker’s code, for example in a pull request, run in the pipeline and use its secrets and access.

quiz.q: Why should CI pipelines use workload identity federation instead of stored cloud keys?
o: Federation makes builds run noticeably faster on shared and self-hosted runners
Short-lived, scoped credentials replace long-lived secrets that can leak
Stored keys can only be used by one pipeline at any one time
Federation removes the need for access control in the cloud
quiz.why: Federated credentials are issued per job, scoped to a repository, branch and environment, and expire quickly.

quiz.q: What does SLSA build level 3 add over level 2?
o: It requires every build to be run manually by two separate engineers
Hardened builds isolated from each other, so provenance can’t be forged
A rule that all artefacts must be stored in a single cloud region
Automatic deployment of every successful build straight to production
quiz.why: Level 3 hardens the build platform, isolating builds and protecting signing material so provenance is trustworthy.

quiz.q: Why should new data land in a quarantine zone before the raw zone?
o: Quarantine storage is much cheaper than raw zone storage
So it can be validated and scanned before anything trusts it
So analysts can edit it before it becomes immutable
Because raw zones can accept new data only once a day
quiz.why: Quarantine holds untrusted data until schema, scanning and hash checks pass, so bad data never enters trusted zones.

quiz.q: Which control BEST preserves evidence of exactly what data arrived in a pipeline?
o: Allowing corrections in place, so that the raw zone always stays accurate
An immutable, versioned raw zone with checksums for each batch
Daily exports of the raw zone to analysts’ laptops for safekeeping
Compressing raw files to keep storage costs as low as possible
quiz.why: Immutability, versioning and checksums preserve the original and make tampering detectable and reversible.

quiz.q: Why tokenise or pseudonymise personal data at ingestion rather than later?
o: Tokens are smaller, which speeds up every later transformation
Later stages, and the people using them, never see raw identifiers
Regulations forbid any processing of identifiers after ingestion
Tokenising at ingestion removes the need for encryption elsewhere
quiz.why: Protecting identifiers at the first opportunity shrinks the number of systems and people exposed to them.

quiz.q: Which detail is MOST important to record about the base model in fine-tuning lineage?
o: Its marketing name, as shown on the provider’s website
Its exact version identifier and its content hash
The number of downloads it has on the model hub
The date on which the model was first announced
quiz.why: Only an exact version and hash identify precisely which weights the fine-tune was built on.

quiz.q: Why should lineage be captured automatically by the pipeline?
o: Automatic records take up less storage than manual ones
Manual records develop gaps and errors; automatic capture is complete
Regulators accept only lineage that was generated automatically by a pipeline
Automatic capture removes the need for a model registry
quiz.why: Lineage is only useful if it is complete and accurate, which manual records rarely are over time.

quiz.q: What makes a pipeline gate enforceable rather than advisory?
o: A dashboard showing how many builds passed each gate last month
Signed gate attestations that deployment verifies before accepting artefacts
An email to the whole team whenever any gate in the pipeline fails
A policy document listing every gate in the pipeline in detail, signed by management
quiz.why: If deployment refuses artefacts without valid attestations, gates can’t be skipped by going around the pipeline.

quiz.q: Why should evaluation thresholds be agreed before a model is tested?
o: So that the model can be trained to hit the thresholds directly
So they can’t be relaxed after a failure to let a release through
Because evaluation tools can’t run until thresholds are configured
So the thresholds can be published to customers in advance
quiz.why: Thresholds set after seeing results invite moving the goalposts; pre-agreed thresholds keep the gate honest.

quiz.q: Which unlearning method gives the HIGHEST assurance that data has been forgotten?
o: Output suppression filters
Retraining without the data
Approximate gradient-based unlearning
Lowering the sampling temperature
quiz.why: A model retrained without the data never learned from it. Suppression hides outputs, and approximate methods may leave traces.

quiz.q: Why must approximate unlearning be verified?
o: It always deletes the model’s training logs as a side effect
Some methods hide rather than remove knowledge, which can resurface
Regulators always require proof in the form of a complete retrain from scratch
It changes the licence terms that apply to the model
quiz.why: Research shows some approximate methods merely suppress knowledge, which can return after further fine-tuning, so test for extraction and leakage.

exam.q: A model-serving image is built from a large GPU base image tagged “latest”, with dependencies installed without version pins. A scan finds 300 vulnerabilities, and the image differs on every rebuild. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Run the vulnerability scanner more often, so that new issues are found sooner
A minimal base pinned by digest, dependencies pinned by hash, and a signed SBOM
Accept the vulnerabilities, because GPU images are always large and complex
Rebuild the image every hour, so that it always has the newest packages
exam.why: Minimal, pinned inputs cut the attack surface and make builds reproducible and verifiable; an SBOM and signature make the result auditable. More scanning finds problems without fixing them, and unpinned rebuilds keep changing what is shipped.

exam.q: A team stores a long-lived cloud access key with production deployment rights in its CI system’s settings. Which change BEST reduces the risk?
o: Rotate the key every 90 days, and restrict who can view or change the CI system’s settings
Use federated, short-lived credentials scoped to the protected branch and environment
Encrypt the key using the CI system’s own built-in secret store feature
Move the key into the repository, so that any changes to it are reviewed
exam.why: Federation removes the standing secret altogether, and scoping limits use to reviewed code deploying to the intended environment. Rotation and encryption still leave a powerful long-lived key; a key in a repository is worse.

exam.q: A fraud model’s training data comes from a transformation job that analysts sometimes edit directly in production to fix urgent issues. An auditor asks how the organisation knows the training data hasn’t been tampered with. What is the BEST response?
o: Show the auditor the job’s current code, which has now been corrected and fully tested
Move transformations to reviewed, versioned code, with immutable data and audit logs
Ask the analysts to keep a written log of any manual changes they make
Restrict manual edits in production to the most senior analysts only
exam.why: Reviewed, versioned transformation code deployed by the pipeline, with immutable data and audit logs, makes the training data reproducible and tampering detectable. Current code says nothing about past runs, and manual logs or seniority don’t make edits controlled.

exam.q: A regulator asks a bank which data and base model built the credit model deployed last March, and to reproduce it. Records were kept in spreadsheets and some are missing. What should the bank implement to avoid this in future?
o: A rule that the shared spreadsheets must be updated within one week of every training run
Automatic lineage linking base model, data snapshots, code, runs and deployments
A policy of retraining every model from scratch at the start of each month
Keeping every model the bank has ever trained in production permanently
exam.why: Automatic, linked lineage records exactly what each deployed model was built from, so it can be explained and reproduced. Spreadsheet rules still rely on people, and retraining or keeping old models doesn’t answer the question.

exam.q: A pipeline has a “skip evaluation” flag that engineers can set themselves. It was used in 40% of releases last quarter. What is the BEST corrective action?
o: Remove the flag, and rely on engineers’ own judgement about releases instead
Replace it with break-glass: independent approval, time limits, logging and review
Keep the flag, but report each use of it to management every quarter
Speed up the evaluations, so that engineers no longer feel any need to skip them at all
exam.why: Emergencies need a route, but it must be controlled: independent approval, expiry, logging and review afterwards. Self-service skipping isn’t a control, quarterly reports are too late, and faster evaluations help but don’t enforce anything.

exam.q: A health app fine-tuned an LLM on patient messages. A patient requests erasure, and lineage shows their data was used in one fine-tuning run. Retraining takes three weeks. What is the BEST approach?
o: Refuse the request, because data held in model weights can’t ever be removed
Delete the data everywhere now, suppress meanwhile, then retrain or unlearn and verify
Apply output suppression permanently, and then close the request as complete
Retrain immediately, and take the whole service offline until the retraining has finished
exam.why: A proportionate response removes the data from all stores at once, limits exposure with interim suppression, and removes its influence on a defined timeline with verification and evidence. Refusal and permanent suppression leave the data in the weights, and halting the service is disproportionate.

exam.q: An organisation wants to offer customers a private assistant that learns from each customer’s documents, with guaranteed removal when a customer leaves. Which architecture BEST supports this?
o: Fine-tune one shared model on all customers’ documents, for the best quality
Per-customer retrieval indexes, with per-customer adapters only where tuning is needed
Train a new base model each year from all customers’ data combined together
Place each customer’s documents in the system prompt of every chat session that they start
exam.why: Keeping customer knowledge in per-customer indexes, and any tuning in per-customer adapters, makes removal a matter of deleting those artefacts. A shared model mixes everyone’s data into the same weights.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN purpose of context boundary validation?
o: To make sure the prompt fits inside the model’s maximum context window
To keep instructions apart from untrusted content, and check what enters the context
To compress retrieved documents so that more of them fit into each prompt sent to the model
To translate every input into English before it reaches the model
quiz.why: Boundary validation separates and labels trusted instructions and untrusted data, and checks content before it is added, which reduces indirect injection.

quiz.q: Why should safety instructions be protected when context budgets are tight?
o: Longer system prompts always produce more accurate and better-grounded answers from the model
If they are truncated to make room for documents, the safeguards silently disappear
Providers charge less for system instructions than for user content
Safety instructions are needed to authenticate the user to the model
quiz.why: Context budgeting should truncate untrusted content first, so that system and safety instructions are never cut to fit long inputs.

quiz.q: What is a key weakness of using an LLM as a content-filter judge?
o: It can only detect patterns such as card numbers and phone numbers
It is slower and costlier, and can be manipulated by the content it inspects
It can’t explain why it reached any of its decisions
It must be retrained from scratch every time the organisation’s content policy changes
quiz.why: Model-based judges are flexible but slow and expensive, and because they read the content, injected instructions can sway them.

quiz.q: In an agent system, where is safety MOST reliably enforced?
o: In the model’s system prompt, which tells it what it must never do
In the harness, which checks and executes every proposed action
In the user interface, which hides dangerous options from users
In the model’s training data, which teaches it good behaviour
quiz.why: The model only proposes actions; the harness decides what runs. Policy checks, approvals, budgets and stop conditions there don’t depend on the model obeying.

quiz.q: Why should a well-understood task use a fixed workflow rather than an open-ended agent?
o: Workflows always produce more creative and varied results for users
Fixed steps are predictable and testable, with a smaller action space
Open-ended agents can’t call tools or use retrieval at all
Workflows remove the need for any input or output guardrails
quiz.why: Fixing the steps in code limits what can happen and makes behaviour testable. Open-ended agents add flexibility, and risk, that a known task doesn’t need.

quiz.q: In the privileged and quarantined model pattern, what can the quarantined model do?
o: Plan the whole task, and then call any of the tools that the plan requires
Read untrusted content and return structured results, but not call tools
Approve high-impact actions on behalf of the human reviewer
Rewrite the system prompt when the user’s request changes
quiz.why: The quarantined model processes untrusted content without any ability to act, so instructions hidden in that content can’t reach the tools.

quiz.q: Why should AI functional tests report pass rates over repeated runs?
o: Repeated runs are needed to warm up the model’s cache before testing
Outputs vary between runs, so a single pass or fail can mislead
Regulators require every test case to be run at least ten times
Repeating tests reduces the cost of each individual evaluation
quiz.why: Non-determinism means the same input can pass once and fail the next time. Pass rates over many runs give a reliable picture.

quiz.q: Which performance measure BEST reflects how responsive a streaming chatbot feels to users?
o: The total number of GPUs available to the serving cluster
Time to first token, tracked at the higher percentiles
The average length of the answers the chatbot gives
The number of tokens in the model’s context window
quiz.why: Users feel the wait before text starts to appear, and tail percentiles show the worst experiences that averages hide.

quiz.q: Why does a load test that uses only short prompts prove very little?
o: Short prompts are blocked by most input guardrails
Cost and capacity scale with tokens, so long requests behave very differently
Load tests are only valid when they use real production personal data from customers
Short prompts make autoscaling switch off during the test
quiz.why: Realistic traffic includes long contexts and outputs, which use far more GPU memory and time. Tiny prompts overstate capacity.

quiz.q: What does a soak test MAINLY reveal?
o: How the system copes with a sudden surge of traffic
Problems that only appear over time, such as memory leaks
The exact point at which the system starts to fail as load keeps rising
Whether malformed inputs crash the request parser
quiz.why: Soak tests apply sustained load for hours or days. Spike, breakpoint and input-extreme tests cover the other cases.

quiz.q: What should a user-facing error message from an AI service contain?
o: The full stack trace, so that users can report the fault precisely
A generic message, with detailed diagnostics written only to internal logs
The system prompt, so that users understand why their request failed
The internal hostname of the failing service, to speed up support
quiz.why: Error messages are a common leak of internals and system prompts. Show users a safe, generic message and keep the details in logs.

quiz.q: Why should agent actions be idempotent where possible?
o: Idempotent actions always run faster than other kinds of agent action
Retrying them after an error won’t duplicate payments or messages
Idempotent actions don’t need any human approval
They let agents skip the harness’s policy checks safely
quiz.why: Failures lead to retries. If repeating an action has the same effect as doing it once, retries can’t cause double payments or duplicate sends.

exam.q: A customer-facing assistant’s input classifier blocks 4% of legitimate requests, and staff report that frustrated customers are switching to an unapproved public chatbot. What should the security team do FIRST?
o: Turn the input classifier off until a better product can be procured and tested
Measure false positives on representative data, then tune thresholds and policy per use case
Block access to the public chatbot at the firewall, so customers have no alternative to use
Tell customers in the interface that the blocks are for their own protection and safety
exam.why: Guardrails need measured error rates in both directions. Tuning against representative data reduces over-blocking without removing protection. Switching the filter off drops a control, blocking alternatives ignores the cause, and messaging doesn’t fix the error rate.

exam.q: A RAG assistant summarises supplier documents. A tester shows that a document containing hidden instructions can make the assistant include a phishing link in its answers. Which combination BEST reduces this risk?
o: A stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions it finds in documents
Labelled boundaries for retrieved content, plus output checks such as URL allow-lists
Retrieving fewer documents per question, so that each answer is based on less content
Retraining the embedding model on a larger and more varied set of supplier documents
exam.why: Layered controls work best: delimit and label untrusted content to reduce injection, and validate output, for example by allowing only approved domains, so a successful injection can’t deliver a malicious link.

exam.q: A finance agent can read invoices and issue payments. An injection test makes it pay a fraudulent invoice of £9,800. Which harness control MOST directly prevents a recurrence?
o: Fine-tuning the agent on examples of fraudulent invoices so it learns to spot them
A pre-execution policy check with payment limits, verified payees and human approval
Telling the agent in its system prompt to double-check every invoice before paying it
Moving the agent to a larger model that is more resistant to prompt injection
exam.why: Controls in the harness don’t rely on the model resisting manipulation: payee verification, limits and approval stop a fooled agent from completing the payment. Fine-tuning, prompts and bigger models all still depend on the model.

exam.q: A research agent browses the web and writes reports into a shared drive. During testing it gets stuck repeating the same search hundreds of times overnight. Which controls should the harness add?
o: A larger context window, so the agent can remember more of what it has already done
Step, time and cost budgets with loop detection, then stopping the run and escalating
Permission to delete old reports, so the shared drive doesn’t fill up during long runs
A second agent that watches the first and restarts it whenever it seems to be stuck
exam.why: Budgets and loop detection bound runaway behaviour, and escalation brings in a person. Bigger contexts don’t prevent loops, extra permissions raise risk, and automatic restarts can repeat the loop.

exam.q: A team updates the system prompt of a production RAG assistant to improve its tone. What is the BEST way to confirm the change is safe to release?
o: Check that the new prompt reads well and has been approved by the product owner
Run the regression, groundedness and guardrail test suites against the new prompt
Release it to all users and monitor the number of complaints over the next week
Compare the new prompt’s length with the old one, to confirm nothing was removed
exam.why: Prompt changes alter behaviour like code changes, so they need the same regression, groundedness and security behaviour tests with agreed thresholds. Approval of wording, complaint monitoring and length checks don’t show safety.

exam.q: During a failure test, the moderation API used to screen a chatbot’s replies times out. Logs show the chatbot sent replies to users without moderation while the API was down. What is the correct finding?
o: The test passed, because the chatbot stayed available throughout the outage
A defect: moderation must fail closed, holding or routing replies until it recovers
A minor issue, because most of the replies would probably have passed moderation anyway
The moderation API should be removed, because it reduces availability
exam.why: Security and safety checks must fail closed. Releasing unchecked content during an outage defeats the control; availability without the check isn’t a pass.

exam.q: An agent that books travel fails halfway through a task: the flight is booked but the hotel booking errors. On retry, it books a second flight. Which design changes BEST address this?
o: Increase the agent’s retry limit, so that it keeps trying until the hotel succeeds
Make bookings idempotent and track task state, so retries resume and partial work is handled
Remove the agent’s ability to book hotels, so that the task can no longer fail halfway
Ask users to check their bank statements for duplicate payments after each trip
exam.why: Idempotent actions and tracked state mean retries continue from where the task stopped instead of repeating completed steps, and partial work can be compensated or flagged. More retries make duplication worse, and the other options avoid the problem rather than fixing it.

quiz.q: Why should each AI agent have its own identity rather than share a service account?
o: Shared accounts are more expensive to license from most identity providers
Its actions can be attributed to it, and it can be revoked without affecting others
Agents run faster when each one authenticates with a different account name
Identity providers refuse to issue any tokens to accounts that are used by more than one agent
quiz.why: Distinct identities make actions attributable and let one agent be scoped, monitored or revoked on its own.

quiz.q: What is the MOST common weakness of non-human identities?
o: They are phished through convincing emails more often than people are
Long-lived secrets and excessive privileges, often with no clear owner
They can’t be given any multi-factor authentication of any kind
They expire too quickly for automated pipelines and services to use
quiz.why: Machine identities tend to accumulate broad rights and static secrets, and outlive the projects and people that created them.

quiz.q: What does a delegated token give that impersonation doesn’t?
o: Access to more data than the user has, which improves the quality of the agent’s answers
A record of both the user and the agent acting for them, with narrower scope
A permanent session, so the agent never needs to re-authenticate
The user’s password, so the agent can sign in to any system as them
quiz.why: Delegation (for example, token exchange with an actor claim) shows who acted for whom, limits the agent to the task, and lets it be revoked separately.

quiz.q: Why do proof-of-possession tokens strengthen accountability?
o: They last longer than bearer tokens, so there are fewer gaps in the logs
They are bound to a key the holder controls, so a stolen token can’t be replayed
They contain the user’s password, which proves who made the request
They can be shared safely between several different agents that are working on the same task
