quiz.why: Binding a token to a key (DPoP or mTLS) means only the legitimate holder can use it, which makes actions harder to fake and easier to attribute.

quiz.q: Which M2M approach removes the need to store a long-lived secret at all?
o: A static API key kept in an encrypted environment variable on every server that uses it
Workload identity federation, exchanging platform identity for short-lived tokens
OAuth client credentials using a shared client secret in configuration
Basic authentication with a long, randomly generated password
quiz.why: Federation relies on the platform vouching for the workload, so there is no stored key to steal or rotate.

quiz.q: Which checks should an API perform on every access token it receives?
o: Only that the token is present and long enough to be genuine
Its signature, issuer, audience, expiry and the scopes it grants
That the token was issued within the last calendar year
That the token’s format matches the one used in the documentation
quiz.why: Full validation stops forged, expired, over-scoped and misdirected tokens, including tokens issued for other services.

quiz.q: Where should a mobile app’s calls to a hosted LLM get their provider API key?
o: From the app bundle, encrypted with a key that is also stored inside the app
Nowhere: the app calls the organisation’s backend, which holds the key
From the user, who pastes their own key into the app’s settings screen
From a public configuration file that the app downloads at start-up
quiz.why: Any key shipped in a client can be extracted by users. A backend or AI gateway keeps the key server-side and enforces limits.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN security benefit of SCIM provisioning for AI tools?
o: It encrypts all of the prompts that are sent from the identity provider to each AI tool
Accounts are created and removed automatically, so leavers lose access promptly
It replaces the need for any multi-factor authentication on the tools
It lets users choose their own passwords for each tool they use
quiz.why: Automated provisioning and deprovisioning closes the gap where former staff keep accounts on tools that were managed by hand.

quiz.q: Which MFA method is phishing-resistant by design?
o: One-time codes sent to the user’s phone by SMS text message
Passkeys and other FIDO2 hardware-backed authenticators
Push notifications that the user simply approves or denies
Security questions about the user’s first school or pet
quiz.why: FIDO2 authenticators are bound to the genuine site’s origin, so credentials can’t be relayed through a fake site.

quiz.q: What does credential brokering for agents achieve?
o: The agent stores credentials more securely in its long-term memory
The tool layer attaches credentials to calls, so the model never sees them
Credentials are shared between agents, so fewer have to be issued
The agent can create brand-new credentials for itself whenever it decides that it needs them
quiz.why: Keeping secrets out of the model’s context means no prompt injection or prompt leak can expose them.

quiz.q: A model provider API key is found in a public repository. What should happen FIRST?
o: Investigate how long the key was public before deciding on any action
Revoke the key and issue a replacement, then review usage and find the source
Delete the file from the repository, which removes the exposure entirely
Email the provider to ask whether anyone has used the key since it leaked
quiz.why: Automated scanners find exposed keys within minutes, so revocation comes first. Deleting the file leaves the key in history and copies.

quiz.q: Why should training datasets be scanned for secrets before use?
o: Secrets make datasets too large to process efficiently on GPUs
Models can memorise secrets in training data and reproduce them later
Data protection law requires every dataset to be free of passwords
Secrets change the tokenizer, which reduces the model’s accuracy
quiz.why: Memorised credentials can be extracted from a model, so scrub secrets from code, documents and crawls before training.

exam.q: An identity review finds 3,000 service accounts and API keys across the AI platform. About 40% have no identifiable owner, and many have administrator rights. What should the identity team do FIRST?
o: Delete every unowned account immediately, whatever pipelines might break as a result
Discover and classify them, assign owners, and prioritise unowned privileged identities for review
Reset the passwords and keys of all 3,000 accounts, and email the new ones to the platform team
Commission a new identity platform, and leave the current accounts in place until it is ready
exam.why: You can’t govern what you haven’t classified or assigned. Ownership and risk-based prioritisation let the team reduce the riskiest identities first without breaking critical services. Mass deletion is reckless, mass resets spread secrets, and waiting leaves the risk in place.

exam.q: A bank’s customer-support agent can issue refunds. Regulators require proof of who authorised each refund. Today the agent uses one service account for every customer. Which design BEST meets the requirement?
o: Keep the service account, but add each customer’s name to the refund description field
Delegated tokens recording customer and agent, step-up approval for refunds, and tamper-evident logs
Give the agent each customer’s online banking password, so that every refund comes from their own account
Ask a supervisor to approve every refund verbally, and note the approval in a spreadsheet
exam.why: Delegation ties each action to both the customer and the agent, step-up authentication captures the authorisation strongly, and tamper-evident logs preserve the evidence. Free-text names, shared passwords and spreadsheets don’t provide non-repudiation.

exam.q: An investigation into a data deletion by an AI agent can’t determine which model version and instructions the agent was running at the time. What should be added to the audit design?
o: Nothing, because the agent’s identity alone is enough to attribute the action
Record the model version, system prompt version and tool configuration with each action
Require the agent to explain each action in plain language, and store its explanations
Keep screenshots of the agent’s user interface for every session it handles
exam.why: An agent’s behaviour depends on its model, prompt and tools, so accountability requires recording the configuration in force when it acted. Self-explanations can be wrong, and screenshots don’t capture configuration.

exam.q: Several internal services call a model inference API using one shared API key that hasn’t been rotated in two years. Which approach BEST improves authentication?
o: Rotate the shared key every month, and announce each new key to teams by email
Give each service its own workload identity, with short-lived, audience-bound tokens
Move the shared key into an environment variable on every server that needs it
Allow the API to be called only during business hours, to limit when misuse could occur
exam.why: Per-service workload identity makes calls attributable, removes the long-lived shared secret, and limits each token to the inference API. Rotation by email still shares one key, environment variables don’t change its nature, and time windows don’t authenticate.

exam.q: Staff are signing up for a popular AI chatbot with their corporate email addresses on personal plans. Security wants control without banning AI. What is the BEST approach?
o: Block the chatbot’s domain at the firewall, and remind all staff of the acceptable use policy for AI
Adopt the enterprise tier with SSO and SCIM, claim the corporate domain, and route staff to it
Ask staff to add their personal accounts to a register kept by the security team
Allow personal plans, but require staff to delete their chat history every week
exam.why: An enterprise tier federated to the IdP brings accounts under corporate MFA, provisioning and data terms, and domain controls stop unmanaged personal sign-ups, while still letting staff use AI. Blocking pushes usage elsewhere, and registers or deletion rules aren’t enforceable controls.

exam.q: An attacker phished an ML engineer’s password and one-time SMS code, then signed in to the model platform console and downloaded weights. Which control would MOST likely have prevented this?
o: Requiring the engineer to change their password every 30 days
Phishing-resistant MFA, such as passkeys, with step-up for weight exports
Sending SMS codes to two different phone numbers instead of one
Adding a prominent warning banner to the console about the value of the model weights
exam.why: FIDO2 passkeys can’t be relayed through a phishing site, and step-up authentication for high-risk actions adds a further barrier. Password rotation, extra SMS codes and banners don’t stop real-time phishing.

exam.q: A team’s MCP server configuration file contains plain-text tokens for five SaaS tools, and is shared across developer laptops. Which change BEST reduces the risk?
o: Encrypt the file with a single strong password that all of the developers share between them
Run tools behind a gateway that injects short-lived, vault-issued tokens per call
Store the file in a private repository, so only the team can read it
Rename the tokens in the file so that attackers won’t recognise them
exam.why: Brokered, short-lived credentials from a vault remove standing secrets from laptops and configuration, and the gateway can enforce policy. A shared password, a private repository and renaming all leave long-lived tokens exposed.

quiz.q: Why are narrow, purpose-built tools safer for agents than generic ones?
o: They run faster, because they make fewer calls to the database server
They limit what a manipulated agent can do, and are easier to test and govern
They don’t need any authentication, because their functions are so limited
They let the agent write its own queries when the narrow function isn’t enough
quiz.why: A narrow tool caps the impact of misuse and has a small, testable surface that policy can describe precisely.

quiz.q: Which situation is a separation of duties failure in an AI system?
o: Two teams run separate models for different products in the same cloud account
An agent can both create a new supplier and approve payments to that supplier
A model is monitored by the security operations centre as well as its own team
Training and deployment pipelines use different service identities and keys
quiz.why: Creating a payee and paying it are maker and checker duties, which shouldn’t sit with one identity.

quiz.q: Why is a second model a weak checker for a first model’s proposed actions?
o: Second models always cost more than human reviewers at scale
Both can be influenced by the same injected content, so errors may pass together
Regulators prohibit any one AI model from checking another AI model’s proposed output
Second models can’t read the output that the first model produces
quiz.why: Model-based checks share the same weaknesses as the model they check. Deterministic policy and human approval are stronger for high-impact steps.

quiz.q: What is the role of a policy enforcement point in AI authorisation?
o: To write and approve new access policies for the organisation each year
To sit in the request path and apply the policy engine’s decision
To train the model to refuse requests that break the access policy
To store the passwords that users need for each AI application
quiz.why: Enforcement points, such as gateways, tools and retrieval layers, intercept requests and apply allow, deny or conditional decisions.

quiz.q: Which access model checks whether a request’s declared purpose is approved for the data?
o: Role-based access control, using each user’s job title
Purpose-based access control, against approved purposes
Discretionary access control, set by each data owner
Mandatory access control, based on clearance labels
quiz.why: PBAC ties access to registered, approved purposes, which directly enforces purpose limitation and consent.

quiz.q: What does just-in-time access remove?
o: The need to authenticate administrators when they sign in
Standing privilege that sits unused for most of the time
The need to log what administrators do during sessions
All approval steps for high-risk administrative tasks
quiz.why: Elevation is granted for a task and revoked automatically, so compromised accounts hold no production rights most of the time.

quiz.q: What defines an agent’s real power?
o: The wording of its system prompt and the instructions in it
What its code can execute and what its credentials can reach
The size of the model it uses and its benchmark scores
The number of users who are allowed to talk to it each day
quiz.why: Prompts can be overridden. Execution boundaries and credential scopes set the actual limits on what an agent can do.

quiz.q: Which sandbox setting MOST reduces the risk of a code interpreter leaking secrets?
o: A larger memory allowance, so that code doesn’t crash during analysis
No credentials inside, and no outbound network access by default
A faster CPU, so that tasks finish before an attacker can act
Running the sandbox in the same network as the production database
quiz.why: With no secrets present and deny-by-default egress, injected code has nothing to steal and nowhere to send it.

quiz.q: What do resource indicators and token audiences achieve?
o: They make tokens last longer, so that agents re-authenticate less often
They bind a token to one API, so it can’t be replayed elsewhere
They let one token work for every API in the organisation
They hide the token’s contents from the API that receives it
quiz.why: Audience restriction stops a token issued for one service from being accepted by another, preventing replay and confused deputy attacks.

quiz.q: Which is an example of excessive autonomy?
o: An agent that summarises internal documents using a read-only enterprise search tool
An agent that sends emails to customers with no review or approval step
An agent that can call only three tools, each with narrow scopes
An agent whose actions are logged and monitored in real time
quiz.why: Excessive autonomy means high-impact actions happen without independent verification or approval.

quiz.q: What does attenuation mean in a chain of agents?
o: Each agent adds its own permissions to the token it passes on
Authority narrows at every hop: scope, amount, audience and lifetime
Agents pass the user’s full token along so that no step fails
The final agent in the chain decides which permissions to keep
quiz.why: Attenuation ensures each delegated agent holds only the slice of authority its task needs, limiting damage if one is manipulated.

quiz.q: Why should shared agent memory be treated as an attack path?
o: Shared memory uses too much storage for large deployments
Poisoned content written by one agent can steer the others that read it
Shared memory makes agents slower to respond to their users
Regulators require each agent to have a completely separate memory store of its own
quiz.why: Content stored by a compromised or manipulated agent can spread instructions to others, so writes need controls, provenance and validation.

exam.q: An HR assistant agent can read employee records, update salary fields, and approve salary changes it has proposed. Which change BEST applies separation of duties?
o: Keep the current design, but log every salary change the agent makes for later review
Let the agent propose salary changes, with approval by an authorised manager in a separate step
Remove the agent’s ability to read employee records, so it can’t see any salary information
Ask the agent in its system prompt to double-check every salary change before approving it
exam.why: Splitting proposal (maker) from approval (checker) means no single identity, and especially no manipulable agent, completes a sensitive change alone. Logging detects but doesn’t prevent, removing reads breaks the use case, and prompts aren’t controls.

exam.q: A data science team’s shared service account can modify training datasets, run training, and mark models as approved in the registry. What is the BEST first remediation?
o: Rotate the service account’s credentials every month and keep the same permissions
Split the duties across separate identities, and remove registry approval from the build team
Enable detailed logging on the account, and review the logs whenever an incident occurs
Restrict the account so that it can be used only from the office network during work hours
exam.why: The account combines data change, build and approval: a toxic combination that lets one compromise poison and promote a model. Separate identities with approval held by independent roles fix the root cause. Rotation, logging and location limits don’t.

exam.q: A RAG assistant answers staff questions from a document store. Junior staff report seeing excerpts from board papers they can’t open directly. Where should the fix be applied?
o: In the system prompt, instructing the model never to quote from any confidential board documents
In the retrieval layer, filtering results to the documents the requesting user may access
In the user interface, hiding answers that mention the word “board”
In the training data, removing board papers from the model’s pre-training corpus
exam.why: Authorisation must be enforced where content is selected: retrieval should only return documents the user is entitled to see. Prompts and keyword filters are bypassable, and RAG content isn’t in the model’s training data.

exam.q: During an incident at 2 a.m., an engineer needs immediate access to a production model’s serving cluster, but the usual approver is unreachable. What should the access design provide?
o: A permanent administrator account for each on-call engineer, used only in emergencies
Controlled break-glass access: fast, time-limited, fully logged and reviewed afterwards
The approver’s password, kept in a sealed envelope in the operations room for emergencies
No access until the approver is available, whatever the impact of the incident
exam.why: Break-glass access balances speed with control: it works without normal approval, but is limited, monitored and reviewed. Standing admin accounts and shared passwords destroy least privilege and accountability, and refusing access can worsen the incident.

exam.q: A browser automation agent books meetings for executives. During testing, it navigates to an attacker’s page that instructs it to visit the company’s internal admin portal, where it is already signed in. Which boundary MOST directly prevents harm?
o: A system prompt telling the agent to ignore instructions it finds on web pages
An isolated browser profile with no internal sessions, and a domain allow-list for the task
A faster model that finishes each booking before any attacker has a chance to interfere with the agent
Asking executives to check the agent’s browser history at the end of each day
exam.why: An isolated profile without privileged sessions, plus allow-listed domains, removes both the reachable target and the path to it. Prompt instructions can be overridden, speed is irrelevant, and history checks only detect afterwards.

exam.q: A procurement agent can raise purchase orders of any value with any supplier, and does so automatically when a request seems valid. A manipulated request leads to a £48,000 order with a fraudulent supplier. Which combination BEST prevents a recurrence?
o: Retraining the agent on thousands of examples of fraudulent purchase requests and invoices
Supplier allow-lists, value caps, and human approval above a set threshold
A disclaimer in the agent’s replies saying that orders may contain errors
Moving the agent to a larger model that is harder to manipulate
exam.why: Removing excessive permissions (any supplier, any value) and excessive autonomy (no approval) stops a manipulated agent completing a high-impact action. Retraining, disclaimers and bigger models still rely on the model resisting manipulation.

exam.q: A security review finds that twelve internal agents share one service account, which can reach the CRM, finance and HR systems. Any one agent being manipulated could reach all three. What should be done?
o: Keep the shared account, but monitor it far more closely for any unusual activity across all three systems
Give each agent its own identity with access only to its systems, and segment the networks
Rename the service account so attackers are less likely to recognise it
Allow the shared account to be used only during business hours
exam.why: Per-agent identities with minimal access and network segmentation stop one compromised agent becoming a path into every system. Monitoring alone, renaming and time windows leave the shared reach in place.

quiz.q: Why must every non-human identity in the inventory have a named owner?
o: Owners are needed to calculate the licence cost of each identity provider seat
Someone must be accountable for its purpose, permissions and retirement
Identity providers refuse to authenticate identities that have no owner field
Owners receive copies of every prompt the identity sends to models
quiz.why: Without an accountable person, non-human identities drift, accumulate rights and are never retired.

quiz.q: Which source do traditional identity tools MOST often miss in AI environments?
o: Employee accounts created in the corporate identity provider
Agents, API keys and MCP server registrations on AI platforms
Group memberships synchronised from the HR system each night
Administrator accounts in the main cloud identity service
quiz.why: AI platforms create their own identities and credentials, which need to be discovered and correlated with the rest of the inventory.

quiz.q: What is a dormant identity?
o: An identity that belongs to an employee currently on annual leave
An identity that hasn’t been used for a long period, such as 90 days
An identity that can sign in only outside normal business hours
An identity whose password is due to expire within the next week
quiz.why: Dormant identities keep their access without being needed, which makes them attractive to attackers and candidates for removal.

quiz.q: Where do excess privileges MOST often accumulate in the identity lifecycle?
o: When new joiners receive their standard birthright access on day one
When people move roles, gaining new access without losing the old
When leavers are disabled in the identity provider
When contractors are given accounts with end dates
quiz.why: Mover processes that only add access leave people with rights from every role they have held.

quiz.q: Why isn’t disabling a leaver’s main account enough in AI environments?
o: Disabling accounts is reversible, so it doesn’t count as removal
Personal API keys, OAuth grants and scheduled jobs can keep working
AI tools ignore the identity provider once a user has signed in once
Regulators require all leaver accounts to be deleted on the same day
quiz.why: Keys, refresh tokens and jobs running under the leaver’s identity survive account disablement unless they are revoked too.

quiz.q: Why should an identity usually be disabled first and deleted later?
o: Deleted identities can never be audited, even while they still exist
Disabling is instant and reversible; deletion can break services or lose evidence
Disabled identities cost less to store in the identity provider than active or deleted ones do
Deletion requires approval from the regulator in most countries
quiz.why: Disable to stop access at once; delete once ownership is transferred, investigations are closed and retention is met.

quiz.q: What makes an access review effective rather than a rubber stamp?
o: Reviewers sign a declaration confirming that they checked every line
Usage and risk context, the right reviewer, and automatic revocation
Reviews are run more often, so each one covers fewer changes
All entitlements are exported into one spreadsheet for review
quiz.why: Reviewers need information and authority to judge access, and decisions must be applied without manual delay.

quiz.q: What does identity security posture management (ISPM) add to periodic reviews?
o: It replaces the need for any human decisions about access
Continuous checks for misconfiguration, excess privilege and stale identities
Real-time blocking of every single sign-in attempt that comes from an unfamiliar location
A single password for each user across every application
quiz.why: ISPM finds identity risk between review campaigns and feeds remediation and the next review.

quiz.q: Why do non-human identities often show the biggest gap between granted and used permissions?
o: Machines are given fewer permissions than people, so the gap is easier to see
Rights are granted generously at creation and rarely trimmed afterwards
Non-human identities can’t use more than one permission at a time
Identity providers hide which permissions machines actually use
quiz.why: Service accounts and agents are often created with broad rights "to make it work", and nobody revisits them.

quiz.q: What should token accounting record for each AI request?
o: The full prompt and response text, so that costs can be explained later
Identity, application, model, token counts, cost and policy decisions
Only the total monthly cost, as shown on the provider’s invoice
The user’s password hash, to prove who made the request
quiz.why: Attribution and usage data support budgets, anomaly detection and audit without storing sensitive prompt content.

quiz.q: A key’s daily token use jumps tenfold overnight, from a new country. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: A normal seasonal increase in customer demand for the product
A leaked credential being used by someone else
A billing error by the model provider that will be refunded
A successful upgrade to a faster model version
quiz.why: Sudden volume changes from new locations against a stable baseline are a classic sign of a stolen key.

quiz.q: Why should agents have maximum run times and step limits per task?
o: Long-running agents produce more accurate answers than short ones
They stop runaway loops consuming tokens, money and capacity
Model providers require agents to stop after a fixed number of steps
They let agents run without any rate limits on their tools
quiz.why: Run-time and step limits bound the cost and impact of agents that loop or go off course.

exam.q: After an incident, investigators can’t tell which systems a compromised AI agent could reach, because its permissions were granted ad hoc and never recorded. What should the organisation implement FIRST?
o: A policy requiring agents to log their own permissions in their system prompts
An automated identity inventory covering agents, with owners and effective permissions
A rule that all agents must be rebuilt from scratch every month to reset permissions
A quarterly survey asking teams which agents they run and what each can access
exam.why: A living inventory with effective permissions answers scope questions immediately and supports reviews and response. Self-reported prompts, monthly rebuilds and surveys are unreliable or disruptive.

exam.q: A contractor’s engagement ended two months ago. Her account was disabled, but an AI coding assistant she connected to the company’s code repositories through an OAuth grant is still pulling code nightly. What is the BEST process fix?
o: Ask contractors to disconnect any AI tools they connected before their last day
Revoke OAuth grants, tokens and keys automatically at deprovisioning, driven by the inventory
Ban all AI coding assistants for contractors, whatever the business need
Review the repository access logs once a year to find any AI tools that are still connected to it
exam.why: Deprovisioning must cover every credential type, including OAuth grants and refresh tokens, automatically. Relying on the leaver, blanket bans or annual log reviews leave the gap open.

exam.q: A team asks for a new autonomous agent with write access to the CRM and email. Which provisioning approach BEST fits identity lifecycle good practice?
o: Let the agent use the requesting team lead’s own account and mailbox, so that it can start work immediately
A request with purpose, sponsor and risk; approved scopes; its own identity, inventory entry and expiry
Create a generic service account with broad access, so future agents can reuse it
Provision the agent first, and complete the approval paperwork within the next quarter
exam.why: Agents need a governed lifecycle: a justified request, approved least-privilege scopes, a distinct identity, inventory registration and an end date. Borrowed human accounts and shared broad accounts break accountability and least privilege.

exam.q: An auditor finds that the AI platform’s access review covered only human users, and 1,800 service accounts and API keys were never reviewed. What is the BEST response?
o: Explain that service accounts are technical, so they fall outside the review’s scope
Extend reviews to non-human identities, with owners, usage data and automatic remediation
Delete every service account and API key that wasn’t reviewed, and recreate them as needed
Ask the platform team to confirm in writing that all service accounts are still needed
exam.why: Non-human identities often hold the broadest, least-used rights, so they must be in scope, reviewed by owners with usage context, and remediated automatically. Exclusion, mass deletion and written assurances don’t give real control.

exam.q: ISPM reports that 30% of identities with access to the model registry don’t have MFA enforced, including two administrator accounts. What should be done FIRST?
o: Schedule the issue for discussion at next year’s access review campaign
Enforce phishing-resistant MFA on the two admin accounts now, then close the other gaps
Remove registry access from every identity, including the people who need it daily
Accept the risk, because the registry can only be reached from inside the corporate network anyway
exam.why: Privileged accounts without MFA are the most urgent exposure, so they are fixed first, followed by the rest. Waiting, blanket removal and accepting the risk on network grounds are all inappropriate.

exam.q: Finance asks for a way to control spending on AI services without blocking legitimate work, and security wants early warning of misuse. Which design BEST meets both needs?
o: A single shared API key for the whole company, with spending reviewed every quarter
Gateway metering per identity, with budgets, baselines and alerts, and caps per team
A ban on AI services until a full business case is approved for every use
Asking teams to estimate their monthly usage, and reconciling it against invoices
exam.why: Per-identity metering at a gateway supports budgets and caps for finance and baselines with alerts for security. Shared keys hide who used what, bans block legitimate work, and estimates don’t detect misuse.

quiz.q: What does "no standing access" mean for AI production systems?
o: Nobody is ever allowed to access production models or data for any reason
Privileged rights are granted just in time for each task, then removed again
Access is granted only to engineers who are physically present in the office
Production access is shared through one team account with a strong password
quiz.why: Standing privileges are an easy target. Just-in-time elevation gives engineers the rights they need, only while they need them, with a record of each use.

quiz.q: Which arrangement BEST shows separation of duties for model releases?
o: The data scientist who trained the model also approves and deploys it, to save time
The author, the approver and the deploying pipeline are separate parties
The model is deployed first, and approved afterwards by the author’s manager
The release is approved by whoever is on call when the model is ready
quiz.why: Separating authorship, approval and deployment means no single person can push an unreviewed or malicious change to production.

quiz.q: What should happen after an emergency change has been deployed?
o: Nothing further, because it was approved by the on-call authority at the time
A post-implementation review within a set time, and updated records
It should be reversed automatically after 24 hours unless it is renewed
It should be reported to the regulator as a deviation from process
quiz.why: Emergency changes trade some up-front scrutiny for speed, so a prompt review confirms the change was right, and records keep it from becoming invisible drift.

quiz.q: Who is usually accountable for decisions about an AI model in production, such as restricting or retiring it?
o: The data scientist who originally built and trained the model
The model owner, typically a senior leader in the business
The security operations centre that monitors the model
The cloud provider that hosts the model’s serving infrastructure
quiz.why: The model owner answers for the model’s use and outcomes, so production decisions are theirs, while technical teams carry them out.

quiz.q: In a RACI matrix, what is the difference between responsible and accountable?
o: Responsible people approve the work; accountable people carry it out
Responsible people do the work; one accountable person owns the decision
Responsible people are internal staff; accountable people are vendors
There is no difference; the two terms are interchangeable in RACI
quiz.why: Several people may be responsible for doing the work, but exactly one person is accountable for each decision.

quiz.q: What is a human override baseline?
o: The maximum number of times a reviewer may override the AI in a day
The normal rate at which reviewers overrule AI outputs, measured in pilots
The minimum accuracy a model must reach before human reviewers are allowed to stop checking it
The number of reviewers needed to override a single AI decision
quiz.why: The baseline describes normal behaviour, so upper and lower thresholds around it can reveal model problems or rubber-stamping.

quiz.q: Why might an override rate falling close to zero be a warning sign?
o: It shows that the model has been retrained on too little data
Reviewers may be rubber-stamping outputs because of automation bias
It indicates that the decision threshold was set too high at launch
It proves that the human reviewers are no longer needed
quiz.why: Overrides near zero, especially with very fast reviews, suggest people have stopped checking, which silently removes the human safeguard.

quiz.q: Why should reject rate thresholds be set in both directions?
o: Because regulators require two thresholds for every metric that is monitored
Both too many and too few rejections can signal a real problem
Because a single threshold can’t be displayed on most dashboards
So that the threshold can be adjusted whenever users complain
quiz.why: Too many rejections suggest over-blocking or a broken model; too few suggest a failed control or eroded safety behaviour.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a playbook and a runbook?
o: Playbooks are written by vendors; runbooks are written in-house
Playbooks cover decisions and roles; runbooks give exact steps for a task
Playbooks are used only in exercises; runbooks are used only in real incidents
A playbook covers technical commands; a runbook covers communications
quiz.why: Playbooks coordinate the response to a type of incident; runbooks are the tested, step-by-step instructions they call on.

quiz.q: What is an inject in a tabletop exercise?
o: A test input sent to a production model during the exercise
New information introduced during the exercise to force decisions
A summary of lessons learned that is circulated after the exercise
A scripted answer that participants read out at each stage
quiz.why: Injects, such as a journalist’s call or new evidence, make the scenario evolve and test how the team decides under pressure.

quiz.q: Which of these is a configuration item for an AI system?
o: How many users signed up for the product in the last month
The system prompt, with its approved version number and hash
The marketing description of the product on the company website
The names of the data scientists who built the first prototype
quiz.why: Anything whose settings shape the system’s behaviour, such as prompts, model versions, guardrails, indexes and tool permissions, is a configuration item.

quiz.q: How does configuration drift differ from model drift?
o: Configuration drift affects only infrastructure; model drift affects only data
Configuration drift means the system was changed; model drift means the world changed
They are the same thing, described by different teams in different ways
Configuration drift is always malicious; model drift is always accidental
quiz.why: Configuration drift is a change to the system itself, such as an edited prompt; model drift comes from changes in the data or environment.

exam.q: An AI platform team uses one shared administrator account for production model changes, so on-call engineers can act quickly at night. An audit finds that nobody can tell who changed a guardrail threshold last month. What is the BEST remediation?
o: Keep the shared account, but change its password every month and limit who knows it
Named individual identities, just-in-time elevation and logged break-glass access
Remove all production access, so that guardrail thresholds can never be changed again
Ask engineers to note their changes in the team chat after each shift
exam.why: Individual identities with just-in-time elevation and logged break-glass access keep speed and restore accountability. Password rotation keeps the account shared, removing all access stops operations, and chat notes are unreliable.

exam.q: A retailer’s recommendation model is found to be using customer purchase data for a purpose customers weren’t told about. The data science team says it only builds models, and the business says the data team approved it. Which gap does this MOST clearly reveal?
o: The model was trained without enough data to produce accurate recommendations
No clear data owner accountable for approving uses of the customer data
The security operations centre failed to detect the misuse in its logs
The company didn’t buy a commercial recommendation engine from a vendor
exam.why: Each side assumes the other approved the use, which shows that nobody is accountable for decisions about the data. A named data owner approves uses, access and retention.

exam.q: A hospital is preparing to release an AI triage assistant. Evaluations have passed and the security review is complete, but no alerts or dashboards exist yet, and the team plans to add them "after go-live". What should the security lead recommend?
o: Release on schedule, because evaluations and the security review were both passed
Delay release until monitoring, alerting and agreed thresholds are in place
Release to all users, but ask clinicians to report any problems they notice
Cancel the project, because the team has shown it can’t be trusted with AI
exam.why: Monitoring is a release requirement: without it, degradation or attacks would go unnoticed in a high-impact setting. Releasing anyway relies on luck or users, and cancelling is disproportionate.

exam.q: Three months after launch, a content moderation guardrail’s block rate drops from 4% of inputs to 0.1% overnight, with no change in traffic. What is the MOST likely explanation to investigate first?
o: Users have become more polite, so fewer of their inputs now need to be blocked
The guardrail may have failed, or been disabled or misconfigured by a change
Attackers have given up trying to misuse the system after launch
The model provider has improved the model, so the guardrail is no longer needed
exam.why: A sudden fall with stable traffic points to a broken or altered control, which is why reject rate thresholds have a lower bound. Behaviour rarely changes overnight like this.

exam.q: A company has a detailed general IT incident response plan. It is adopting several AI agents that can act on customer accounts. During a review, which gap is MOST important to address?
o: The plan’s contact list hasn’t been updated with the AI vendor’s sales team
No AI-specific playbooks, such as agent misbehaviour, or exercises to test them
The plan is stored as a PDF instead of in a collaborative online editor
The plan doesn’t include a glossary explaining AI terms for new staff
exam.why: AI incidents need specific triggers, containment such as disabling agents, and evidence such as tool-call logs, and teams must practise them. The other gaps are minor.

exam.q: During a tabletop exercise on training data poisoning, participants realise they can’t identify which production models were trained on the suspect dataset. What should the organisation do as a result?
o: Retrain every production model immediately, in case any of them were affected
Implement data and model lineage tracking, and add lineage checks to the playbook
Stop running tabletop exercises, because they create unnecessary concern among staff
Ask data scientists to keep personal notes of the datasets used for each model
exam.why: Lineage lets responders scope a poisoning incident quickly, and the playbook should use it. Retraining everything is disproportionate, stopping exercises hides gaps, and personal notes are unreliable.

exam.q: A financial firm calls a hosted LLM through the provider’s "latest" model alias. After a provider update, output formats change and a downstream payment workflow breaks. Which control would BEST have prevented this?
o: Asking the provider to give at least a week’s notice before changing any model
Pinning a dated model version, and testing each new version before switching
Building a second workflow that can be used whenever the first one breaks
Monitoring the provider’s status page for announcements of model releases
exam.why: A pinned version can’t change underneath the workflow, and new versions are adopted only after testing. Notice periods and status pages don’t stop the change, and a second workflow adds cost without fixing the cause.

exam.q: A retraining pipeline automatically deploys a new fraud model every night if training completes without errors. Which change BEST reduces the risk of this process?
o: Run the retraining pipeline weekly instead of nightly, so there are fewer releases
Treat each retrained model as a candidate gated by evaluations and approval
Let the pipeline deploy, but email the data science team a summary each morning
Disable automated retraining, and retrain manually only once a year
exam.why: Finishing without errors doesn’t mean a model is good or safe. Evaluation gates and risk-based approval keep the automation while stopping poor or poisoned models reaching production.

quiz.q: Why should every AI telemetry event carry a shared trace ID?
o: So that events can be deleted together when the retention period ends
To join events from the gateway, agent, retrieval, model and tools for one request
To let the model provider bill each request to the correct customer account
To encrypt each event with a key derived from the request identifier
quiz.why: A trace ID lets analysts follow a single request through every layer, which is essential for reconstructing what an AI system did.

quiz.q: Which telemetry would BEST reveal that a RAG assistant returned a document the user wasn’t entitled to see?
o: Gateway logs showing the number of tokens sent and received in each request
Retrieval logs with document IDs and the access filter applied
Model serving logs showing the latency of each response
Billing records showing the monthly cost of the assistant
quiz.why: Only retrieval telemetry shows which documents came back for which user, and whether access filtering was applied.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record model and system prompt versions with AI events?
o: Versions are needed to work out the provider’s charges for each request
Behaviour depends on them, so investigators need them to explain outputs
Regulators require version numbers to be shown to users in every response
Version numbers make the logs smaller, because content can then be dropped
quiz.why: The same input can produce different behaviour under a different model or prompt version, so versions are part of the evidence.

quiz.q: What is the main role of SOAR in AI incident response?
o: Storing AI telemetry for long-term compliance and audit purposes
Running playbooks that enrich alerts and automate response actions
Training detection models on the organisation’s historical incidents
Sharing indicators with other organisations through industry groups
quiz.why: SOAR platforms orchestrate enrichment, triage and response steps, such as pausing an agent or revoking a key.

quiz.q: Why are sequence rules useful for detecting AI attacks?
o: They run faster than any other type of correlation rule in the SIEM
Weak signals in order, such as injection then exfiltration, reveal attacks
They remove the need to collect telemetry from AI agents and tools
They let analysts review every alert in the order it was received
quiz.why: Individually weak events become strong evidence when they occur in a meaningful order within one trace or time window.

quiz.q: What do STIX and TAXII provide?
o: A method for encrypting logs before they are forwarded to the SIEM platform
A standard format for threat intelligence, and a protocol to exchange it
A framework for scoring and classifying the severity of AI vulnerabilities
A certification scheme for security operations centre analysts
quiz.why: STIX describes threat intelligence in a standard structure, and TAXII exchanges it automatically between platforms and partners.

quiz.q: Why should AI logs be forwarded off the source system as they are created?
o: Local disks on AI servers are usually too small to hold all their telemetry
An attacker who compromises the host can’t then erase the record
Central storage is always cheaper than local storage
Model providers require logs to be stored in a central SIEM
quiz.why: Logs that stay on a compromised host can be altered or deleted, so they must leave it immediately for protected storage.

quiz.q: What is log injection?
o: Adding extra logging statements to an application to improve its visibility
Untrusted input written unescaped, so crafted text forges log entries
Copying logs from one SIEM into another during a migration
Sending logs to the SIEM faster than it can process them
quiz.why: Prompts, outputs and tool results are untrusted input; escaping them before logging stops forged or corrupted entries (CWE-117).

quiz.q: Why should analysts work on copies of log evidence rather than the originals?
o: Copies are smaller, so analysis tools can process them more quickly
The originals stay unaltered, so findings can be verified against them
Original logs are encrypted, so most analysis tools can’t read them at all
Copies can be shared publicly without needing any approval
quiz.why: Preserved, hashed originals let anyone confirm that the evidence analysed is exactly what was collected.

quiz.q: Which masking technique keeps correlation working without allowing the value to be reversed?
o: Redaction, which removes the value entirely
Keyed hashing, which gives a consistent pseudonym
Tokenisation, which stores the original in a vault
Format-preserving encryption, which keeps the format
quiz.why: A keyed hash maps the same value to the same pseudonym every time, but can’t be reversed without the key. Tokenisation and encryption are reversible; redaction breaks correlation.

quiz.q: Why should masking happen at collection rather than inside the SIEM?
o: The SIEM can’t search data that has been masked by another system
Otherwise raw data sits in transit, buffers and storage before masking
Masking in the SIEM is prohibited by most data protection laws
Collection-time masking removes the need for any access controls
quiz.why: Masking at the edge means raw personal data and secrets never travel or rest in the analytics pipeline.

quiz.q: Why is a weekly report not enough to monitor AI agents?
o: Weekly reports can’t include charts of agent activity over time
Agents can cause serious harm in minutes, long before a weekly review
Regulators require AI agents to be monitored every hour of every day
Weekly reports are too expensive to produce for each agent
quiz.why: Agents act at machine speed, so detection and containment must work in seconds or minutes, with batch reports for trends.

quiz.q: What is embedding drift?
o: A gradual increase in the size of the vector database over time
A shift in input embeddings away from a baseline, as user topics change
The loss of precision when embeddings are stored as smaller numbers
A change of embedding model made by the provider without telling its customers
quiz.why: Embedding drift shows that the content of inputs has moved away from what the system was built and tested for.

exam.q: An organisation’s AI gateway logs every request’s metadata, but its agents call internal APIs directly, and those calls aren’t logged. After a suspected data leak, investigators can’t tell what the agents did. What should be implemented FIRST?
o: A policy requiring agents to describe their actions in their final responses
Tool-call telemetry from the agent framework, linked to requests by trace ID
A second AI gateway in front of the first, to capture the same metadata twice
A monthly review of agent permissions by each agent’s business owner
exam.why: Tool-call telemetry, joined to requests, shows what agents actually did. Self-descriptions are unreliable, a second gateway sees the same traffic, and permission reviews don’t record actions.

exam.q: A company wants to capture full prompt and response content for all 40 of its AI applications, "in case it is ever needed". The privacy officer objects. What is the BEST compromise?
o: Capture full content for every application, but delete it after five years
Metadata for all; content by risk, flagged sessions or sample, in a restricted store
Capture no telemetry at all, so that there is no privacy risk from AI logging
Capture full content, but only for requests made by employees, not customers
exam.why: Metadata supports most detection; selective content in a restricted store supports investigations while respecting minimisation. Blanket capture, no capture and arbitrary splits by user type fail one goal or the other.

exam.q: A SOC wants to automate responses to AI alerts. Which action is MOST suitable for full automation without human approval?
o: Rolling back the model for all customers to a version from last year
Pausing an agent and holding its outbound message pending review
Deleting the training dataset that a poisoning alert refers to
Notifying the regulator that a serious AI incident has occurred
exam.why: Pausing and holding are safe and reversible, so they suit automation. Fleet-wide rollbacks, data deletion and regulatory notification are disruptive or irreversible and need human decisions.

exam.q: Threat intelligence reports that a set of IP addresses is systematically querying AI APIs across the financial sector to copy model behaviour. What should the SOC do with this intelligence?
o: Wait until the same addresses are actually seen attacking the organisation’s own systems
Add the indicators to gateway enrichment and detections, and hunt for past activity
Forward the report to all staff, asking them to watch for unusual AI behaviour
Ask the model provider whether it has seen the addresses, and do nothing else
exam.why: Operationalising intelligence means using it in detection and enrichment now, and hunting for earlier activity. Waiting, broadcasting to staff or relying on the provider leaves the organisation exposed.

exam.q: An attacker who gained administrator access to an AI platform deleted the platform’s local audit logs. Which control would BEST have preserved the evidence?
o: Daily email summaries of audit events sent to the platform administrators
Forwarding events in real time to a separately administered, write-once store
Encrypting the local audit logs with a key held by the platform administrators
Increasing the local audit log retention period from 30 days to one year
exam.why: Logs forwarded immediately to storage the attacker doesn’t control, and can’t modify, survive the compromise. Summaries, local encryption and longer local retention don’t.

exam.q: Investigators preparing AI logs for a legal case must show they haven’t been altered since collection. Which practice BEST supports this?
o: Storing the exported logs in a shared folder that only members of the legal team can see
Hashing each export, preserving originals, and recording the chain of custody
Printing the logs and asking the investigators to sign every page
Converting the logs into a summary report written by the lead investigator
exam.why: Hashes prove integrity, preserved originals allow verification, and a custody record shows who handled the evidence. Folder permissions, signatures on printouts and summaries don’t prove the data is unchanged.

exam.q: A SOC needs to track individual users’ activity across AI applications to detect abuse, but analysts mustn’t see customers’ identities. Which approach BEST meets both needs?
o: Remove all user identifiers from AI telemetry before it reaches the SIEM
Replace identifiers with consistent keyed-hash pseudonyms at collection
Show analysts full identities, but log every search they make in the SIEM
Ask customers to consent to their identities being visible to analysts
exam.why: Consistent pseudonyms preserve correlation without revealing identity. Removing identifiers breaks detection, logging searches doesn’t prevent exposure, and consent isn’t a substitute for minimisation.

exam.q: An employee pastes a production database password into an AI assistant’s prompt. The telemetry pipeline’s secret scanner detects it. What should happen?
o: Store the prompt as normal, because the SIEM is already access-controlled
Remove the secret from all telemetry and trigger rotation of the password
Tokenise the password, so investigators can recover it later if needed
Hash the password, so analysts can tell whether it is used again elsewhere
exam.why: Secrets should never be stored in telemetry, and once exposed to an AI system they must be rotated. Storing, tokenising or hashing them keeps an exposed credential in use.

exam.q: A bank’s customer chatbot shows a sudden doubling of refusals and a jump in jailbreak-detector hits from a small set of accounts. What is the MOST appropriate real-time response?
o: Wait for next week’s batch report to confirm the trend before taking any action
Throttle the accounts automatically, alert the SOC and investigate the pattern
Switch the chatbot off for all customers until the model can be retrained
Lower the jailbreak detector’s sensitivity, so it raises fewer alerts
exam.why: A targeted, reversible guard on the suspicious accounts, plus investigation, contains a likely attack campaign without affecting other customers. Waiting, a full shutdown or desensitising the detector are all poor responses.

exam.q: An AI agent that normally makes about 20 API calls an hour makes 3,000 in ten minutes, all to an internal HR system. What should the monitoring design have ensured?
o: That the agent’s owner reviews a summary of its activity at the end of each month
An alert from its per-agent baseline, with an automatic, reversible pause
That the HR system’s administrators are told to watch for unusual traffic
That the agent is rebuilt from scratch every week to reset its behaviour
exam.why: Per-agent baselines catch abnormal action rates quickly, and an automatic pause limits the damage while people investigate. Monthly reviews, informal watching and weekly rebuilds don’t detect or stop the activity.

quiz.q: Why should retrieved documents be scanned for injected instructions, not just user prompts?
o: Retrieved documents are usually larger, so scanning them is cheaper overall
Indirect injection arrives through content the model reads, not what the user types
User prompts can’t contain injection attempts once they pass the gateway
Scanning retrieved documents removes the need for any output monitoring
quiz.why: Attackers who can place content where the system will read it don’t need access to the prompt box at all.

quiz.q: What is a canary token used for in AI runtime detection?
o: Measuring how quickly a model responds to each request while under heavy load
Revealing leakage when a planted unique string appears where it shouldn’t
Encrypting sensitive fields in prompts before they reach the model
Counting the tokens each user consumes against their monthly quota
quiz.why: A unique string planted in a system prompt or document has no legitimate reason to appear in outputs or elsewhere, so its appearance is a high-confidence leak signal.

quiz.q: Which signal MOST suggests a denial-of-wallet attack?
o: A single user receiving several refusals in a row from the model
One key sending many maximum-length requests, far above its baseline
A slight increase in the average response latency during normal business hours
A new model version being deployed through the standard pipeline
quiz.why: Repeated maximum-length requests from one key drive up cost by design, especially when far outside that key’s normal pattern.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between an unauthorised identity and an over-privileged agent?
o: Unauthorised identities are always external attackers, and agents are always internal
One is access that shouldn’t exist; the other is legitimate access that’s too broad
Over-privileged agents can’t be detected, while unauthorised identities can
There is no practical difference, as both are handled in exactly the same way
quiz.why: Unauthorised access is revoked and rotated; excess privilege is reduced to what the agent actually needs, and its recent actions reviewed.

quiz.q: Why is the first use of a high-risk tool by an agent a useful detection signal?
o: First uses are always caused by bugs in the agent framework’s code
It may indicate hijacking, over-delegation or an unapproved change
Tools can only be used once before they need to be re-approved
It shows the agent has become more capable and needs more access
quiz.why: A change in an agent’s behaviour outside its purpose profile is often the first visible sign that it has been manipulated or misconfigured.

quiz.q: What does a large gap between an agent’s granted and used permissions indicate?
o: The agent is working efficiently and needs no changes to its access
Excess privilege that could be abused if the agent is manipulated
The identity provider is failing to record the agent’s activity
The agent should be given even more permissions for future tasks
quiz.why: Unused rights add risk without value: a manipulated or stolen agent identity could use them.

quiz.q: A secret is found in a prompt sent to an external model provider. What is the MOST important action?
o: Delete the prompt from the organisation’s own logs so nobody else sees it
Revoke and rotate the secret, then check whether it has been used
Ask the provider to confirm it hasn’t trained on the prompt
Remind the employee of the policy on sharing secrets with AI tools
quiz.why: Once a secret has left your control it must be treated as compromised. Rotation makes the exposed copy useless.

quiz.q: Which tool-call pattern is the strongest exfiltration signal?
o: An agent calling the same read-only tool several times in a row
A sensitive read followed by a send to a new external destination
An agent using a tool with arguments that match its usual, approved ranges
A tool call that is approved by a human before it is executed
quiz.why: Read-then-send chains to unfamiliar destinations are how hijacked agents move data out.

quiz.q: Why should secrets never be placed in system prompts?
o: System prompts are limited to a few hundred characters by most providers
System prompts can leak through outputs, logs and deliberate attacks
Secrets in system prompts make the model’s answers less accurate
Providers charge extra for system prompts that contain credentials
quiz.why: System prompt leakage is a recognised risk (OWASP LLM07), so credentials should be fetched by tools server-side, never placed in the model’s context.

quiz.q: What should an admission check do before a model server loads a model?
o: Measure the model’s accuracy on a small sample of production traffic
Verify the model’s signature and hash against the approved registry
Compress the model files so they load into memory more quickly
Ask the model owner to confirm by email that the model is the right one
quiz.why: Cryptographic verification at load time stops unsigned, unknown or tampered models from serving traffic.

quiz.q: Which knowledge base event MOST deserves investigation?
o: A scheduled nightly sync from the approved document management system
A bulk insert of hundreds of pages from a source not on the approved list
A librarian correcting a typing error in one existing policy document
A routine re-index after the embedding model was upgraded through change control
quiz.why: Bulk content from an unapproved source is a classic sign of knowledge base poisoning.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of an AI assistant that reads raw log content in the SOC?
o: It will use too much storage when it saves summaries of each alert
Attacker-controlled log fields can carry instructions aimed at the assistant
It can only read logs in English, so foreign-language attacks are missed
It will make analysts faster, which reduces the size of the SOC team
quiz.why: File names, user agents and email subjects are attacker-controlled, so the SOC’s assistant must treat them as untrusted data.

quiz.q: What should a good threat hunt produce, beyond its immediate findings?
o: A longer list of open alerts for analysts to review next week
A durable improvement, such as a new detection or a fixed visibility gap
A report for the board describing the tools the hunters used
A permanent increase in the number of analysts assigned to hunting
quiz.why: Hunts should leave the SOC better able to detect the same behaviour automatically next time.

exam.q: Monitoring shows a customer assistant’s responses increasingly contain image links to an unfamiliar domain, with long strings of characters in the URLs. What is the MOST likely concern?
o: The assistant is using a new content delivery network to speed up image loading
Data may be leaking out through the URLs, possibly after injected instructions
The model has started to hallucinate images that don’t exist anywhere online
Customers have asked the assistant to include more pictures in its answers
exam.why: Links to unknown domains carrying encoded data are a known exfiltration channel, often triggered by indirect injection. The other explanations don’t account for the encoded strings.

exam.q: A company’s RAG assistant uses rules to block known jailbreak phrases. Red teamers bypass it easily by rephrasing and translating their attempts. Which improvement BEST strengthens detection?
o: Add the red team’s exact phrases to the rule list after each exercise
Add ML classifiers and behavioural baselines alongside the existing rules
Block all inputs that are not written in English, to prevent translation tricks
Replace the rules with a single classifier and remove all other checks
exam.why: Layering methods covers each one’s blind spots: classifiers generalise across wording and baselines catch unusual behaviour. Adding exact phrases, blocking languages or relying on one classifier are easily evaded or harmful.

exam.q: An API key issued to a backend summarisation service is seen making requests from an employee’s home broadband connection. What should the SOC do FIRST?
o: Ask the employee to stop using the key from home in future
Revoke and rotate the key, then investigate how it was obtained
Increase the key’s rate limit so the extra traffic doesn’t cause errors
Add the home address to the key’s list of approved networks
exam.why: A service key used outside its workload is compromised, whoever is using it. Rotation contains it; investigation finds how it escaped. The other options leave it usable.

exam.q: An HR agent was given read and write access to all employee records "to avoid errors". Monitoring shows it only ever reads records for the employee who is chatting with it. What is the BEST action?
o: Leave the access unchanged, because the agent hasn’t misused it so far
Reduce its access to reading the current user’s records, and review recent actions
Give the agent administrator rights too, so it never fails on future tasks
Disable the agent permanently, because it was given excessive access at launch
exam.why: Usage data shows what the agent needs, so right-size its access and check nothing was done with the excess. Leaving or widening access keeps the risk, and disabling a useful agent is disproportionate.

exam.q: A SOC finds that an agent’s traces, including OAuth refresh tokens, have been written in plain text to an observability platform that 200 engineers can read. What should happen FIRST?
o: Restrict the observability platform to the SOC team only, and continue as before
Revoke the exposed tokens, then purge them and stop tokens being logged
Ask the 200 engineers to confirm they haven’t looked at the traces
Encrypt the observability platform’s disks so the tokens are protected
exam.why: Exposed tokens must be revoked first, because anyone who copied them could still use them. Then remove the copies and fix the logging. Restricting access, asking for assurances or encrypting disks leaves valid tokens in circulation.

exam.q: A code-executing data analysis agent repeatedly attempts outbound network connections, which its sandbox blocks. What is the BEST interpretation?
o: The sandbox is misconfigured and should allow outbound connections
A strong signal of manipulation or misuse that warrants investigation
Normal behaviour, because data analysis agents often need internet access
A sign that the agent needs a larger compute allocation to finish
exam.why: Repeated attempts to break sandbox boundaries are high-confidence signals that the agent is running code it shouldn’t, possibly because of injected instructions. Loosening the sandbox would remove the control.

exam.q: A new self-hosted runner and a new repository secret appeared in the ML deployment pipeline overnight, with no change ticket. What is the MOST appropriate response?
o: Wait for the next scheduled deployment and check whether it succeeds
Treat it as possible pipeline compromise: freeze deployments and investigate
Delete the runner and secret, and say nothing to avoid alarming the team
Approve the change retrospectively, since engineers often forget tickets
exam.why: Unapproved runners and secrets are classic indicators of pipeline compromise, which could push tampered models to production. Freezing and investigating preserves evidence and stops harm.

exam.q: Retrieval monitoring shows that a set of recently added documents now ranks first for many common employee questions. The documents came from a newly created contributor account. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Promote the documents to the official policy library, since employees find them useful
Quarantine the documents, snapshot the index and investigate the contributor
Rebuild the entire vector index from scratch using a new embedding model
Ask employees whether they found the recent answers helpful and accurate
exam.why: New content dominating retrieval from a new account suggests poisoning. Quarantine stops the harm, a snapshot preserves evidence, and the investigation establishes intent. Rebuilding destroys evidence; promoting or surveying users ignores the risk.

exam.q: A SOC introduces AI triage. After three months, analysts override its scores in under 1% of cases, and a missed intrusion was scored "low" by the assistant. What should the SOC do?
o: Remove human review entirely, because the assistant has clearly proven itself accurate
Investigate automation bias: sample decisions, measure accuracy and refresh training
Switch off AI triage permanently and return to fully manual processes
Ask the vendor for a model update and make no other changes to the process
exam.why: A near-zero override rate combined with a missed intrusion suggests rubber-stamping. Sampling and measuring reveal the real accuracy, and training restores meaningful review.

exam.q: Threat intelligence warns that attackers are stealing AI agent tokens from developer laptops. Which proactive activity BEST fits?
o: Wait for an alert from the existing detections before doing anything
A hypothesis-driven hunt for agent tokens used from unexpected hosts
A company-wide email asking developers whether they have been hacked
Buying a new SIEM with more built-in rules for AI-related threats
exam.why: Threat hunting turns intelligence into a testable hypothesis and searches for evidence that detections may have missed. Waiting, surveys and new tools don’t look for current compromise.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a vulnerability register and an exposure register?
o: One is kept by security, the other by the legal team for regulators
One records weaknesses; the other records who can reach each AI asset
One covers models, the other covers only traditional software components
One is updated daily, the other only after each annual risk assessment
quiz.why: Weakness plus reachability gives urgency: a flaw nobody can reach matters less than one exposed to the internet.

quiz.q: Why should a register entry be retested before it is closed?
o: Retesting is required by every regulator for each AI vulnerability
To confirm the fix works, rather than trusting that a ticket was closed
To generate more findings for the next quarterly metrics report
Retesting lets the team skip assigning an owner to each entry
quiz.why: Verification proves the weakness is gone. Closed tickets alone often hide incomplete or failed fixes.

quiz.q: When is a model behaviour such as hallucination treated as a security vulnerability?
o: Always, because any incorrect output is a security failure by definition
When an attacker can reliably trigger it to cause harm or bypass a control
Never, because hallucinations are only ever a model quality issue, not security
Only when the model has been deployed for more than a year
quiz.why: Limitations become vulnerabilities when they can be exploited deliberately; otherwise they belong in quality and risk management.

quiz.q: Why can the same CVE warrant different priorities in two AI deployments?
o: CVE scores are recalculated for every organisation by the CVE Program
Exposure, data, privileges and consequence differ between deployments
Older deployments are always lower priority than newer ones
Priorities depend on which team found the vulnerability first
quiz.why: Context changes how likely exploitation is and how much harm it would cause, even when the flaw is identical.

quiz.q: What does EPSS estimate?
o: The financial loss an organisation would suffer from a vulnerability
The probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days
The number of systems in the world affected by a vulnerability
The time a vendor will take to release a patch for a vulnerability
quiz.why: EPSS, from FIRST, adds a likelihood signal that base severity scores don’t provide.

quiz.q: Which factor MOST increases the urgency of patching a flaw in an AI agent platform?
o: The flaw was found by an internal team rather than an external researcher
The flaw is in CISA’s KEV catalogue and the agent is internet-facing
The platform’s vendor is headquartered in a different country from yours
The flaw has an unusually long and complicated technical description
quiz.why: Known exploitation plus exposure means attackers are likely to use the flaw against you soon.

quiz.q: Why should model evaluations be part of testing an inference framework patch?
o: Evaluations are faster to run than functional tests for most frameworks
Framework updates can subtly change model outputs and safety behaviour
Regulators require evaluations for every software change in any system
Evaluations replace the need for any functional or security testing
quiz.why: Changes to frameworks, drivers or tokenizers can shift outputs, so behaviour must be checked as well as function.

quiz.q: What is a virtual patch?
o: A patch that is downloaded automatically from the vendor’s website
A control that blocks exploitation while the real fix is prepared
A patch applied only to test environments, never to production
A simulated patch used in tabletop exercises to train staff
quiz.why: Gateway rules, network blocks or restrictions can stop exploitation of a known flaw until the fix is tested and deployed.

quiz.q: What does an AIBOM add to a traditional SBOM?
o: A list of the people who approved each software component in a build
Models, datasets and other AI-specific components and their versions
Encryption of all the component names so attackers can’t read them
The prices paid for each commercial component in the system
quiz.why: An AIBOM lets you match advisories and issues affecting models and datasets, not just software packages.

quiz.q: What makes a control a valid compensating control?
o: It is cheaper to implement than the control it replaces
It meets the intent and rigour of the requirement it replaces
It has been approved by the vendor of the legacy system
It is implemented by a different team from the original control
quiz.why: A compensating control must provide comparable protection to the control that can’t be applied, not just exist.

quiz.q: Why should exceptions for legacy models have an expiry date?
o: Expiry dates are needed so that the exception can be billed annually
Open-ended exceptions turn temporary risks into permanent ones
Models stop working when their exception expires
Regulators only allow exceptions that last exactly twelve months
quiz.why: Expiry forces a fresh decision: replace, retire or consciously renew with the risk owner’s approval.

quiz.q: Which is a meaningful posture metric rather than a vanity metric?
o: The number of AI security awareness emails sent to staff each month
The share of AI assets with an owner and a current security review
The number of vulnerability scanning tools the organisation licenses
The total number of pages in the organisation’s AI security policy
quiz.why: Coverage of assets by ownership and review reflects actual control over risk, unlike activity counts.

quiz.q: What does AI security posture management typically do?
o: Train new models with improved safety behaviour for the organisation
Discover AI assets, check configurations and find attack paths
Replace the need for human security reviews of AI systems
Negotiate security terms in contracts with AI providers
quiz.why: AI-SPM provides continuous visibility of assets, misconfigurations and attack paths, feeding human-led reviews and remediation.

exam.q: A red team finds that a customer assistant can be made to reveal internal pricing rules through role-play prompts. The finding is noted in a slide deck, but no one owns it, and three months later it is still exploitable. What is the BEST process improvement?
o: Ask the red team to present its findings more forcefully at the next review
Record findings in a register with an owner, due date and retest before closure
Remove the role-play capability from every model used anywhere in the organisation
Reduce the frequency of red team exercises, so fewer findings are left open
exam.why: A register with ownership, deadlines and verification turns findings into fixes. Presentation style, blanket capability bans and fewer exercises don’t create accountability.

exam.q: A vulnerability with a CVSS base score of 6.5 affects the vector database behind an internal HR assistant that retrieves salary and disciplinary records. EPSS is high, and exploit code is public. How should it be prioritised?
o: Low, because its base score is below the organisation’s critical threshold
High, because exploitation is likely and the records are highly sensitive
Low, because the assistant is internal and employees are trusted users
Defer, until the vendor rates the vulnerability as critical in an update
exam.why: Likely exploitation combined with highly sensitive data raises the contextual priority well above the base score. Internal systems still face insider and compromised-account threats.

exam.q: Which approach to vulnerability prioritisation BEST suits an organisation with hundreds of AI deployments and limited staff?
o: Fix vulnerabilities strictly in order of CVSS base score, highest first
Combine exploitation data, exposure, data sensitivity and consequence
Fix the vulnerabilities in the oldest systems first, whatever their risk
Let each development team decide which findings to fix, if any
exam.why: Risk-based prioritisation focuses scarce effort where exploitation is likely and harm would be greatest. Base-score ordering, age and team preference ignore context.

exam.q: A new release of a popular agent orchestration library fixes a flaw that allows code execution through crafted tool outputs. The organisation uses the library in 30 services, but nobody is sure which versions. What should be done FIRST?
o: Wait for each service team to notice the advisory and upgrade when convenient
Use SBOM data to identify affected services and versions, then prioritise patching
Upgrade all 30 services immediately in production without any testing
Ban the library from future projects and leave existing services as they are
exam.why: Identifying exactly where vulnerable versions run is the first step to prioritised, tested patching. Waiting, untested mass upgrades and future-only bans all leave risk unmanaged.

exam.q: After a GPU driver and framework update, a fraud model’s outputs shift slightly, and its false negative rate rises by 3 points. The update passed all functional tests. What does this show?
o: Functional tests are unnecessary and can be dropped for future updates
Patch testing must include model evaluations, not just functional tests
GPU driver updates should never be applied to AI systems running in production
The fraud model should be retrained after every infrastructure change
exam.why: Infrastructure changes can alter model behaviour, so evaluations must be part of patch testing. Dropping functional tests, avoiding driver patches or routine retraining are wrong lessons.

exam.q: A manufacturer’s quality inspection model runs on an unsupported serving stack with a known remote code execution flaw. Replacement is scheduled in nine months. Which approach BEST manages the risk meanwhile?
o: Accept the risk informally, because the replacement is already scheduled
Isolate and restrict it, with monitoring, under a time-limited exception
Disable the model now and inspect all products manually for nine months
Ask the original vendor to support the stack again for one more year
exam.why: Isolation, restricted access and monitoring reduce exploitability, and a formal exception keeps the risk owned until replacement. Informal acceptance, disruptive shutdowns and hoping for vendor support don’t manage the risk.

exam.q: A legacy chatbot can’t be updated to resist newer jailbreak techniques. The business wants to extend it to anonymous public users. What should the security team advise?
o: Approve the extension, because the chatbot has worked well for its internal users
Keep it to named internal users, with gateway guardrails, until it is replaced
Approve the extension, but add a disclaimer that answers may be inaccurate
