Retrain the chatbot on public data so that it is ready for external users
exam.why: A model that can’t resist known techniques should not gain a larger, anonymous attack surface. Restrictions and guardrails contain it until replacement; disclaimers and retraining on public data don’t fix the weakness.

exam.q: An organisation reviewed each AI system’s security only at launch. Two years later, many agents have gained new tools and data sources. What should it introduce?
o: A second launch review for each system, held once at the two-year anniversary
Trigger-based and risk-tiered reviews, supported by continuous posture checks
A rule that AI systems can never gain new tools after their launch review
An annual survey asking system owners whether anything important has changed
exam.why: Reviews triggered by significant change and scheduled by risk tier, with continuous automated checks, keep assessments current. One-off reviews, change freezes and surveys don’t.

exam.q: The board receives a monthly AI security report listing scans run, policies published and training completed. Which change would make it MOST useful for decision-making?
o: Add more activity counts, such as meetings held and emails sent to staff
Replace activity counts with trended outcome metrics and decisions required
Remove all metrics, and present a narrative summary from the CISO instead
Send the report weekly instead of monthly, so the board sees more data
exam.why: Boards need outcome metrics trended against targets, with clear decisions to make. More activity data, no data or more frequent reports don’t support decisions.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a jailbreak and indirect prompt injection?
o: A jailbreak targets image models; indirect injection targets text models only
A jailbreak is usually by the user; indirect injection often comes via third-party content
Jailbreaks are always harmless experiments; indirect injections are always attacks
There is no difference; the two terms describe exactly the same attack
quiz.why: The attacker and delivery route differ, so do the harms and the playbooks: jailbreaks bypass safety rules, injection hijacks the model’s task or tools.

quiz.q: Why should incidents involving poisoned models be rated higher for persistence?
o: Poisoned models run faster, so they affect more users each minute
The harm continues until the model and its data are cleaned
Poisoned models are always detected by antivirus tools
Persistence ratings decide which vendor must pay for the incident
quiz.why: Poisoning, corrupted memory and tainted indexes keep causing harm on every request until they are removed.

quiz.q: Which question is MOST important when scoping an AI agent incident?
o: Which programming language was used to build the agent framework
What data the agent accessed and what actions it took, on whose behalf
How many other agents the organisation is planning to build next year
Whether the agent’s model was the newest version available at the time
quiz.why: Data accessed and actions taken define the impact, and the delegated identity shows whose authority was used.

quiz.q: Why should legal and privacy join an AI incident early when personal data is exposed?
o: They are the only people allowed to use the incident ticketing system
Notification clocks, such as the GDPR’s 72 hours, may already be running
They must approve every technical containment action before it can be taken
They are responsible for rolling back models in most organisations
quiz.why: Deadlines run from awareness, not from the end of the investigation, so assessment must start in parallel.

quiz.q: Who typically carries out a model rollback during an AI incident?
o: The communications team, after approval from the press office
MLOps or platform engineers, on the decision of the model owner
The legal team, to make sure the rollback meets contractual terms
The model provider’s sales team, under the support contract
quiz.why: MLOps is responsible for executing the rollback, while the model owner is accountable for the decision.

quiz.q: Under NIS2, an entity has sent its early warning of a significant incident. By when must it submit the fuller incident notification?
o: Within one month
Within 72 hours
Within 7 days
Within 24 hours
quiz.why: NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month.

quiz.q: Why must a rollback after data poisoning target a verified clean version?
o: Older versions are always more accurate than newer ones
Recent versions may also have been trained on the poisoned data
The registry deletes any version that is older than one month
Regulators require organisations to keep only one model version
quiz.why: Lineage shows which versions were trained after the poisoned data arrived; rolling back to one of them restores the poison.

quiz.q: What is quiet containment?
o: Taking a system offline at night, when fewer customers are affected
Restricting and monitoring an attacker without alerting them, to keep evidence
Containing an incident without telling the organisation’s management
Using only automated containment, with no human involvement at all
quiz.why: For theft or insider cases, restricting and watching first preserves evidence and avoids prompting the attacker to destroy traces.

quiz.q: Which containment action is usually the LEAST disruptive?
o: Taking the whole AI service offline with its kill switch
Tightening guardrails to block the specific attack pattern
Rolling back every model in the organisation to last year’s versions
Isolating the entire data centre that hosts the model
quiz.why: Targeted guardrail changes sit at the bottom of the containment ladder; take more disruptive steps only if they don’t stop the harm.

quiz.q: Why should an agent be stopped by revoking credentials rather than by instructing it to stop?
o: Instructions cost far more tokens than credential changes, so they are slower
A hijacked agent may ignore instructions, but can’t act without credentials
Credentials expire automatically after any incident anyway
Revoking credentials also deletes the agent’s memory for investigators
quiz.why: Controls outside the model work whatever the agent’s state; a manipulated model may not follow instructions to stop.

quiz.q: Which step is often missed when suspending an AI pipeline during a poisoning incident?
o: Notifying the vendor that supplied the training hardware
Pausing scheduled retraining and re-indexing jobs as well
Updating the model card to describe the suspected poisoning
Renaming the datasets so that attackers can’t find them
quiz.why: Scheduled jobs can redeploy a poisoned model or re-index poisoned documents overnight if only ingestion is paused.

quiz.q: Why should artefacts be collected in order of volatility?
o: The most valuable evidence is always stored in the very largest files
The most fragile evidence, such as agent memory, disappears first
Volatile evidence is not admissible, so it can be collected last
Collecting large files first makes the investigation cheaper
quiz.why: Runtime state, queues and caches vanish on restart or rotation, so they are captured before durable stores.

quiz.q: Why can’t investigators simply rerun a model to see what it said during an incident?
o: Rerunning models is forbidden under most data protection laws
Outputs are often non-deterministic, and inputs or versions may have changed
Models delete their own outputs automatically after each conversation
Rerunning the model would cost too much in tokens to be worthwhile
quiz.why: Recorded outputs, plus the exact model, configuration and context, are the evidence; reruns can give different answers.

exam.q: An HR assistant begins approving leave requests that managers rejected. Logs show employees added text to their requests telling the assistant that managers had already approved. How should this be classified and handled?
o: As a jailbreak, by blocking the employees from using all AI tools permanently
As prompt injection in request content, restricting tools during investigation
As data poisoning, by retraining the model on a cleaned set of leave requests
As model theft, by revoking the assistant’s access to the HR system entirely
exam.why: Instructions embedded in content the assistant processes, changing its task, are prompt injection. Restricting the approval tool contains it while the investigation and fixes proceed.

exam.q: Model weights for a proprietary fraud model were downloaded at 03:00 by a service account that normally only reads inference logs, and sent to an unknown external IP address. Which category and FIRST concern apply?
o: Data poisoning; retrain the fraud model on fresh data immediately
Model theft; contain the account and preserve evidence of the transfer
Jailbreaking; tighten the guardrails on the fraud model’s outputs
Drift; schedule a performance review of the fraud model for next month
exam.why: Unauthorised copying of weights to an external destination is model theft. Containing the account and preserving evidence come first; the other categories don’t fit.

exam.q: A critical AI incident occurs at 02:00 on a Sunday. The on-call engineer can’t reach anyone with authority to approve taking the customer-facing agent offline. What should have been in place?
o: A rule that critical incidents are only handled during business hours
Pre-agreed escalation paths, deputies and decision rights for each severity
A requirement for the engineer to email the whole company before acting
A policy that customer-facing agents are never taken offline under any circumstances
exam.why: Escalation paths with deputies and pre-agreed decision rights let responders act quickly at any hour. The other options delay or prevent necessary action.

exam.q: A provider of a high-risk AI system learns of a serious incident in which a malfunction contributed to a patient’s death. Once Article 73 applies, what is the maximum time to report it under the EU AI Act?
o: 72 hours
10 days
15 days
30 days
exam.why: Article 73 sets 10 days where a death is involved, 2 days for widespread infringement or critical infrastructure, and 15 days otherwise.

exam.q: A chatbot is being manipulated by a coordinated jailbreak campaign from about 40 accounts. Legitimate customers are unaffected so far. Which containment is MOST appropriate?
o: Take the chatbot offline for all customers until the campaign stops
Block or throttle those accounts and tighten filters, watching for over-blocking
Roll back the chatbot’s model to the version used two years ago
Do nothing, because jailbreaks only ever affect the accounts that carry them out
exam.why: Targeted blocking and filter changes stop the campaign with minimal disruption. A full shutdown is disproportionate, an old model is likely weaker, and jailbreak outputs can still cause harm.

exam.q: After rolling back a support model to fix an incident, the team finds the old model still behaves badly. Investigation shows the system prompt and retrieval index had also changed before the incident. What lesson applies?
o: Model rollbacks never work in practice, so models should always be retrained instead
Roll back the whole known-good set: model, prompt, guardrails and index
System prompts should never be changed once a model is deployed
Retrieval indexes should be deleted during every AI incident
exam.why: Behaviour comes from the combination of model, prompt, guardrails and index, so a clean rollback restores the whole known-good configuration.

exam.q: A poisoning incident is confirmed. The team rolls back the model, but the next morning the poisoned behaviour returns. What MOST likely went wrong?
o: The rollback was performed by the wrong member of the MLOps team
The pipeline wasn’t suspended, so scheduled retraining redeployed the poison
The model provider released an update that reintroduced the poison
Users remembered the poisoned answers, and kept asking the same questions again
exam.why: Without suspending ingestion, scheduled retraining and deployment, the pipeline rebuilds and redeploys a poisoned model.

exam.q: A hijacked agent queued 200 outbound customer emails before it was stopped; 50 had already been sent. What is the BEST next action?
o: Delete the queue and the agent’s logs, so the incident can be closed quickly
Hold the remaining 150 emails, assess the 50 sent, and notify those affected as needed
Release the remaining emails, since the agent has now been stopped and is safe
Restart the agent immediately so that it can send corrected versions of the emails
exam.why: Holding pending actions prevents further harm, and assessing sent messages drives notification and recall. Deleting evidence, releasing the queue or restarting the agent are all unsafe.

exam.q: Investigators need to establish what an AI agent believed its instructions were when it transferred funds. The agent has since been restarted. Which artefact would have been MOST valuable?
o: The agent’s source code repository, showing its latest commits
A snapshot of its memory and context taken before the restart
The model provider’s published model card for the base model
The finance team’s monthly reconciliation report for the account
exam.why: The agent’s memory and context show what instructions it was following, including any planted by an attacker. Restarting without a snapshot destroys this.

exam.q: A team must roll back a tampered model within the hour, but its weights are 400 GB. What is the BEST way to preserve evidence?
o: Skip preservation, because the files are too large to copy in time
Lock the suspect version in the registry with its hash, then roll back
Email the weights to the legal team as an attachment before rolling back
Keep the suspect model running in production until a full copy is made
exam.why: A retention-locked, hashed registry version preserves the evidence without delaying containment. Skipping preservation loses it, email is impractical and insecure, and leaving it running prolongs harm.

quiz.q: In an agent incident, what is the "pivot point" in the trace?
o: The moment the user first logged in to the application that hosts the agent
The step where the agent’s plan diverged from what the user had asked for
The point at which the agent’s session reached its maximum token budget
The last tool call made before the security team stopped the agent
quiz.why: The pivot shows when untrusted content took control, and the content just before it is usually the carrier of the attack.

quiz.q: Why do investigators of a poisoning incident work backwards through lineage?
o: Lineage records are the only logs that regulators allow investigators to read
To trace the model to its datasets and sources, and find every affected asset
Working forwards would alert the attacker that an investigation has started
Lineage tools automatically remove poisoned data as they are queried
quiz.why: Lineage connects a model to the data versions and sources it learned from, and to other models and indexes that used the same data.

quiz.q: How does persistence typically differ in AI attacks compared with traditional attacks?
o: AI attacks never persist, because models forget everything between sessions
It can live in agent memory, poisoned indexes or modified model weights
It always requires malware to be installed on the model serving hosts
Persistence only happens when attackers have administrator credentials
quiz.why: AI systems store state in memory, indexes and weights, which can carry an attacker’s influence long after the initial access.

quiz.q: Why must timestamps be normalised to UTC when building an incident timeline?
o: UTC timestamps take up less storage space than local times do
Sources in different time zones or with clock offsets otherwise misalign
Regulators only accept incident reports that are written in UTC
UTC timestamps can’t be altered by attackers, unlike local times
quiz.why: Merging sources without normalisation can reverse the apparent order of events and send the investigation the wrong way.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a proximate cause and a root cause?
o: The proximate cause is always technical; the root cause is always a person
The proximate cause is the immediate trigger; the root cause let it happen
The proximate cause is found by the SOC; the root cause by the auditors
They are the same thing, described at different points in the investigation
quiz.why: Fixing only the proximate cause leaves the gap that allowed it, so the incident can recur in another form.

quiz.q: Why should a "no findings" result from a backdoor scan be treated with caution?
o: Backdoor scans only work on models that were trained in the last year
No method finds every backdoor, so absence of findings isn’t proof
Backdoor scans always produce false negatives for language models
A clean scan means the model must be retrained to confirm the result
quiz.why: Scans can find some triggers, but a clean result doesn’t prove a model is free of backdoors; combine it with lineage and testing.

quiz.q: Which evidence is generally MOST reliable for clustering attacker activity?
o: IP addresses, because attackers rarely change the infrastructure they use
Tactics, techniques and procedures, which are harder to change
The language used in planted instructions, which can’t be faked
The time zone in which the attack’s first events were recorded
quiz.why: Infrastructure and language are easy to change or fake; consistent techniques are more stable indicators of the same actor.

quiz.q: Why is hacking back not an appropriate response to an AI attack?
o: It takes too long, so it is less effective than simply blocking the attacker
It is unlawful in most jurisdictions and can harm innocent third parties
It only works against attackers who are based in the same country
Attackers always detect it, so it reveals the investigation too early
quiz.why: Attackers often use compromised systems belonging to others, and unauthorised access is a crime regardless of motive.

quiz.q: Why should poisoned records be quarantined rather than deleted?
o: Deleting records is slower than moving them into a quarantine area
They are evidence, needed to understand and prove what happened
Quarantined records can safely be used again for training later
Regulators require all training data to be kept forever
quiz.why: Quarantine removes them from use while preserving them for analysis, attribution and any legal action.

quiz.q: When is fine-tuning from a clean checkpoint appropriate after poisoning?
o: Whenever it is cheaper than retraining, whatever the checkpoint’s history
When lineage proves the checkpoint was produced before the poisoned data was used
Only when the provider of the base model gives written permission first
Never, because fine-tuning always reintroduces the original poisoned data
quiz.why: A checkpoint is only clean if lineage shows it predates the poisoned data; otherwise the backdoor may already be learned.

quiz.q: Which hidden location could bring a poisoned model’s behaviour back after eradication?
o: The organisation’s published model card on its public website
A model fine-tuned from the poisoned one, or a backup used in a restore
The monitoring dashboard that first detected and charted the poisoned behaviour
The incident ticket in which the poisoning was first recorded
quiz.why: Derived models inherit poisoning, and restoring from an old backup can redeploy it, so both must be found and cleaned.

quiz.q: What is an incident replay set?
o: A recording of the whole incident response meeting, kept for later review
The attack inputs from an incident, with variants, kept for regression tests
A backup of the production system taken just before the incident
A list of the people who were involved in responding to the incident
quiz.why: Replaying the attack and its variants proves the fix works, and keeps the weakness from quietly returning later.

quiz.q: Why should pass criteria be agreed before safety regression testing starts?
o: Testing tools can only run when the criteria are stored in their configuration
So results aren’t interpreted to fit a deadline after they are known
Because criteria agreed afterwards can’t legally be included in reports
So that the testing team can finish more quickly than usual
quiz.why: Criteria set in advance keep the decision evidence-based, even under pressure to restore service.

exam.q: An investigation into a support agent that issued unauthorised refunds finds the refund instructions came from text in a customer’s uploaded PDF. What is the MOST important next step in reconstructing the attack?
o: Block all PDF uploads permanently for every customer of the business
Find other sessions and agents that read the same or similar content
Retrain the agent’s model on a dataset that excludes PDF documents
Ask the customer who uploaded the PDF to explain why they did it
exam.why: Hunting for the same carrier elsewhere establishes the full scope of the attack. A permanent ban, retraining and asking the customer don’t reveal other affected sessions.

exam.q: A model trained on scraped public data shows backdoor behaviour. Investigators have identified the poisoned web pages. What should they establish NEXT?
o: Whether the pages are still online, so they can be reported
Every model, fine-tune and index that used data from those web pages
The name of the person who wrote each of the poisoned web pages
Whether the scraping tool was the latest version when it ran
exam.why: Lineage from the poisoned sources to every affected asset defines what must be contained and cleaned. Reporting pages, identifying authors and checking tool versions come later or matter less.

exam.q: During root cause analysis, the team finds an agent leaked data because untrusted email content wasn’t separated from instructions. The engineering lead proposes closing the RCA with "agent followed malicious email". What should the security lead say?
o: Agree, because the agent following the email is clearly what caused the leak
That is the proximate cause; record the design gaps as root causes, with fixes
Close the RCA, but add a recommendation to train staff on phishing emails
Ask the email provider to explain why it delivered the malicious message
exam.why: The root causes are the design gaps that allowed the agent to be manipulated and to leak data. Recording only the proximate cause leaves them unfixed.

exam.q: Investigators can’t line up gateway logs with agent traces because the timestamps disagree by several minutes. What should they do?
o: Discard the gateway logs completely, and rely only on the agent traces instead
Measure each source’s offset, normalise to UTC and record the correction
Assume the gateway logs are correct, since gateways are more reliable
Average the two sets of timestamps to produce a compromise timeline
exam.why: Measured, documented corrections produce a defensible unified timeline. Discarding sources loses evidence, and assumptions or averages introduce errors.

exam.q: A company’s model was extracted through thousands of queries from many cloud accounts. The CEO wants to name the competitor suspected of being behind it in a press release. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Name the competitor, because only a competitor would want the model
Assess attribution with stated confidence, keep evidence and take legal advice
Launch an attack on the competitor’s systems to gather proof of the theft
Ignore attribution entirely, since it never affects the security response at all
exam.why: Public claims need well-founded attribution and legal advice; evidence supports any legal or law enforcement action. Assumptions, hacking back and ignoring attribution are all wrong.

exam.q: Which statement BEST describes the role of attribution in an AI incident?
o: It must be completed before any containment action is allowed to begin
A confidence judgement that informs defences, sharing and reporting
A formal legal finding that proves who carried out the attack
An optional exercise that only matters for nation-state attacks
exam.why: Attribution is a judgement with stated confidence that helps defenders and authorities. It never delays containment and is not proof.

exam.q: A poisoned customer service model was retrained on cleaned data, but an investigation shows the same poisoned data was also used to fine-tune a sales assistant. What should happen?
o: Nothing, because the sales assistant hasn’t shown any problems in production so far
Treat the sales assistant as affected: test it, and rebuild it from clean data
Delete the sales assistant permanently, as it can never be trusted again
Add a disclaimer to the sales assistant’s responses about possible errors
exam.why: Any model trained on the poisoned data may carry the backdoor, even if it hasn’t been triggered yet. Testing and rebuilding from clean data eradicates it.

exam.q: Planted instructions from an attack were written into an agent’s long-term memory. The vulnerable tool has been patched. Is eradication complete?
o: Yes, because patching the tool removes the attacker’s way in
No: the memory entries must be purged, or they may re-trigger the behaviour
Yes, as long as the agent’s model is also updated to the very latest version
No: the agent must be deleted, because memory can never be cleaned
exam.why: Memory is a persistence mechanism: planted instructions can be read again and restart the attack. Patching the entry point alone isn’t enough.

exam.q: A fixed model blocks every replayed attack prompt, but customer complaints about refusals of legitimate requests rise sharply in the canary. What should the team conclude?
o: The fix is successful, because every attack prompt was blocked
The fix causes over-refusal, failing quality regression, so it needs work
The complaints are probably from attackers testing out the new controls on purpose
The canary should be expanded to all users to gather more feedback
exam.why: Regression testing covers what must keep working as well as what must now fail. Over-refusal is a regression in quality and usefulness.

exam.q: Which reintroduction approach BEST balances speed and safety after a serious agent incident?
o: Restore full service as soon as the incident’s exact inputs are blocked
Pre-agreed criteria, regression and red team testing, then shadow and canary
Keep the agent offline permanently, replacing it with a manual process
Restore full service, and rely on users to report any remaining problems
exam.why: Evidence-based gates and staged rollout restore service with confidence. Testing only exact inputs, permanent shutdown or relying on users are poor choices.

quiz.q: Why should a vector store be restored to staging before production?
o: Staging restores are cheaper because they use less powerful hardware
So retrieval can be validated and verified changes re-added safely
Production systems can’t accept restored data under most licences
Restoring to staging deletes the poisoned documents automatically
quiz.why: Staging lets the team re-add legitimate changes and test retrieval with golden queries and canaries before users depend on it.

quiz.q: What does a recovery point objective (RPO) describe?
o: How quickly a service must be restored after any disruption
The amount of recent data or change you can afford to lose
The point in a process where AI first becomes involved
The location of the backup data centre used for recovery
quiz.why: RPO sets how far back recovery may go; RTO sets how quickly service must return.

quiz.q: Why must snapshot retention reach back far enough for AI recovery?
o: Older snapshots are always smaller and faster to restore than new ones
Poisoning can go unnoticed for weeks, so a clean point must predate it
Regulators require every snapshot to be kept for at least ten years
Newer snapshots can’t be restored once an incident has been declared
quiz.why: If every retained snapshot already contains the poison, the only option is a slow rebuild from verified sources.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a circuit breaker and a kill switch?
o: Circuit breakers are hardware; kill switches are always software
Breakers trip automatically; kill switches are pulled deliberately
Kill switches only affect test environments, never production
There is no difference; the terms are used interchangeably
quiz.why: Circuit breakers respond to thresholds without waiting for people; kill switches are authorised human decisions to stop a capability.

quiz.q: Why must a kill switch work outside the model?
o: Models are usually far too slow to process stop instructions in an emergency
A manipulated or failing model may not obey an instruction to stop
Kill switches inside models are prohibited by the EU AI Act
External kill switches are cheaper to build than internal ones
quiz.why: Gateways, feature flags and credential revocation work regardless of what the model does.

quiz.q: What should an AI service do if its guardrail service becomes unavailable?
o: Continue serving responses, because availability matters most
Fail closed: stop or divert traffic until the protection returns
Switch to a larger model, which is less likely to be manipulated
Ask users to report any harmful responses they receive meanwhile
quiz.why: Running without a protective control exposes users and data; failing closed, with a fallback, is the safe default.

quiz.q: Why must a second model provider be tested before it is needed?
o: Contracts with second providers can only be signed after testing
Models differ in behaviour, safety and formats, so prompts may not transfer
Second providers always charge more for models that are untested
Testing in advance guarantees both providers will never fail together
quiz.why: Switching models changes behaviour, so prompts, guardrails, safety evaluations and output formats must be prepared in advance.

quiz.q: What is concentration risk in AI continuity planning?
o: The risk that staff lose concentration during long incident calls
Many services depending on one provider, region or model family
The risk that GPUs overheat when too many models run at once
A measure of how much data is concentrated in a single index
quiz.why: When many services share one dependency, a single failure can stop them all at once.

quiz.q: What makes a post-incident review "blameless"?
o: Nobody is allowed to mention any mistakes that were made
It focuses on systems, not blame, so people share what happened
The review is written by an external firm with no internal input
Only senior managers attend, so junior staff aren’t blamed
quiz.why: People speak openly about decisions and mistakes only when the aim is to fix systems, not punish individuals.

quiz.q: What does a TTP register link together?
o: Staff training records and their certification expiry dates
Observed attacker techniques and the defences and tests for them
Third-party contracts with AI suppliers and their termination clauses
Tokens, transactions and payments processed by AI agents
quiz.why: The register connects what attackers have done with the detections, mitigations and regression tests that now address it.

quiz.q: What does TLP:AMBER signal when sharing threat intelligence?
o: The information may be published openly, on any public website or forum
Share only on a need-to-know basis within your organisation and clients
The information is unverified and should not be acted upon at all
The incident is still active and the sender needs urgent help
quiz.why: TLP labels set sharing limits: AMBER allows limited disclosure on a need-to-know basis within the recipient organisation and its clients.

quiz.q: Why is disabling a model’s endpoint not enough to decommission it?
o: Endpoints can’t be disabled without the model provider’s permission
Keys, identities, artefacts and data copies remain until removed
Disabled endpoints restart automatically after thirty days
Decommissioning is only complete once the model is retrained
quiz.why: Leftover credentials and copies keep risk alive; decommissioning removes or archives them and verifies the result.

quiz.q: What is algorithmic disgorgement?
o: A technique for compressing models so they use less memory
An order to delete models built with improperly obtained data
A method for extracting training data from a model’s outputs
A process for splitting a model across several providers
quiz.why: The US FTC has used this remedy to require deletion of models and algorithms derived from unlawfully obtained data.

exam.q: A support assistant’s model was tampered with. Last week’s signed version is verified clean, and the prompts and index haven’t changed since. What is the FASTEST trustworthy recovery?
o: Rebuild the model from scratch using freshly collected training data
Roll back to last week’s signed version from the registry, then monitor
Restore the whole platform from the oldest backup that is available
Keep the tampered model running while a new one is being trained
exam.why: A verified clean, signed version can be redeployed in minutes. Rebuilding is slow, the oldest backup loses legitimate changes, and the tampered model must not keep serving.

exam.q: A poisoned vector store is restored from a clean snapshot taken five days ago. Legitimate policy updates were added during those five days. What should happen to them?
o: Discard them, because anything added after the snapshot may be poisoned
Re-add them from verified sources, then validate retrieval before cutover
Copy them across directly from the poisoned index to save time
Ask employees to remember the policy changes and re-enter them
exam.why: Verified sources restore legitimate content without bringing the poison back, and validation confirms retrieval works. Copying from the poisoned index risks reintroducing it.

exam.q: An agent’s tool calls suddenly rise to ten times its baseline in two minutes, at 03:00 when nobody is watching. Which control would have limited the impact MOST?
o: A weekly report of agent activity sent to the agent’s business owner
A circuit breaker that pauses the agent when action rates exceed a threshold
A kill switch that only the CEO is authorised to activate, in person, on site
A policy forbidding agents from running outside business hours
exam.why: An automatic breaker acts in seconds without waiting for people. Reports are too slow, a CEO-only kill switch is impractical at night, and policies don’t stop running agents.

exam.q: During a game day, the team finds that pulling the kill switch for a customer agent takes 40 minutes to take effect across all regions. What should happen?
o: Accept it, because kill switches are rarely needed in practice
Treat it as a finding: redesign for speed, retest, and track the fix
Remove the kill switch entirely, since it clearly doesn’t work as intended
Ask staff to pull the kill switch 40 minutes earlier in future
exam.why: Exercises exist to find exactly this. A slow kill switch must be fixed and retested; accepting, removing or working around it leaves the gap.

exam.q: A bank’s fraud model depends on a single GPU cluster in one region, and its manual review team has been reduced. Business impact analysis sets an RTO of 15 minutes. What is the BEST continuity improvement?
o: Increase the RTO to 24 hours, so that it matches current capability
A tested secondary deployment and a rules-based degraded mode
Buy more GPUs for the same cluster in the same region
Ask the fraud team to work overtime whenever the model is unavailable
exam.why: A tested secondary deployment meets the RTO, and a degraded mode keeps essential screening running. Changing the RTO ignores the business need; more GPUs in one region keep the single point of failure.

exam.q: Which item is MOST important to include in an AI dependency map for a critical service?
o: The service’s user interface design and accessibility features
Providers, regions, data stores, tools, identity and safety services
The names of all the staff who have used the service in the past year
The marketing plan and budget for promoting the service to customers
exam.why: Continuity depends on the technical and supplier dependencies that can fail, each with an owner, objective and fallback.

exam.q: An AI incident’s post-incident review produced 14 recommendations. Six months later, three have been implemented and nobody knows the status of the rest. What is the BEST fix?
o: Hold another review to produce a fresh set of recommendations
Give each action an owner, date and verification, tracked to closure
Reduce the number of recommendations in future reviews to three
Close all the remaining recommendations, since the incident is now quite old
exam.why: Lessons become improvements only when actions are owned, scheduled, verified and tracked. More reviews, fewer recommendations or closing them unaddressed don’t fix the process.

exam.q: After an indirect injection incident, which update BEST captures the knowledge for future defence?
o: A note in the incident ticket describing the attack in general terms
A TTP register entry linked to ATLAS, detections, mitigations and tests
An email to all staff warning them about suspicious web pages
A reminder in the system prompt telling the agent to ignore injections
exam.why: A structured register entry connects the technique to concrete defences and regression tests. Ticket notes get lost, staff emails don’t protect agents, and prompt reminders are weak controls.

exam.q: A fine-tuned model must be removed because its training data was collected unlawfully. Which remediation gives the STRONGEST assurance?
o: Apply an approximate unlearning method, and assume that it has worked
Terminate the model and its derived models, deleting the unlawful data
Add a guardrail that blocks outputs mentioning the unlawful data
Restrict the model to internal users, so that fewer people ever see its outputs
exam.why: Termination, including derived models and the data, removes the unlawful processing completely. Approximate unlearning is hard to verify, and guardrails or restrictions leave the model in use.

exam.q: A company ends its contract with an AI provider that hosted its fine-tuned model and stored training files. What should the decommissioning process include?
o: Nothing, because the provider’s data is the provider’s responsibility
Deletion of the fine-tune, files and logs, with written confirmation
Asking the provider to keep the files in case they are needed again
Downloading the files to a personal laptop for safekeeping
exam.why: Provider-held copies are part of the decommissioning scope; deletion should be requested and confirmed in writing, in line with the contract.

quiz.q: What is PASTA’s main distinguishing feature as a threat modelling method?
o: It focuses only on privacy threats to personal data held in systems
A risk-centric, seven-stage process tied to business objectives
It can only be used for agentic AI systems with multiple agents
It replaces data flow diagrams with fully automated code scanning
quiz.why: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) links threats and attack simulations to business impact through seven stages.

quiz.q: What does MAESTRO add for agentic systems?
o: A scoring system for the severity of software vulnerabilities
Seven layers to analyse, including threats that cross between layers
A certification scheme for agent developers and their organisations
A list of approved foundation models for use in agent frameworks
quiz.why: MAESTRO decomposes agentic systems into seven layers and highlights cross-layer threats, such as poisoned memory hijacking tools.

quiz.q: Why should AI threat models cover the whole pipeline, not just the deployed application?
o: Regulators only accept threat models that are longer than fifty pages
Data sourcing, training, registries and deployment have their own threats
Applications built on AI never contain any security weaknesses
Pipeline threats are always more serious than application threats
quiz.why: Poisoning, backdoors, model swaps and pipeline compromise happen before the application ever runs.

quiz.q: Which four attacker goals does NIST AI 100-2 use?
o: Speed, scale, stealth and simplicity
Availability, integrity, privacy and misuse enablement
Reconnaissance, access, execution and exfiltration
Confidentiality, authentication, authorisation and audit
quiz.why: NIST’s adversarial ML taxonomy classifies attacks by these goals, with misuse enablement specific to generative AI.

quiz.q: Which actor combines the most dangerous access and capability for AI systems?
o: An opportunistic user trying jailbreaks found online
A malicious insider with machine learning skills
A careless employee using a public chatbot
A competitor reading the company’s published model card
quiz.why: Legitimate access plus the skill to poison data, plant backdoors or copy weights makes skilled malicious insiders especially dangerous.

quiz.q: Why should agents and tools be considered potential threat actors in threat models?
o: Agents are always deliberately malicious, because of how they are designed
If compromised, they act with legitimate permissions at machine speed
Tools can’t be secured, so they must be removed from all systems
Threat models are required to include at least one non-human actor
quiz.why: A hijacked agent or malicious tool can do anything its permissions allow, very quickly, which drives least agency and monitoring.

quiz.q: At which stage does an evasion attack take place?
o: During data collection, before any training has begun
At inference, using crafted inputs to a deployed model
During training, through corrupted or flipped labels
In the model registry, by swapping the model files
quiz.why: Evasion manipulates inputs to a deployed model; poisoning and backdoors happen at training time.

quiz.q: Why do backdoors often survive normal model evaluation?
o: Evaluation suites never test language models
The trigger is rare, so clean accuracy looks normal
Backdoors only activate during the evaluation itself
Evaluation is always skipped for fine-tuned models
quiz.why: Without the trigger, a backdoored model behaves normally, so standard test sets don’t reveal it.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of model extraction?
o: Encrypting the training data at rest in the data lake
Rate limiting and returning only the minimum output detail
Adding more layers to the neural network architecture
Publishing the model card, including full architecture details
quiz.why: Extraction depends on many queries and detailed outputs, so limiting both slows or prevents it.

quiz.q: What did the PoisonedRAG research show?
o: RAG systems can’t be poisoned if the model is large enough
A handful of crafted documents can steer answers in a huge knowledge base
Poisoning only works when attackers control the embedding model
Knowledge bases holding millions of documents are effectively immune to poisoning
quiz.why: Five crafted texts per target question, among millions, achieved around 90% attack success, and tested defences were insufficient.

quiz.q: What is package hallucination?
o: A package manager installing the wrong version of a library
A model inventing a package name that attackers can then register
A library that produces random outputs during automated testing
Duplicate packages appearing in a software bill of materials
quiz.why: Hallucinated package names recur, so attackers can register them with malicious code ("slopsquatting").

quiz.q: Which OWASP agentic risk describes planted instructions in an agent’s persistent memory?
o: Agent goal hijack (ASI01)
Memory and context poisoning (ASI06)
Insecure inter-agent communication (ASI07)
Cascading failures (ASI08)
quiz.why: ASI06, memory and context poisoning, covers corrupted memory or shared context that affects later work.

quiz.q: What is the BEST defence against deepfake requests for urgent payments?
o: Training staff to spot the visual glitches that reveal fakes in calls
Verifying through a separate known channel, with dual approval
Requiring executives to keep their cameras on during calls
Using the newest video conferencing software available
quiz.why: Process controls work however convincing the fake; spotting glitches becomes harder as deepfakes improve.

quiz.q: Why can AI availability attacks succeed without large traffic floods?
o: AI systems have no rate limits of any kind, by design
Single requests can be very costly in tokens and compute
Floods are blocked automatically by every model provider
AI systems always run on a single server with no redundancy
quiz.why: Context stuffing, output amplification and agent loops make individual requests expensive.

quiz.q: What is a sponge example?
o: A training example designed to absorb labelling errors from others
An input crafted to maximise a model’s computation and latency
A small, clean dataset used to dilute poisoned records
A prompt that makes a model forget its earlier instructions
quiz.why: Sponge examples, described in 2021 research, target energy use and latency, an availability attack.

quiz.q: What distinguishes PGD from FGSM when crafting adversarial examples?
o: PGD needs only the model’s labels, while FGSM needs its gradients
PGD takes many small steps, projecting back into the budget each time
PGD changes a few pixels a lot, while FGSM changes all pixels a little
PGD works only on text models, while FGSM works only on image models
quiz.why: FGSM takes a single step along the sign of the input gradient. PGD iterates many smaller steps from a random start, projecting back inside the budget after each, which makes it a much stronger attack.

quiz.q: An attacker can’t query a target model before an attack, but has an openly available model trained on similar data. Which approach is MOST practical?
o: A decision-based attack, walking along the target’s boundary
A transfer attack, using examples crafted on the open model
A score-based attack, estimating gradients from confidence
A membership inference attack, using shadow models of it
quiz.why: Adversarial examples often transfer between models trained for similar tasks, so the attacker can craft them on the open model without querying the target. Score-based and decision-based attacks need queries.

quiz.q: Why do researchers report membership inference results as the true-positive rate at a low false-positive rate?
o: Average accuracy is always 50%, so it can’t distinguish between attacks
Confidently identifying even a few individuals is the real privacy harm
Low false-positive rates make attacks run faster on large datasets
Regulators require that exact metric in every privacy impact assessment
quiz.why: An attack can look weak on average yet identify some people with high confidence, which is what matters for privacy. Carlini and colleagues argued for this measure when introducing LiRA.

quiz.q: Which sign MOST suggests that a defence relies on obfuscated gradients?
o: Accuracy under attack falls steadily to zero as the budget grows
Single-step attacks succeed more often than iterative attacks do
Clean accuracy is a few points lower than the undefended model’s
The defence was evaluated with AutoAttack and adaptive attacks
quiz.why: Iterative attacks should be at least as strong as single-step ones. When they do worse, the defence is probably breaking gradient-based attacks rather than resisting them, and adaptive attacks are likely to succeed.

exam.q: A bank is building a customer-facing agent that can move money. The security architect needs a threat modelling approach that links threats to business impact and supports detailed attack simulation. Which is MOST appropriate?
o: LINDDUN, because customer data is involved
PASTA, supplemented with MAESTRO for the agent’s layers
A STRIDE review of the login page only
No threat model, since the vendor has certified the agent platform
exam.why: PASTA ties threats to business impact through attack simulation, and MAESTRO covers agent-specific layers. LINDDUN is privacy-focused, a login-only review is too narrow, and vendor certification doesn’t replace a threat model.

exam.q: A threat model for an AI system was completed at design time two years ago. Since then, the system has gained web browsing, a new vector database and three new tools. What should happen?
o: Nothing, because the original threat model was approved by the architecture board
Update the threat model for the new components, data flows and trust boundaries
Remove the new capabilities, so that the original threat model remains valid
Commission a penetration test instead, as threat models become outdated
exam.why: Threat models must evolve with the system; new tools and data sources add trust boundaries and threats. Testing complements threat modelling rather than replacing it.

exam.q: Which scenario BEST describes a non-human threat actor?
o: An employee who forgets to lock their laptop in a café
An agent hijacked by injected content, acting with its own permissions
A competitor who carefully reads all of the company’s published research papers
A contractor who works remotely from another country
exam.why: A hijacked agent acts against the organisation using its own legitimate access, which is why agents belong in threat models as potential adversaries.

exam.q: An ML engineer downloads full model weights to a personal cloud storage account two days before resigning. Which control set would MOST likely have prevented or detected this?
o: Annual security awareness training for all engineering staff
Least privilege on weights, with DLP and monitoring of downloads
A non-disclosure agreement signed on the engineer’s first day
Encrypting weights at rest with a key the engineer could access
exam.why: Restricting access, blocking or flagging transfers to personal storage, and monitoring downloads address the insider path. Training and NDAs deter but don’t stop it, and accessible keys don’t help.

exam.q: Attackers have discovered they can slightly modify malware so that a security vendor’s ML classifier labels it benign. What type of attack is this, and which defence is MOST relevant?
o: Poisoning; retrain the classifier on its original, unmodified training data
Evasion; adversarial training and robustness testing of the classifier
Model extraction; remove the classifier from all public download sites
Membership inference; apply differential privacy during training
exam.why: Crafted inputs that fool a deployed model are evasion; adversarial training and robustness testing improve resistance. The other attack types don’t match the scenario.

exam.q: A healthcare model’s API returns detailed confidence scores, and researchers show they can infer whether specific patients were in its training data. Which mitigation BEST addresses this?
o: Increase the model’s accuracy so that its predictions are more reliable
Reduce output detail, and retrain the model with differential privacy
Move the model to a faster GPU cluster to reduce response times
Add a disclaimer to every response about the use of patient data
exam.why: Membership inference exploits detailed outputs and overfitting; reducing output detail and differential privacy directly limit it.

exam.q: A legal research assistant retrieves from a large public case-law corpus that anyone can contribute to. Which threat should be prioritised in its threat model?
o: Model extraction through very high volumes of API queries from partners
Knowledge poisoning through crafted documents added to the corpus
Physical theft of the servers that host the vector database
Typographic attacks using text embedded in images
exam.why: Open contribution makes knowledge poisoning and injection carriers the primary risk, and research shows a few crafted documents can steer answers.

exam.q: A procurement agent accepted fabricated supplier "facts" from a research agent and initiated payments, which a human approved because both agents agreed. Which OWASP agentic risks are MOST evident?
o: Unexpected code execution, and rogue agents acting alone
Cascading failures and human-agent trust exploitation
Agentic supply chain flaws and insecure inter-agent messages
Identity abuse and unexpected code execution
exam.why: An error spreading from one agent to another is a cascading failure, and approval based on the agents’ agreement is human-agent trust exploitation.

exam.q: An insurer’s claims assistant accepts photos of damage. Testers find that text written on a photographed object can change the assistant’s assessment. What is the BEST response?
o: Stop accepting photos, and require customers to describe damage in text
Treat text found in images as untrusted input, and validate assessments
Increase the image resolution, so the model reads the text more accurately
Train customers not to include any text in the photos they submit
exam.why: This is a typographic injection; all modalities are untrusted input, and assessments need validation. Banning photos loses value, and higher resolution or customer training doesn’t stop attackers.

exam.q: A startup’s public chatbot is hit by a few accounts sending maximum-length prompts that trigger long agent workflows. Monthly costs triple. Which control would have limited the damage MOST?
o: A web application firewall with signatures for known attack strings
Per-account quotas, input and output caps, and per-task agent budgets
A larger committed-use discount negotiated with the model provider
Moving the chatbot to a different cloud region with more capacity
exam.why: Quotas, token caps and agent budgets directly bound the cost each account and task can incur. Signatures, discounts and more capacity don’t limit abuse.

exam.q: Why is cost per hour often the earliest signal of an AI availability attack?
o: Providers send cost alerts before any other monitoring signal exists
Attacks can use few, expensive requests that barely change traffic volume
Cost data is the only telemetry most AI platforms bother to collect
Network monitoring tools can’t see any of the traffic sent to AI services
exam.why: Resource exhaustion often comes from a small number of costly requests, so token and cost metrics move before traffic volume does.

exam.q: A fraud detection API returns a score from 0 to 100 for each transaction. Attackers are probing it to find the smallest changes that avoid detection. Which change would MOST raise the cost of this attack?
o: Publishing the model card, so partners understand its limitations
Returning only an approve or review decision, with query limits
Increasing the score’s precision from whole numbers to decimals
Retraining the model monthly on the latest legitimate transactions
exam.why: Detailed scores let attackers estimate gradients; returning only a decision forces slower decision-based attacks, and query limits and monitoring cap the probing. More precision would help the attacker.

exam.q: A hospital wants to know whether its published diagnostic model reveals which patients were in its training data. Which test BEST answers this?
o: An evasion test, using PGD attacks at several perturbation budgets
A membership inference test, measured at a low false-positive rate
A reproducibility test, checking that answers repeat across runs
A fairness test, comparing accuracy across different patient groups
exam.why: Membership inference directly tests whether someone can tell that a record was used in training, and measuring at a low false-positive rate shows whether individuals can be identified confidently.

exam.q: During threat modelling, an architect notes that anyone can download the open-source base model the company fine-tuned for its content filter. Which risk does this MOST increase?
o: Model inversion, since the base model contains the company’s fine-tuning data
Transfer attacks, since examples crafted on the base model may also work
Denial of service, since attackers can run the same model at a large scale
Licence breach, since fine-tuned models can’t be used commercially
exam.why: A fine-tuned model stays close to its base, so adversarial inputs crafted on the public base model are likely to transfer. The base model doesn’t contain the company’s fine-tuning data.

quiz.q: What does LLMOps add to traditional MLOps?
o: Faster GPU clusters for training very large models from scratch
Managing prompts, evaluations, guardrails and RAG pipelines
A ban on using any models from external providers or open source
Manual human approval of every individual user request
quiz.why: Applications built on language models change through prompts, retrieval and guardrails as much as through models, so these become managed artefacts.

quiz.q: Why should evaluation gates be automated in the AI pipeline?
o: Automated gates remove the need for any security testing elsewhere
Releases that fail agreed thresholds are blocked consistently
Manual reviews are prohibited for AI models under the EU AI Act
Automation makes models more accurate during training
quiz.why: Automated gates apply the same thresholds to every release, and can’t be skipped under deadline pressure.

quiz.q: What is NIST SP 800-218A?
o: A technical standard for encrypting model weights when stored at rest
An AI-specific profile of the Secure Software Development Framework
A list of approved generative AI providers for US agencies
A testing tool for prompt injection vulnerabilities
quiz.why: SP 800-218A adds practices for generative AI and dual-use foundation models to NIST’s SSDF.

quiz.q: Why should models move between environments only through the registry?
o: The registry compresses models, so they deploy much faster
Everything in production stays traceable, verified and approved
Environments can’t share network connections of any kind
Registries are required before models can be trained on GPUs
quiz.why: A single controlled path means every production model is a registered, signed and approved version.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of copying production personal data into development notebooks?
o: Notebooks run more slowly when they process real data
The data leaves production’s controls and spreads to more people
Development environments can’t store data larger than a gigabyte
Models trained in notebooks are always less accurate
quiz.why: Development environments have weaker controls and wider access, so copies multiply exposure; use synthetic or masked data instead.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST secures integration with a model provider’s API?
o: One shared key embedded in the application code for simplicity
Scoped, short-lived credentials over private paths, with response validation
Sending all the data available, so the model has the most context possible
Allowing the integration host to reach any internet destination
quiz.why: Scoped, short-lived credentials limit misuse, private paths reduce exposure, and validating responses treats model output as untrusted.

quiz.q: Which change requires AI change management even though no application code changes?
o: Restarting the serving containers during routine maintenance
Switching the retrieval index to a new embedding model
Adding a new dashboard to the monitoring tool
Renewing the TLS certificate on the API gateway
quiz.why: A new embedding model changes what is retrieved, and therefore what the system says.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a release manifest for an AI system?
o: To advertise new features to customers, in the release notes
To pin every behaviour-changing component, for reproducibility
To record which engineers worked on the release, for payroll purposes
To replace the need for any evaluation before release
quiz.why: Pinning model, data, prompt, index, guardrail and tool versions lets a release be reproduced, compared and rolled back as a unit.

quiz.q: What is a standard change in AI change management?
o: Any change made by a senior engineer, whatever its risk
A pre-approved, low-risk change that follows an agreed pattern
A change that must always be approved by the board of directors
A change that bypasses all testing, to save time in urgent cases
quiz.why: Standard changes, such as scheduled index refreshes from approved sources, are pre-approved because their risk is understood and controlled.

quiz.q: What makes shadow deployment different from a canary release?
o: Shadow deployments only run at weekends, when traffic is lower
In shadow mode, users never see any of the new version’s outputs
Shadow deployments skip monitoring, to avoid slowing users down
Canary releases never use real traffic, only synthetic test data
quiz.why: Shadow mode compares behaviour on real inputs with no user exposure; a canary exposes a small share of real users.

quiz.q: Why should a rollback restore the whole release bundle, not just the model?
o: Restoring only the model is always slower than restoring everything
An old model with a new prompt or index may behave unpredictably
Regulators prohibit rolling back models without rolling back logs
Bundles are smaller than individual models
quiz.why: Behaviour depends on the combination, so the last known-good combination is what must be restored.

quiz.q: When should rollback triggers be agreed?
o: After the first complaints arrive from customers
Before the rollout starts, as part of the release plan
Only after an incident has been declared by the SOC
At the end of the year, during the annual review
quiz.why: Triggers agreed in advance allow automatic, uncontested rollback when signals breach their limits.

exam.q: A company’s AI projects run security reviews only in the week before launch, and findings often delay releases by months. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Skip the reviews for projects that are behind schedule
Build security into every lifecycle stage, with automated gates
Hire an external firm to perform the same review in less time
Move the review to after launch, so it no longer delays releases
exam.why: Security built into each stage finds issues early, when they are cheap to fix, and automated gates keep releases moving. Skipping, outsourcing the same late review or reviewing after launch don’t fix the cause.

exam.q: Which artefact set should an LLMOps pipeline version and test, in addition to code?
o: Only the model weights, since everything else is configuration
Prompts, retrieval indexes, guardrail settings and tool definitions
The marketing materials that describe the application to customers
The personal laptops and phones used by the development team
exam.why: These artefacts change behaviour as much as code or model weights, so they need versioning, testing and approval.

exam.q: A research team runs Jupyter notebooks on a server reachable from the internet, with a shared administrator token and production database credentials stored in notebook cells. Which change is MOST important FIRST?
o: Upgrade the server’s GPUs, to improve the speed of everyone’s experiments
Remove internet exposure, rotate credentials, require individual logins
Ask researchers to delete any old notebooks they no longer use
Add a warning banner to the notebook server’s login page
exam.why: Internet exposure with a shared token and stored production credentials is an open door: close it, rotate the exposed credentials and require individual authentication.

exam.q: An agent that executes generated code runs in the same network as internal databases. Which environmental control BEST reduces the risk?
o: Giving the agent read-only database credentials instead of write access
A sandbox isolated from internal networks and secrets, with egress limits
Asking the model to avoid generating code that connects to databases
Logging all code the agent runs for review at the end of each month
exam.why: Isolation removes the paths a manipulated agent could use. Read-only credentials still allow data theft, instructions to the model are weak, and monthly reviews are too late.

exam.q: A provider announces it will retire the model version an application uses. The team plans to switch to the provider’s newest model the day before retirement. What should change management require?
o: Nothing, because the provider has tested the new model thoroughly
Comparative evaluation and approval well ahead, with a rollback plan
A contract clause preventing the provider from ever retiring models
Rebuilding the application from scratch around a different provider
exam.why: A provider model change is a behaviour change: evaluate it against the current version early, approve it by risk and keep a fallback. The other options are unrealistic or disproportionate.

exam.q: A team loosened a guardrail threshold to reduce customer complaints, treating it as a minor configuration tweak with no review. What does this indicate?
o: Good agility, since guardrails should be tuned freely by any engineer
A behaviour-changing change made without impact analysis or approval
A problem with the customers, who should accept the guardrail’s decisions
Nothing of concern, as guardrail thresholds don’t affect security
exam.why: Guardrail thresholds directly affect safety and security, so changes need impact analysis, evaluation and approval.

exam.q: Under the EU AI Act, why might a major update to a high-risk AI system need special attention in change management?
o: Updates to high-risk systems are prohibited once they are on the market
A substantial modification can trigger a new conformity assessment
High-risk systems may only be updated once every three years
The Act requires all updates to be approved by the European Commission
exam.why: Substantial modifications can require a new conformity assessment, so impact analysis must consider regulatory as well as technical effects.

exam.q: A bank releases a new credit model to 5% of applicants first, watching approval rates by group, error rates and complaints, with automatic reversion if any breach agreed limits. Which practice is this?
o: A blue-green deployment with an instant full switch
A canary release with pre-agreed rollback triggers
A shadow deployment, since only some applicants are affected
A ring deployment limited to internal staff
exam.why: A small share of real traffic, with monitored signals and automatic reversion, is a canary with rollback triggers. Shadow mode wouldn’t affect real applicants.

exam.q: After a rollback, an agent keeps behaving like the new version for some users. Investigation shows the new version wrote instructions into users’ persistent memory. What should the rollback procedure have included?
o: Rolling back the model only, since memory doesn’t affect behaviour
Handling state: reverting or cleaning memory written by the new version
Deleting all users’ accounts, so that they start again from scratch
Waiting for the memory entries to expire naturally over several months
exam.why: Rollbacks must handle state that the new version created, such as memory, caches and data changes, or the old behaviour won’t fully return.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a SOC 2 Type I and a Type II report?
o: Type I covers security; Type II covers only privacy and processing integrity
Type II also tests whether the controls operated effectively over a period
Type I is written by an auditor; Type II is the vendor’s own self-assessment
Type II applies only to vendors that provide AI or ML services
quiz.why: Type I assesses control design at a point in time; Type II adds testing of operating effectiveness over a period, typically 6 to 12 months.

quiz.q: In a SOC 2 report, what does it mean when a subservice organisation is "carved out"?
o: Its controls are covered in more detail than the vendor’s own controls
Its controls are excluded, so separate evidence is needed for it
It failed the audit and was removed from the vendor’s supply chain
It is owned by the vendor, so it needs no separate assessment
quiz.why: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organisation’s controls are excluded from the report, so you need its own assurance.

quiz.q: Why is a CSA STAR for AI level 1 entry weaker evidence than an independent audit?
o: It covers physical data centre security rather than AI controls
It is the vendor’s own self-assessment, without independent checks
It expires after thirty days and is rarely renewed by vendors
It is only available to vendors that are based in the United States
quiz.why: Level 1 is a published self-assessment against the AI Controls Matrix questionnaire; level 2 adds independent assurance.

quiz.q: What does the OSI’s Open Source AI Definition require beyond published weights?
o: A commercial support contract with the model’s original developer
Access to the code and detailed information about the training data
Certification of the model under ISO/IEC 42001 by an accredited body
A guarantee that the model has never produced a harmful output
quiz.why: The 2024 definition requires the weights, the code and sufficiently detailed information about the training data. Most "open" models publish weights only.

quiz.q: Why should a model’s licence be checked along its whole pedigree?
o: Only the most recent licence in a chain of derived models is binding
Derived models may carry obligations from every parent and dataset
Model hubs merge all licences in a chain into one permissive licence
Older licences expire once a model is fine-tuned or quantised
quiz.why: Fine-tunes, merges and copies may inherit the conditions of their base models and tuning data, so obligations accumulate.

quiz.q: Which contract position BEST protects the inputs an organisation sends to an AI vendor?
o: Inputs become the vendor’s property, in exchange for a lower price
Customer ownership, no training without consent, limited retention
The vendor may use inputs to improve services if it anonymises them
The vendor decides retention according to its operational needs
quiz.why: Clear ownership, no training without explicit consent and defined retention keep the organisation in control of its data.

quiz.q: What does OMB M-25-22 require US federal AI contracts to say about non-public agency data?
o: Vendors must publish it, so that others can compete for future AI contracts
Vendors may not use it to train public or commercial AI without consent
Vendors must store it only in data centres located outside the United States
Vendors must share it with all model providers to improve government AI
quiz.why: The April 2025 memorandum requires contracts to permanently prohibit vendors from training publicly or commercially available AI on non-public agency data without explicit consent.

quiz.q: What is a model’s pedigree?
o: The number of downloads and likes it has received on a public hub
Its lineage: parents, derivation steps, data and who did each step
The digital signature its original publisher applied to the files
The legal entity that currently owns the copyright in its weights
quiz.why: Pedigree is the family tree: ancestors, derivation steps such as fine-tuning or merging, and the data and producers involved.

quiz.q: What does a valid digital signature on a model prove?
o: That the model contains no backdoors or hidden behaviours
Who signed it, and that it hasn’t changed since signing
That the model was trained only on lawfully obtained data
That the model performs well on standard benchmarks
quiz.why: Signatures prove authenticity and integrity, not safety, lawful data or quality.

quiz.q: Why should models from public hubs be pinned to a commit hash rather than a name?
o: Commit hashes download faster than names on most public model hubs
A name can be re-pointed or re-registered; a commit hash can’t change
Names are case-sensitive, which causes frequent download failures
Hubs charge extra fees for downloads that refer to models by name
quiz.why: Pinning to an immutable revision means a renamed, transferred or re-registered namespace can’t silently substitute a different model.

quiz.q: Which hardware details belong in an AIBOM?
o: The office floor plans and seating plans of the data science team
Accelerator models, driver and firmware versions, settings like ECC
The purchase prices and warranty dates of every GPU the firm owns
Only cloud region names, since hardware is the provider’s concern
quiz.why: Hardware flaws affect isolation and integrity, so accelerators, drivers, firmware, toolkits and security settings need recording.

quiz.q: What is a VEX statement?
o: A vendor’s marketing claim that its AI product has no vulnerabilities
A statement of whether a product is actually affected by a vulnerability
A list of every library version installed anywhere across the organisation
An emergency patch that fixes a vulnerability without needing a restart
quiz.why: VEX records whether a product is affected, not affected (with a justification), fixed or under investigation, so teams focus on real exposure.

quiz.q: Why should AIBOMs be generated by the pipeline rather than written by hand?
o: Hand-written AIBOMs are prohibited for high-risk systems under the EU AI Act
Generated AIBOMs reflect the artefacts actually built, and can be verified
Pipeline-generated AIBOMs are smaller and take up less storage space
Hand-written AIBOMs can’t record any information about datasets
quiz.why: Generating AIBOMs from the real artefacts, and signing one for each release, keeps them accurate and verifiable.

exam.q: An organisation finds that its document management vendor has added an AI summarisation feature, switched on by default, which sends files to a third-party model provider. The contract predates the feature. What should the organisation do FIRST?
o: Keep using the feature, since the vendor’s existing certifications already cover it
Switch the feature off, then assess the new data flow, fourth party and terms
Terminate the vendor contract at once and migrate all documents elsewhere
Ask staff to avoid summarising sensitive documents until the next renewal
exam.why: The feature creates a new data flow to a fourth party outside the assessed scope. Switching it off contains the exposure while the flow, provider and terms are assessed. Existing certifications may not cover it, termination is disproportionate, and relying on staff behaviour is unreliable.

exam.q: An AI vendor supplies a SOC 2 Type II report with an unmodified opinion. The report’s period ended ten months ago, and the vendor offers a bridge letter for the gap. How should the assessor treat the bridge letter?
o: As equivalent to an audit, because it extends the auditor’s opinion up to today
As management’s unaudited statement, weaker evidence than the report itself
As a sign that the vendor failed its audit, so the report should be rejected
As irrelevant, because SOC 2 reports never need to cover recent months
exam.why: A bridge letter is vendor management’s own statement about the period since the report ended. It is useful but unaudited, so weigh it accordingly and ask when the next report is due.

exam.q: An AI chat tool connected to a company’s CRM is compromised at the vendor, and attackers use its OAuth tokens to export CRM records. Which control would MOST have reduced the impact?
o: Requiring the vendor to hold an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covering its offices
Least-privilege scopes, activity monitoring and no secrets kept in CRM records
Asking users to sign out of the chat tool at the end of every working day
Changing the CRM administrator password once a year as a routine task
exam.why: Narrow scopes limit what stolen tokens can reach, monitoring spots bulk exports, and keeping secrets out of records stops attackers pivoting further. A certificate doesn’t limit token access, and user sign-outs and annual password changes don’t affect integration tokens.

exam.q: A team wants to build a commercial product on an open-weight model released under a community licence with an acceptable use policy and a monthly active user threshold. What is the BEST approach?
o: Proceed freely, because open-weight models can be used for any purpose at all
Review the licence and policy against the use case, growth plans and obligations
Avoid all open-weight models, because their licences can’t be complied with
Rename the model in the product so that the licence terms no longer apply
exam.why: Community licences usually allow commercial use, with conditions: prohibited uses, attribution or naming rules, and a separate licence above a user threshold. Review them against the use case and expected scale.

exam.q: A bank is negotiating a contract to fine-tune a provider’s model on its own data. Which term is MOST important for avoiding lock-in?
o: A discount for committing to the provider for at least five years
Exclusive ownership of the fine-tune, exportable in a usable format
A clause letting the provider reuse the fine-tune for other customers
Monthly reports on the provider’s overall model usage statistics
exam.why: Owning the fine-tune, and being able to export it with its prompts and evaluation sets, preserves the bank’s investment if it changes provider. The other terms increase dependence or don’t address portability.

exam.q: A dataset hub lists a scraped text dataset as "CC BY 4.0", but the original source’s terms say "non-commercial research only". Which terms should guide a commercial project’s decision?
o: The hub label, because hubs verify every dataset licence before publishing
The original source’s terms, verified at source, which are more restrictive
Whichever licence is more permissive, since the user may choose either one
Neither, because data scraped from the web carries no licence obligations
exam.why: Audits have found hub licence labels are often missing or wrong, and the original licence is frequently more restrictive. Follow the terms verified at the original source, and seek legal advice where needed.

exam.q: A security team must approve a quantised model that a community member derived from a lab’s signed release. The lab’s signature doesn’t cover the quantised files. What is the BEST way to establish trust?
o: Accept it, because the lab’s signature on the original covers all its derivatives
Quantise the verified original in-house through the pipeline, and sign the result
Check that the quantised model has many downloads and positive comments
Run a malware scan, and approve the model if no malicious code is found
exam.why: Reproducing the derivation from the verified, signed original in your own pipeline gives you provenance you control. The lab’s signature doesn’t cover altered files, popularity isn’t evidence, and a clean scan can’t reveal hidden behaviours.

exam.q: A deployment pipeline checks that model signatures are valid, but not who signed them. What is the MAIN weakness?
o: Valid signatures slow deployment down, so they should be checked less often
An attacker could sign a substitute model with their own valid identity
Signatures can only be verified by the model’s original training team
Signature checks stop models from loading on GPU-based servers
exam.why: A signature means something only when checked against an expected identity or key. Accepting any valid signature lets an attacker sign a malicious model with their own credentials.

exam.q: Which practice gives the STRONGEST chain of custody for third-party models inside an organisation?
o: Downloading the latest version from the hub every time a service starts up
Digests recorded on entry and verified at each step; counter-signing on approval
Keeping a spreadsheet of model names and the dates on which they were downloaded
Letting engineers copy approved models between servers whenever they are needed
exam.why: Verifying the same digest at every hand-off, and counter-signing approved artefacts, lets admission control trust one internal identity. The other options allow substitution or lose track of what runs.
