exam.q: A public dataset is reported to be poisoned. Which AIBOM content lets the organisation MOST quickly find every affected model, including fine-tunes of affected models?
o: The names of the data scientists who trained each affected model
Dataset identifiers and versions per model, plus pedigree links
GPU driver versions and firmware settings for each training cluster
The licence terms of every serving library used by the platform
exam.why: Dataset entries show which models trained on the poisoned data, and pedigree links reveal descendants that inherited it. People, drivers and library licences don’t answer the question.

exam.q: A GPU container toolkit vulnerability allows container escape on shared clusters. The organisation’s AIBOMs record models, data and libraries, but not infrastructure. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Stop using containers for AI workloads, and run every model on bare-metal servers
Record drivers, toolkits, firmware and settings in AIBOMs, generated automatically
Ask the cloud provider to confirm in writing that its GPUs are always kept secure
Record infrastructure details, but only for clusters that host high-risk models
exam.why: Recording infrastructure dependencies automatically lets infrastructure advisories be matched as quickly as software ones. Abandoning containers is disproportionate, written assurances don’t locate exposure, and partial records leave gaps.

quiz.q: Why should an AI security assessment scope the whole system rather than just the model?
o: Models can’t be tested directly, so only the surrounding system can be assessed
Many serious failures happen where components meet, such as retrieval and tools
Regulators prohibit testing models that were developed by a third-party provider
The model is always the most secure component, so testing it adds little value
quiz.why: Real failures often occur at the joins: retrieved content reaching tools, outputs reaching downstream systems, or approvals that can be bypassed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of rules of engagement in an AI red team exercise?
o: To list the attacks testers must avoid mentioning on social media afterwards
To set the authority, scope, limits and stop rules before testing starts
To guarantee that the system will pass the test without any findings at all
To describe the product’s features for the marketing team’s launch plan
quiz.why: Signed rules of engagement make testing authorised, bounded and safe, with clear stop rules and reporting.

quiz.q: What does grey box testing mean in an AI assessment?
o: Testers start with no information at all about the system that they are testing
Testers get some internal knowledge, such as the architecture and system prompts
Testers get full access to code, weights and training data from the very start
Testers may only use automated tools, and never any manual testing techniques
quiz.why: Grey box testing shares partial knowledge, so testers spend their time finding weaknesses rather than guessing how the system works.

quiz.q: What is a canary tool in an indirect injection test?
o: A tool that blocks every instruction found inside the retrieved documents
A harmless tool that records it was called, proving an instruction was obeyed
A tool that alerts users whenever an agent is about to transfer any money
A monitoring tool that measures the agent’s response time under heavy load
quiz.why: A canary tool has no real effect; its only job is to show that the agent followed an instruction planted in data.

quiz.q: Which test is specific to retrieval-augmented generation?
o: Checking that the chatbot’s login page enforces multi-factor authentication
Checking whether retrieval returns documents the user isn’t permitted to see
Checking that the model’s weights are encrypted when they are stored at rest
Checking that the GPU cluster’s drivers are patched to the latest version
quiz.why: Permission-aware retrieval is a RAG-specific control: retrieval must enforce the requesting user’s document permissions.

quiz.q: Why are AI security test results reported as attack success rates?
o: Rates are required by every AI regulation for all types of AI system
Outputs vary between attempts, so a rate shows how often attacks work
Rates are easier to present to executives than a list of findings
Most automated testing tools can’t record the result of a single test
quiz.why: Because AI systems are stochastic, the same attack can succeed on some attempts and fail on others; a rate over many attempts captures that.

quiz.q: Which agentic test checks whether an injected instruction can affect later sessions?
o: A runaway loop test that counts how many tool calls the agent makes
A memory persistence test, across later sessions and other users
A permission-aware retrieval test run against the document index
A load test that measures the agent’s latency during peak traffic
quiz.why: Memory persistence tests check whether planted instructions survive in an agent’s memory and influence future sessions.

quiz.q: Which stage of the AI red team cycle follows reporting?
o: Planning next year’s budget for the whole security team
Fixing the weaknesses that were found, and then retesting
Deleting all test logs to protect the testers’ privacy
Publishing the findings openly on the company website
quiz.why: Red teaming is a break-fix cycle: builders mitigate, and the red team retests to confirm the fixes.

quiz.q: What does the CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide provide?
o: A certification scheme for organisations that develop agentic AI products
Twelve threat categories for red teaming agents, such as memory manipulation
A list of approved AI agent vendors for government procurement in the EU
A legal template for contracts between agent developers and customers
quiz.why: The 2025 guide, developed with the OWASP AI Exchange, sets out twelve agentic threat categories with test approaches.

quiz.q: Why do AI red teams emulate benign users as well as attackers?
o: Benign users are easier to emulate, which keeps testing costs to a minimum
Ordinary users can trigger harms by accident, which matter as much as attacks
Regulations require at least half of all red team personas to be benign users
Attackers always pretend to be benign users, so the two personas are identical
quiz.why: Many AI harms, such as dangerous advice or privacy leaks, arise from ordinary use, so red teams test benign personas too.

quiz.q: What role does the scorer play in automated red teaming?
o: It generates new adversarial inputs from the seed objectives
It judges whether each response shows a successful attack
It deploys the target system into the staging environment
It writes the final report for non-technical stakeholders
quiz.why: A scorer, such as a classifier or an LLM judge, decides whether each response counts as a success, and its verdicts feed back to the attacker.

quiz.q: Why must LLM judges be calibrated against human labels?
o: LLM judges can only score responses that are written in English
They can be lenient, strict or manipulated, distorting the results
Human labels are needed before any model can legally be deployed
Calibration makes the judge run faster on very large test sets
quiz.why: Uncalibrated judges can hide failures or raise false alarms, and the system under test may even manipulate them.

quiz.q: What is the "lethal trifecta" for AI agents?
o: Three agents working together, so no single agent can be compromised
Untrusted content, access to private data and external communication
Three failed sign-in attempts, after which an agent’s account is locked
Training, fine-tuning and deployment, all done in a single environment
quiz.why: An agent with all three can be steered by injected instructions into stealing data; removing any one breaks the path.

quiz.q: A model refuses a harmful request in English but answers the same request translated into a low-resource language. Which root cause does this illustrate?
o: Competing objectives: helpfulness overrides safety training
Mismatched generalisation: ability outreaches safety training
Context overflow: the system prompt was truncated in translation
Model drift: the provider updated the model between the two tests
quiz.why: The model can understand the language, but its safety training didn’t cover it well, so its abilities generalise further than its safety behaviour. That is mismatched generalisation.

quiz.q: Many-shot jailbreaking depends MOST on which model feature?
o: Access to the model’s gradients through an open-weight release
A long context window that can hold hundreds of examples
Tool use that lets the model fetch content from the web
A high sampling temperature that makes outputs more random
quiz.why: The attack packs hundreds of fabricated dialogues into one prompt, which only fits in a long context window. Its success rises with the number of examples.

quiz.q: A team’s jailbreak tests show a 2% attack success rate after a new classifier is added, down from 30%. What else must the report include for a fair view of the change?
o: The names of the testers who ran each of the attack families
How often benign requests are wrongly refused, before and after
The model’s accuracy on general knowledge benchmarks only
The exact prompts used, published for the whole company to see
quiz.why: A defence that blocks attacks by also blocking legitimate requests can look excellent on attack success alone. Pairing attack success with false refusals shows the real trade-off.

quiz.q: An attacker submits thousands of slightly varied versions of a refused request, changing capitalisation and spacing, until one succeeds. Which control MOST directly counters this approach?
o: A longer system prompt that restates the safety policy in detail
Rate limits, and monitoring for bursts of near-identical requests
Lowering the sampling temperature for every request to zero
Translating every request into English before it reaches the model
quiz.why: Best-of-N attacks rely on volume: success keeps rising with the number of attempts. Rate limits and monitoring cap the attempts and reveal the pattern. Varied inputs still produce varied outputs at a temperature of 0.

exam.q: A bank plans an assessment of a customer chatbot that uses RAG and can open support tickets. The project manager proposes testing only the underlying model with a public jailbreak benchmark. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, because the model is where all of the chatbot’s security weaknesses originate
Scope the whole system, including retrieval, ticket actions, guardrails and monitoring
Agree, provided the benchmark is run twice, to allow for the model’s randomness
Replace the assessment with a review of the model vendor’s SOC 2 report instead
exam.why: Benchmarks of the model miss system-level risks such as retrieval permissions, injection through documents and ticket actions. Scope the whole system, with scenarios drawn from its threat model.

exam.q: During a red team exercise, a tester sees what appears to be real customer data in the staging assistant’s responses. The rules of engagement include a stop rule for this case. What should the tester do FIRST?
o: Continue testing to find out how much real data can be extracted, then report it
Stop testing at once and notify the engagement lead, as the stop rule requires
Delete the responses from the logs so that the real data isn’t retained
Post the finding in the team’s open chat channel to warn colleagues quickly
exam.why: Stop rules exist for exactly this situation: halt, escalate and let the lead manage the potential data exposure. Continuing, deleting evidence or broadcasting the finding are all inappropriate.

exam.q: Which success criterion is BEST for a red team test of a support agent’s refund tool?
o: The agent should generally behave securely and responsibly in most situations
Unauthorised refunds succeed in under 0.5% of 500 attempts per technique class
The testers should feel satisfied that they tried their hardest to break the agent
The agent must never produce any output that the testers find surprising
exam.why: A good criterion is measurable and agreed in advance, accounting for repeated attempts. Vague or subjective criteria can’t support a decision.

exam.q: A legal research assistant retrieves from a shared index. Testers find that a junior employee’s question returned a confidential board memo. Which control failure does this MOST likely indicate?
o: The model wasn’t fine-tuned on enough legal documents during its development
Retrieval isn’t enforcing the requesting user’s document permissions
The assistant’s guardrails were set too strictly for the legal domain
The index was too large for the embedding model to handle accurately
exam.why: Returning documents a user isn’t entitled to see is a failure of permission-aware retrieval, not of model quality or guardrail strictness.

exam.q: Testers want to show that an email agent can be steered by instructions hidden in incoming messages, without risking harm. Which approach is BEST?
o: Send real phishing emails to staff, and see whether the agent forwards them on
Plant a test email that asks the agent to call a monitored canary tool
Ask the agent directly whether it would follow instructions found in emails
Review only the agent’s code, since its behaviour can’t be tested
exam.why: A canary proves the weakness safely and observably. Real phishing harms people, asking the agent proves nothing, and code review alone can’t show model behaviour.

exam.q: An agent passed every single-prompt injection test, but a red teamer succeeded by spreading an attack across six conversation turns. What does this show about the test design?
o: Single-prompt tests are sufficient, so the red teamer’s result can be ignored
The test suite needs multi-turn cases, since attacks can build up gradually
Conversations longer than five turns should be blocked for every user
The red teamer should have kept to the existing single-prompt test cases
exam.why: Multi-turn attacks escalate gradually and evade single-prompt safeguards, so suites must include them. Blocking long conversations is disproportionate.

exam.q: An organisation wants to start red teaming a new agent with novel capabilities. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Run an automated tool’s default test library only, since it covers known attacks
Explore manually first, then automate variants and regressions of what is found
Wait until a public benchmark covers the agent’s capabilities before testing
Ask the developers to red team their own agent, since they know it best
exam.why: Human exploration finds novel, contextual weaknesses in new capabilities; automation then scales and preserves them. Default libraries, waiting and self-testing all leave gaps.

exam.q: A red team shows that an agent can be manipulated into exfiltrating data, but the SOC saw no alerts during the whole exercise. Which practice would have MOST improved the outcome?
o: Running the exercise without telling anyone, to keep it as realistic as possible
Purple teaming, so that defenders tune detections during the engagement
Reducing the number of attacks, so that the SOC isn’t overwhelmed by alerts
Repeating the same exercise next year, with exactly the same test cases
exam.why: Purple teaming turns each attack into a detection test, so monitoring gaps are found and fixed during the engagement.

exam.q: A team’s autonomous testing agent began probing a third-party API that was out of scope, after following a link in a response. Which control was MISSING?
o: A larger compute budget for the testing agent, so that it could finish sooner
Technical scope limits on targets and actions, enforced outside the agent
A better system prompt asking the agent politely to stay within its scope
A faster model, so the agent spends less time on each individual target
exam.why: Autonomous testers can be steered like any agent, so scope must be enforced technically, outside the model, for example with network allow-lists.

exam.q: An automated pipeline reports that a new guardrail blocks 99% of adversarial prompts. What should ALSO be measured before relying on it?
o: How long the guardrail’s vendor has been in business
The false positive rate on benign requests, by category
How many engineers reviewed the guardrail configuration
Whether the guardrail was bought or developed in-house
exam.why: A guardrail that blocks attacks but also blocks many legitimate requests may be unusable; results by category also reveal weak spots hidden in the average.

exam.q: A red team lead is planning jailbreak testing for a multilingual customer assistant that accepts text, images and file uploads. Which test plan is BEST?
o: Run the public HarmBench suite in English and report its overall score
Cover each attack family in every supported language and input channel
Test text prompts thoroughly, since images and files are lower risk
Focus on optimised suffixes, as they are the most advanced technique
exam.why: Jailbreaks exploit gaps in safety training, which are often language-specific and channel-specific. A public benchmark in one language, or one family alone, leaves those gaps untested.

exam.q: After a perplexity filter is deployed, a red team finds that machine-optimised jailbreak strings are blocked, but readable jailbreaks written by an attacker model still succeed. What is the BEST next step?
o: Lower the perplexity threshold until the readable attacks are blocked too
Add complementary defences, such as classifiers on inputs and outputs
Close the finding, since automated suffix attacks were the main threat
Ban attacker models from being used in future red team exercises
exam.why: Perplexity filters catch unnatural text, not fluent attacks. Pushing the threshold far enough to block fluent text would block normal users too, so layered classifiers and other controls are needed.

exam.q: A bank’s red team reports that a jailbreak succeeded in 4 of 100 attempts. The product owner wants it marked as not reproducible because it failed when re-run once. What is the BEST response?
o: Mark it not reproducible, since it failed when it was re-run
Report it as a 4% success rate, since outputs are probabilistic
Discard it, since anything below 5% is within normal tolerance
Retest at a temperature of 0 and report only the single result
exam.why: Model outputs vary between runs, so a single failed retry proves nothing. Findings are reported as rates over repeated trials, then judged against the system’s risk tolerance.

quiz.q: Why is reproducibility reported as a success rate for AI findings?
o: Success rates are mandatory under every AI security regulation in force
AI outputs vary, so the rate shows how often the attack actually works
A rate is easier to calculate than recording the result of a single test
Rates hide the details of the attack from anyone who reads the report
quiz.why: Because outputs vary between attempts, a rate over many runs, with settings recorded, is the meaningful measure of reproducibility.

quiz.q: Why should findings be deduplicated during triage?
o: Duplicates make reports longer than executives are willing to read
Variants with one root cause need one fix, so they are one finding
Deduplication lowers the severity of each finding that remains afterwards
Most frameworks only allow one finding per assessment to be reported
quiz.why: Grouping variants under one root cause gives one owner, one fix and one retest, with the variants kept as evidence.

quiz.q: Why does a finding that went undetected during testing deserve a higher priority?
o: Undetected findings are always easier to fix than detected ones
An attacker could exploit it without anyone noticing or responding
Detection tools are only required for high-risk AI systems by law
Monitoring teams are responsible for fixing every undetected finding
quiz.why: Without detection, exploitation could continue unnoticed, so the exposure lasts longer and response is delayed.

quiz.q: What makes a finding a security vulnerability rather than a model limitation?
o: It appears in more than half of all the test attempts that were made
It lets someone cross a security boundary, reaching data, actions or systems
It was found by the security team rather than by the data science team
It involves a model that was provided by an external third-party vendor
quiz.why: Vulnerabilities break security boundaries and can be exploited deliberately; limitations are inherent behaviour seen in normal use.

quiz.q: When does a hallucination become a security concern?
o: Whenever the model is used by more than a thousand people each day
When attackers can exploit it, as with invented package names
Only when the hallucination appears in an image rather than text
Never, because hallucinations are only quality problems
quiz.why: Hallucination is a limitation, but invented package or URL names can be registered by attackers, creating supply chain risk.

quiz.q: Where should a finding about biased outputs in a hiring tool usually be routed?
o: To the network team, as a firewall configuration problem
To safety and responsible AI review, given its legal stakes
To the help desk, as a routine user complaint about tone
To nobody, since bias is not a security issue of any kind
quiz.why: Bias is a responsible AI issue with legal implications, such as discrimination law and high-risk obligations, so it needs its own review.

quiz.q: What does MITRE ATLAS add when mapping a finding?
o: A severity score that replaces the organisation’s own risk rating
The adversary technique involved, linked to tactics and case studies
A legal opinion on whether the finding must be reported to regulators
A ready-made patch for the vulnerability, supplied by MITRE itself
quiz.why: ATLAS describes how adversaries attack AI systems, with tactics, techniques and real case studies.

quiz.q: Which CWE entry describes improper neutralisation of input used for LLM prompting?
o: CWE-79, which covers cross-site scripting in web pages
CWE-1427, which covers input used for LLM prompting
CWE-89, which covers SQL injection into databases
CWE-200, which covers exposure of sensitive information
quiz.why: CWE-1427 names the weakness behind prompt injection; CWE-1426 covers improper validation of generative AI output.

quiz.q: What should a reproduction package for an AI finding include?
o: A single screenshot of the most convincing output, with no other detail at all
Versions, settings, transcript, traces, expected and observed results, and a rate
The tester’s opinion of how serious the finding is, with no supporting data
The full text of every attack prompt, pasted into the report’s executive summary
quiz.why: Those elements let anyone repeat the test under the same conditions and verify the fix later.

quiz.q: Why should evidence files be hashed when they are captured?
o: Hashing compresses evidence so it takes less storage space
It proves later that the evidence hasn’t been altered
Hashes make evidence readable by automated report tools
Regulators only accept evidence stored in hashed form
quiz.why: A hash recorded at capture, with a chain of custody, lets anyone confirm the evidence is unchanged.

quiz.q: What does "bottom line up front" mean in an executive summary?
o: Listing every finding in order of when it was discovered
Leading with the decision that is needed, and its impact
Placing the budget request on the final page of the report
Starting with the technical method used by the testers
quiz.why: Leaders need the decision and its consequences first; supporting detail follows.

quiz.q: How should a flaw found in a third-party AI product be disclosed?
o: Published immediately on social media, to warn the vendor’s other customers
Reported privately to the vendor, with time to fix before any publication
Kept secret indefinitely, since disclosure could embarrass the vendor
Sent to all the vendor’s competitors, so that they can check their products
quiz.why: Coordinated vulnerability disclosure, as described in ISO/IEC 29147, protects users while giving the vendor time to fix.

quiz.q: Why should an assessment report include positive observations?
o: To make the testing team look good to the people who hired them
To show which controls held, which helps decisions and teams
To reduce the number of findings that need to be fixed later
To satisfy a legal requirement in every country for reports
quiz.why: Knowing what worked helps leaders judge overall risk, and tells teams which controls to keep and extend.

exam.q: A red team reports a jailbreak that makes a public chatbot produce mildly offensive jokes in 45% of attempts, and an indirect injection that leaks other customers’ order details in 2% of attempts. Which should receive the HIGHER priority?
o: The jailbreak, because its 45% success rate makes it far more reproducible
The injection, because leaking customers’ data is far more severe at scale
Both equally, because every finding should always share the same priority
Neither, because both success rates fall below the 50% threshold for action
exam.why: Severity and business impact dominate: a data leak affecting customers is serious, and 2% is frequent at scale. The jailbreak still needs fixing, at lower priority.

exam.q: During triage, an engineer argues that a finding should be closed because the fix "has been deployed". The retest hasn’t been run. What should happen?
o: Close it, since the engineer has confirmed that the fix was deployed
Keep it open until a retest under the original conditions passes
Lower its priority to P3, since a fix now exists in production
Delete the finding, so it doesn’t appear in the next report
exam.why: Closure requires evidence: a retest using the reproduction package confirms the fix works and hasn’t been bypassed.

exam.q: An assistant sometimes recommends a software library that doesn’t exist. Researchers note that attackers have started registering such names. How should this finding be treated?
o: As a harmless hallucination, for the model’s quality backlog only
As a limitation with security impact, needing supply chain controls
As a direct jailbreak, to be handled through content moderation alone
As out of scope, since the library names were never real
exam.why: The hallucination is a limitation, but because attackers can register the names, it creates supply chain risk that needs controls such as allow-listed registries.

exam.q: A vendor’s AI bug bounty programme lists jailbreaks and direct prompt injection as out of scope, but rewards data exfiltration. A tester finds that a planted document makes the vendor’s assistant send users’ files to an outside address. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Don’t report it at all, since prompt injection is listed as out of scope
Report it through the programme as data exfiltration, a security impact
Publish the finding at once, since the programme won’t accept it anyway
Report it only through in-product feedback, as a content issue
exam.why: Indirect injection that exfiltrates data has a security impact, which is exactly what such programmes reward. The exclusions cover content-only issues.

exam.q: A team maps its findings only to internal labels such as "chatbot weirdness" and "agent problem". What is the MAIN drawback?
o: Internal labels can’t be stored in standard ticketing systems at all
Findings can’t be compared, shared or checked for coverage consistently
Internal labels always overstate severity compared with frameworks
The team must pay a licence fee to use internal labels in reports
exam.why: Mapping to ATLAS, OWASP and CWE gives a common language, supports coverage analysis and links findings to known controls and threats.

exam.q: A dashboard shows findings mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, and an executive concludes that LLM01 findings are always the most severe. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, since the OWASP list is ordered by severity in every system
Explain that categories describe the type of risk, not its severity here
Remove LLM01 findings from the dashboard to avoid further confusion
Re-rate every LLM01 finding as critical, to match the executive’s view
exam.why: Framework categories classify the kind of problem. Severity depends on context, so mapping and rating must stay separate.

exam.q: Engineers can’t reproduce a finding that the red team recorded a month ago. The record shows the provider has since updated the model behind the API. What does this MOST suggest about evidence practice?
o: Findings from hosted models should never be recorded in the first place
Record the provider’s model version or snapshot, and retest after changes
The red team must have invented the finding, so it should be closed
Engineers should be given administrator access to the provider’s systems
exam.why: Recording the exact provider model version explains changed results, and retesting after provider updates checks whether the risk remains.

exam.q: A red team’s report pastes full attack transcripts, including working injection text and customer names, into the main body. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Encrypt the PDF with a strong password, and keep the content exactly as it is
Redact personal data, store attack text separately, and refer to it by name
Delete all of the evidence immediately, so that nobody can ever misuse it
Email the report only to the executives, and not to any of the engineers
exam.why: Reports circulate. Redaction and restricted evidence storage, referenced by name, protect people and stop the report from becoming an attack kit, while engineers can still reproduce the finding.

exam.q: A CISO must brief the board on an AI red team exercise with two serious findings and many minor ones. Which approach is BEST?
o: Present every finding in technical detail, so the board sees how thorough the work was
Lead with the two risks in business terms, the decisions needed and the options
Mention only the minor findings, to avoid alarming the board unnecessarily
Present the most shocking raw outputs, to make sure the board takes AI seriously
exam.why: Boards need the bottom line: business impact, decisions and options, with proportion. Detail, minimisation and shock tactics all undermine good decisions.

exam.q: A product owner asks whether the absence of findings in one category means the assistant is safe in that area. What is the MOST accurate answer?
o: Yes: no findings means the category has now been proven to be completely safe
Testing reduces uncertainty, but can’t prove absence; check coverage and limits
No: categories with no findings are always the most dangerous ones in practice
It depends only on how much the testing cost, not on what was tested
exam.why: Honest communication states what testing can and can’t show: coverage, attempts and conditions determine how much confidence is justified.

quiz.q: Which mitigation targets the root cause of training data poisoning?
o: Rate limiting the model’s public API by user and by token count
Provenance tracking and data validation before training
Watermarking every output that the model generates
Adding a disclaimer to the application’s user interface
quiz.why: Poisoning enters through data, so verifying where data comes from and validating it before training addresses the root cause.

quiz.q: What is a known limitation of adversarial training?
o: It can only be used on models that have fewer than a million parameters
It hardens models against attacks seen, but new techniques can still succeed
It permanently removes the need for any input or output filtering at all
It makes models completely immune to every possible kind of evasion attack
quiz.why: Adversarial training improves robustness to known attacks, often at some cost to accuracy, and needs repeating as attackers adapt.

quiz.q: What is the core principle behind design patterns that contain prompt injection?
o: Every agent should use the largest and most capable model available
Once untrusted input is read, it mustn’t trigger consequential actions
Agents should be given broad tools, so that they can recover from attacks
System prompts should be kept secret, so attackers can’t learn their rules
quiz.why: Patterns such as plan-then-execute and dual LLM constrain agents so that untrusted content can’t change which consequential actions run.

quiz.q: Why should a content filter be tuned using both adversarial and benign test sets?
o: Benign sets are needed to make the filter run faster in production
To measure missed attacks and false positives, and balance the two
Because regulators require equal numbers of each kind of test
Adversarial sets alone are too expensive to create in most cases
quiz.why: A filter that blocks attacks but also blocks many legitimate requests may be switched off; both error types must be measured.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST describes a well-designed code execution sandbox?
o: Long-lived, shared by every user, with cloud keys for convenience
Isolated, short-lived, with no secrets and allow-listed egress
Running inside the production database server, for speed
Open network access, so code can install anything it needs
quiz.why: Isolation, short life, no secrets and restricted egress contain the damage if executed code is malicious or an agent is manipulated.

quiz.q: Why should AI rate limits consider tokens and cost, not just request counts?
o: Request counts are impossible to measure accurately at an API gateway
Just a few very long requests can consume huge resources and money
Token limits are required for every AI system under the EU AI Act
Cost-based limits make every individual response noticeably faster
quiz.why: One request can carry an enormous prompt or trigger a long agent loop, so limits on tokens, cost and steps prevent floods and denial of wallet.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an interim control?
o: To replace the permanent fix, so that it never needs to be built
To contain a risk now, while the full fix is still being built
To document a risk for auditors without changing anything
To transfer all responsibility for the risk to the vendor
quiz.why: Interim controls, such as disabling a tool or adding approval, close the exposure immediately while strategic fixes are delivered.

quiz.q: Which is a risk treatment option in standards such as ISO/IEC 27005?
o: Ignore the risk, until an incident proves that it was real
Avoid the risk, for example by removing the risky capability
Hide the risk from the board, to avoid causing any alarm
Delay all decisions until the next annual risk review
quiz.why: Risks can be modified, avoided, shared or retained; avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all.

quiz.q: Why should a regression suite include variants of a reported attack?
o: Variants make the suite take longer to run, which gives better coverage
To check the fix addresses the weakness, not just the reported input
Variants are needed so that the report looks more thorough to readers
Because the original reported input is usually impossible to rerun
quiz.why: A fix that only blocks one string is overfitted. Variants, including held-out ones, show whether it generalises.

quiz.q: What does a release gate do in a regression testing pipeline?
o: It lets anyone deploy a change without running any tests first
It blocks changes that push results past agreed thresholds
It records test results only after a release has gone live
It replaces the need for an independent retest by the red team
quiz.why: A gate stops a change from shipping when security or utility results cross their thresholds, unless an exception is approved.

quiz.q: Why must benign requests be part of mitigation validation?
o: Benign requests are the easiest test cases for any team to write quickly
A fix that breaks normal use may be switched off, bringing back the risk
Regulators require benign tests before any AI system is allowed to launch
Benign requests reveal new attack techniques faster than red teams
quiz.why: Utility matters: over-blocking frustrates users and creates pressure to remove the control, reintroducing the risk.

quiz.q: Which event should trigger reassessment of an accepted residual AI risk?
o: A routine change to the colour scheme of the user interface
A provider model update, or a new tool given to the agent
A new employee joining the marketing department
A scheduled office move to another floor of the building
quiz.why: Model updates and new capabilities change behaviour and exposure, so accepted risks must be re-tested and re-rated.

quiz.q: What should happen when a production canary record appears in an AI output?
o: Delete the canary record, so it can’t appear in any more outputs
Treat it as a potential incident, and investigate how it leaked
Ignore it, because canary records are only used during testing
Raise the guardrail threshold, so that fewer outputs are checked
quiz.why: Canaries should never appear in normal use, so a hit signals possible misuse or leakage that needs investigation.

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of PGD adversarial training?
o: It can only be applied to models with fewer than a billion parameters
Robustness mainly covers the attack type and budget used in training
It removes the need to test the model with new attacks after release
It improves clean accuracy so much that robustness becomes unnecessary
quiz.why: Adversarial training hardens a model against the threat model it trained on, such as one norm and budget. Other norms, patches and new attack types can still succeed, and clean accuracy usually falls.

quiz.q: What does a certificate from randomised smoothing guarantee?
o: No change an attacker could make, however large, can alter it
No change within a stated L2 radius can alter that input’s label
Every input from the training distribution is classified correctly
Gradient-based attacks fail, though black-box attacks may succeed
quiz.why: Randomised smoothing certifies, for a specific input, that no perturbation within a stated L2 radius can change the smoothed classifier’s output. It says nothing about larger changes or overall accuracy.

quiz.q: A team adds an open-weight guardrail model that screens prompts for jailbreak attempts. Which evaluation is MOST important before relying on it?
o: Confirm the guardrail model is larger than the main model it protects
Measure missed attacks, false blocks and evasion with obfuscated inputs
Check that the guardrail’s developer is certified under ISO/IEC 27001
Verify that it blocks every prompt containing suspicious keywords
quiz.why: A guardrail has to be measured on your own traffic for misses and false positives, and tested against deliberate evasion, which research shows can defeat detectors. Size, certification and keyword blocking don’t show it works.

quiz.q: A small prompt injection classifier has a 512-token context window, but the application accepts documents of up to 20,000 tokens. What should the design do?
o: Scan only the first 512 tokens, since attacks usually appear at the start
Split long inputs into segments and scan each, alongside other controls
Remove the classifier, since it can’t process complete documents
Raise the classifier’s threshold, so it flags less of each document
quiz.why: Content beyond the window would go unscanned, and attackers can place instructions anywhere. Splitting inputs into segments and scanning each, as Meta recommends for Prompt Guard 2, keeps coverage, with other controls behind it.

exam.q: A bank’s fraud model is being evaded by small, deliberate changes to transaction features. Which mitigation BEST targets this threat?
o: Watermarking the model’s outputs, so evasion attempts can be traced back
Adversarial training on such changes, validated against held-out attacks
Adding a longer system prompt telling the model to watch for manipulation
Increasing the API rate limit, so the model can process more transactions
exam.why: Adversarial training targets evasion directly, and validating it on held-out attacks checks it generalises. Watermarks, prompts and rate limits don’t address evasion of a fraud model.

exam.q: A research assistant agent reads web pages and can send emails. Testing shows injected page text can make it email confidential notes. Which change addresses the root cause MOST effectively?
o: Adding a filter that looks for suspicious phrases in each web page
Redesigning so web content can’t change actions, with approval for emails
Asking users not to research any topics on unfamiliar or untrusted websites
Switching to a different model provider with stronger safety training
exam.why: Containing untrusted content by design, for example plan-then-execute or a quarantined reader, with approval for consequential actions, removes the attack path. Filters, user advice and model changes only reduce it.

exam.q: After a new output filter is deployed, the help desk reports that the assistant now refuses many legitimate questions about medication doses from pharmacists. What should the security team do FIRST?
o: Remove the filter immediately, since user satisfaction is the priority
Measure false positives on labelled benign sets, and retune for this use
Tell the pharmacists to rephrase their questions to avoid the filter
Keep the filter unchanged, since some over-blocking is always acceptable
exam.why: Measuring false positives with labelled benign data, then retuning thresholds or adding context-aware rules, keeps protection while restoring utility. Removing, ignoring or working around the filter are poor responses.

exam.q: A provider’s API is being queried systematically by a small number of accounts in what looks like a model extraction attempt. Which response is BEST?
o: Publish the model’s weights, since extraction is now inevitable anyway
Throttle those accounts, minimise output detail, and investigate them
Double the rate limits for all users, to keep the service responsive
Watermark all outputs, and take no other action against the accounts
exam.why: Per-identity throttling, returning less detail and investigating raise the cost of extraction and confirm intent. Watermarks help prove theft later but don’t stop it.

exam.q: A serious finding has two fixes: an approval step that takes two days to add, and a redesign that takes two months. The product launches in a week. What is the BEST plan?
o: Launch, and start the two-month redesign immediately after the launch
Add the approval step before launch, and fund the redesign as planned work
Delay the launch by two months, until the redesign is fully complete
Launch, and add the approval step if an incident occurs afterwards
exam.why: The quick win reduces risk before launch, and the redesign addresses the root cause later. Delaying two months may be disproportionate if the interim control brings risk within appetite.

exam.q: A residual risk remains after mitigation, and a team lead informally agrees to "live with it". What is MISSING from good practice?
o: Nothing, since any team lead can accept risks of any size on their own
Acceptance by an owner with authority, within appetite, with a review date
A press release explaining the risk to the organisation’s customers
An immediate decision to stop using AI anywhere in that business process
exam.why: Residual risk must be formally accepted by someone with authority, within the risk appetite, recorded in the register and reviewed.

exam.q: A fix for an injection finding blocks the exact prompt from the report. Testers then find that a translated version of the same attack still works. What does this show?
o: The fix works, since translated attacks are always out of scope for testing
The fix is overfitted; validate with variants, including held-out ones
Translation tools should be blocked for every user of the system
The original finding was a false positive, and can now be closed
exam.why: A fix that fails on simple variants addresses the string, not the weakness. Validation needs variants across languages, formats and turns, including held-out cases.

exam.q: A team tunes its injection classifier until it scores perfectly on the regression suite, using the suite’s own cases as tuning data. Why is the perfect score unreliable?
o: Perfect scores are always caused by a software bug in the harness
The suite has been contaminated, so it no longer tests generalisation
Classifiers can never be tuned without the model provider’s consent
Regression suites must be rebuilt from scratch for every release
exam.why: Tuning on test cases inflates results. Held-out variants that are never used for tuning keep the suite an honest measure.

exam.q: Scheduled automated red teaming shows attack success on a key category rising from 2% to 11% after a newly published technique was added to the tests. What should happen NEXT?
o: Remove the new technique from the tests, so the results return to normal
Treat it as a breached KRI: reassess, mitigate and add regression cases
Wait for the next annual review to discuss the change in results
Accept the new level, since accepted risks can’t be reopened
exam.why: A breached key risk indicator triggers reassessment and treatment, with new cases added to the regression suite, so the risk returns within appetite.

exam.q: Which approach BEST maintains confidence in an AI system’s residual risk between formal assessments?
o: Relying on the most recent penetration test report until the next one
KRIs, scheduled testing, canaries and triggered reassessments
Asking users to report problems, with no other monitoring
Freezing the system, so that its risk can never change again
exam.why: Continuous signals, scheduled testing and triggers keep residual risk visible as models, tools and threats change. Point-in-time reports go stale, and freezing the system is rarely practical.

exam.q: An organisation relies on a single guardrail model to block prompt injection for an agent that can make payments. Testing shows character-level obfuscation evades the guardrail 40% of the time. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Replace the guardrail with a larger model from a different vendor
Keep the guardrail, and add least privilege and approval for payments
Accept the risk, since 60% of obfuscated attacks are still blocked
Remove the guardrail, since it gives a false sense of security
exam.why: Guardrails can be evaded, so high-impact actions need controls that hold when a classifier misses: least privilege and human approval. A larger model may be evaded too, and removing a working layer weakens defence in depth.

exam.q: A guardrail service sometimes times out under heavy load. For an agent that can change customer records, what should happen to requests when the guardrail times out?
o: Fail open: let requests through so customers aren’t delayed
Fail closed: hold or block requests until the check completes
Send requests to the model unchecked, but log them for review
Retry once, then let the request through if it times out again
exam.why: For an agent with write access to customer records, an unchecked request can cause real harm, so the safe failure mode is to hold or block until the check succeeds. Failing open hands attackers a way round the control: overload it.

exam.q: A hospital must choose between an imaging model with empirical robustness from adversarial training and a smoothed model certified against small changes, which sometimes abstains. It needs provable assurance and has radiologists available. Which option fits BEST?
o: The empirical model, since adversarial training is a mathematical proof
The certified model, with abstentions routed to radiologist review
The certified model, with abstentions treated as negative results
The empirical model, since certified models can’t be used in healthcare
exam.why: Only the certified model provides provable assurance within its radius, and its abstentions need a safe fallback such as specialist review. Treating abstentions as negative results could miss disease.

quiz.q: About how long can you spend on each question if you want to finish the pilot exam on time?
o: About 30 seconds, since most questions are simple recall
About 67 seconds each, for 160 questions in three hours
About two minutes, with review time added at the end
About five minutes, as the exam has only 40 questions
quiz.why: 180 minutes for 160 questions is about 67 seconds each, so pacing checkpoints matter.

quiz.q: Why is "instruct the model not to do it" rarely the best answer?
o: Prompts are far too expensive to maintain at any real scale of use
Instructions guide a model; enforced controls outside it stop harm
Regulators prohibit the use of system prompts in production
Models ignore every instruction written in their system prompt
quiz.why: A prompt is guidance the model may not follow under manipulation; permissions, isolation and approvals are enforced regardless.

quiz.q: A question asks what to do FIRST after discovering an AI security incident. Which answer is usually best?
o: Rebuild the affected system immediately from scratch
Contain the incident, and preserve the evidence
Publish a full statement to all customers at once
Retrain the model on fresh data straight away
quiz.why: Containment with evidence preservation comes first; rebuilding or retraining early destroys evidence and may miss the cause.

quiz.q: Which NIST AI RMF function covers culture, policies and accountability?
o: Map, which sets the context and identifies risks
Govern, which is cross-cutting across the others
Measure, which analyses and tracks identified risks
Manage, which prioritises and treats the risks
quiz.why: Govern is the cross-cutting function covering culture, policies, roles and accountability.

quiz.q: Why can accuracy mislead when evaluating a detector for rare attacks?
o: Accuracy can only be calculated for image classification models
A detector that flags nothing can still score very highly
Accuracy always overstates recall by exactly a factor of two
Rare attacks can never be included in evaluation datasets
quiz.why: When attacks are rare, predicting "benign" every time gives high accuracy and zero recall.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, who carries most obligations for a high-risk AI system?
o: The end users who interact with the system each day
The provider who places the system on the market
The cloud company that hosts the underlying model
The national standards body in each member state
quiz.why: Providers carry most duties, such as conformity assessment and technical documentation; deployers have their own, narrower duties.

quiz.q: Why should training datasets be versioned by content hash?
o: Hashes compress datasets, so training runs much faster
To prove exactly which data trained a model, and roll back
Regulators require hashes for every spreadsheet in use
Hashing removes personal data from datasets automatically
quiz.why: Content hashes tie each model to the exact data it used, supporting investigations, rollback and integrity checks.

quiz.q: What does just-in-time access provide for AI platform administrators?
o: Permanent administrator rights, for faster troubleshooting
Time-limited, approved access that is revoked automatically
Shared administrator accounts for everyone in the team
Access granted only to models and never to any people
quiz.why: Just-in-time access removes standing privilege: access is requested, approved, scoped, recorded and revoked automatically.

quiz.q: Which step on the AI containment ladder is LEAST disruptive?
o: Taking the whole AI system offline until further notice
Tightening guardrails and filters around the system
Rolling back the system to an earlier model version
Isolating the system completely from the network
quiz.why: The ladder climbs from tighter guardrails, through throttling, restriction, isolation and rollback, to taking the system offline.

quiz.q: Which threat modelling method is designed around the layers of agentic AI systems?
o: STRIDE, which classifies threats into six categories
MAESTRO, which models threats layer by layer for agents
PASTA, which is a seven-stage risk-centric process
DREAD, which scores threats by damage and exploitability
quiz.why: MAESTRO structures threat modelling across the layers of agentic AI systems, including cross-layer threats.

quiz.q: Why are AI security test results reported as success rates over repeated attempts?
o: Rates are required by every AI regulation now in force
Outputs vary, so a single attempt can prove very little
Repeated attempts make the model more secure over time
Rates hide the attack details from people reading reports
quiz.why: The same input can succeed on one attempt and fail on another, so a rate over many attempts is the meaningful measure.

quiz.q: What is an AI bill of materials MAINLY used for?
o: Setting the price of AI services for different customers
Finding affected systems fast when a component is compromised
Replacing the model card that documents each model in use
Training models faster on newly purchased GPU hardware
quiz.why: An AIBOM records models, data, software and hardware dependencies, so advisories can be matched to affected systems quickly.

exam.q: A hospital deploys an AI triage assistant. Clinicians accept its recommendations 99% of the time, including when it is wrong. Which concern does this MOST indicate?
o: The model’s accuracy is too high for it to be used in clinical settings
Automation bias is undermining effective human oversight of the system
The hospital has too many clinicians reviewing the assistant’s outputs
The assistant needs a larger context window to give better answers
exam.why: Near-total acceptance, even of wrong outputs, indicates automation bias: oversight exists on paper but isn’t effective. Training, interface design and monitoring of override rates help.

exam.q: A company wants to fine-tune a model on customer support transcripts that contain personal data. Which step should come FIRST?
o: Start fine-tuning now, and anonymise the data afterwards if anyone asks
Confirm the purpose and lawful basis, and complete a DPIA first
Buy a larger GPU cluster to speed up the fine-tuning process
Publish the transcripts, so customers can review what is used
exam.why: Purpose, lawful basis and a data protection impact assessment come before processing, and determine minimisation and other safeguards.

exam.q: An internal audit finds several AI models in production with no named owner and no risk tier. What is the BEST corrective action?
o: Decommission every model without a named owner immediately
Assign owners, tier each model, and record both in the inventory
Ask each model’s vendor to take full ownership of its model
Wait for the next audit, to see whether the problem persists
exam.why: Accountability and risk-based control depend on named owners and tiers recorded in the inventory. Decommissioning everything is disproportionate, and vendors can’t own your risk.

exam.q: A model registry accepts uploads from any engineer, and deployments pull the "latest" version. Which change MOST improves integrity?
o: Allow only senior engineers to upload models to the registry
Pipeline-only writes, signed versions, and deployment by digest
Back up the registry every night to a second cloud region
Rename the models clearly, so engineers always pick the right one
exam.why: Restricting writes to the pipeline, signing versions and deploying by immutable digest stop tampering and substitution. Seniority, backups and naming don’t.

exam.q: An agent uses one long-lived API key with full CRM access for every task. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Rotate the key once a year, and keep its full set of permissions
Per-task, scoped, short-lived tokens issued through a broker
Put the key in the system prompt, so the model can use it
Share the key with the support team, so they can audit its use
exam.why: Scoped, short-lived, per-task credentials limit what a manipulated agent can do. Annual rotation keeps excessive privilege, and keys in prompts or shared are exposed.

exam.q: Researchers can reconstruct parts of a model’s training data by querying its API. Which combination BEST reduces this risk?
o: Publishing the training data, so reconstruction no longer matters
Deduplicating training data, limiting outputs, and monitoring queries
Increasing the model’s temperature setting for every single response
Moving the API to a new, unpublished domain that is harder to find
exam.why: Duplication drives memorisation, while output limits, rate limits and monitoring raise the cost of extraction. Publishing, temperature changes and obscurity don’t address the cause.

exam.q: A SOC sees a spike in tool calls from one agent to an external file-sharing service. What should happen FIRST?
o: Delete the agent and all its logs, to stop the activity at once
Contain: pause or restrict the agent, and preserve the traces
Email the file-sharing service and ask it to investigate
Wait to see whether the activity stops on its own
exam.why: Containment that preserves evidence stops possible exfiltration and keeps the traces needed for investigation.

exam.q: After a poisoning incident, a team plans to "unlearn" the poisoned samples instead of retraining. What is the BEST advice?
o: Unlearning is always preferable, because it is faster and cheaper
Prefer retraining on clean data, or restoring a verified checkpoint
Keep the model unchanged, because poisoning effects fade over time
Add a warning to all outputs, and continue operating as normal
exam.why: Machine unlearning offers weaker guarantees. Retraining on cleaned, verified data, or restoring a verified clean checkpoint, gives stronger assurance.

exam.q: A vendor’s SOC 2 Type II report carves out the model provider the vendor depends on. What should the assessor do?
o: Accept the report, since carved-out suppliers are covered by it anyway
Obtain assurance for the model provider, or agree compensating terms
Reject the vendor, since carve-outs always show a dishonest supplier
Ask the vendor to delete the carve-out section from its report
exam.why: Carved-out suppliers aren’t covered, so separate evidence or compensating contractual and technical controls are needed.

exam.q: A red team reports that indirect injection makes an agent send data externally in 4% of attempts. Leadership asks whether 4% is low enough to ignore. What is the BEST answer?
o: Yes, since any rate under 5% is considered acceptable by default
No: at scale it will happen often, and the impact is a data breach
Yes, because the red team could only make it work occasionally
No, but only because regulators ban any non-zero failure rate
exam.why: Low rates are frequent at scale, and the impact is severe, so the finding needs mitigation. Acceptance must be based on risk, not on an arbitrary threshold.

exam.q: Which response is MOST likely to be correct when a question asks how to manage employees using unapproved AI tools?
o: Block every AI website permanently at the corporate firewall
Discover the use, assess it, and offer approved alternatives
Discipline every employee who is found using the tools
Ignore it, since personal productivity tools are low risk
exam.why: Shadow AI is managed by discovering and assessing use, then enabling safe, approved options. Blanket bans and punishment drive use underground.

exam.q: A model provider updates its model, and scheduled tests show attack success rising above the agreed threshold. What should happen?
o: Nothing, until the next annual review of the accepted risks
Treat it as a breached KRI: reassess, mitigate and gate releases
Switch off the monitoring until the provider fixes its model
Raise the threshold, so that the latest result passes again
exam.why: A breached key risk indicator triggers reassessment and treatment, with release gates preventing further exposure.
